speaker: Jonathan Harker
text: A narrow stair goes down beneath the chapel. A heavy door bars the foot of it; the Count's keys hang in my hand. Below, I can hear the Szgany loading boxes of earth.

speaker: Jonathan Harker
text: The key turns. This is my last throw. Whatever lies below - better to die like a man than to wait for those women.

speaker: Narrator
text:
30 June. Castle Dracula.

"I shall try to scale the castle wall once more, and get away. It is the last chance I have. Good-bye, all! Mina!"

But that night, far away on the English coast, another story had already begun...

speaker: Hostess
text: Must you go, Herr Harker? It is the eve of St. George's Day. Do you not know that at midnight all the evil things in the world will have full sway?

speaker: player
text: I must. A client waits at the castle.

speaker: player
text: What evil things?

speaker: Hostess
text: Then take this for your mother's sake. Wear it round your neck.

speaker: Hostess
text: Ah, the Count's land is not as ours. At night the dead ride fast. Please, take this.

speaker: Landlord
text: Herr Engländer... the Count's castle is no place... *he stumbles, shakes his head*. Eat. Rest. The coach comes at midnight.

speaker: Driver
text: *In a deep, hollow voice* We are early tonight, sir. The wolves have been bold. Get in.

speaker: player
text: Do you know the Count?

speaker: Driver
text: *His eyes glint red.* Everyone in this land knows the Count, sir. Few have seen him.

speaker: Count Dracula
text: Welcome to my house! Enter freely and of your own will! The night is cold, and you need to eat and rest.

speaker: player
text: Your English is flawless, Count.

speaker: player
text: I am pleased to be here. I have the papers for Carfax.

speaker: Count Dracula
text: I am anxious to speak as the English do. Here I am noble; I am a Count. But in London no one would know me. I should be as the others - a stranger.

speaker: Count Dracula
text: Good. Whenever you want anything, ring. Only - you will remember? - do not sleep anywhere in my house save in your own room.

speaker: Fair woman
text: 'Go on! You are first, and we shall follow. Yours is the right to begin.' *They giggle, silvery and cold.*

speaker: Fair woman
text: *She hisses, falls back.* 'Take that away! He will not let us feed on you tonight. Not yet.'

speaker: Lucy
text: Mina, darling! I was just thinking of you. Do sit with me.

speaker: player
text: Tell me about the three proposals, Lucy.

speaker: player
text: Poor Dr. Seward, among his madmen. Let me hear how he fares.

speaker: player
text: How are you sleeping, Lucy?

speaker: player
text: How do you feel today?

speaker: player
text: Never mind. Drink your tea.

speaker: Lucy
text: Oh Mina, such a day! Three proposals, and I have not breathed since. Dr. Seward first, grave and kind, very much in earnest, so I said no and felt like a wicked girl.

speaker: Lucy
text: Then Mr. Quincey P. Morris, from Texas, who came in so drolly. I was in the middle of laughing when he told me it was serious, and then I was quite undone. He took it like the gentleman he is.

speaker: Lucy
text: And then dear Arthur, Lord Godalming's son. He had only to look at me, and I had only to say yes. Oh Mina, why can't a girl marry three men, or as many as want her, and save all this trouble?

speaker: player
text: You must marry the man you love, and no regrets.

speaker: player
text: Tell them gently, and tell them soon. Delay is cruel.

speaker: Lucy
text: You are the sweetest. I shall write to them tonight, and if I weep on the paper you must not tell. Now, what shall I do with all this happiness?

speaker: Lucy
text: Dr. Seward? He sent me a long letter, quite exhausted. He is a man of science, he says, and likes best to be among those whose minds are broken, because he can learn from them. Poor man. Poor madmen.

speaker: player
text: Not now.

speaker: Mina
text: I close my eyes, and for a moment I am somewhere else, in a study full of books and the smell of carbolic. A phonograph is waiting...

speaker: Narrator
text: Dr. Seward's Diary, 25 April. Kept in phonograph.

speaker: Lucy
text: Like a top, Mina! Only I woke two nights ago with my feet wet and my slippers on the wrong feet, and you scolding me. Oh, and I dreamed of the sea.

speaker: player
text: You walk in your sleep, Lucy. We must be careful tonight.

speaker: player
text: Just a dream, darling.

speaker: Lucy
text: Do you really think so? Mother will be so alarmed. Promise not to tell her. Lock the door, if you must, and keep the key, and I will not mind a bit.

speaker: Lucy
text: Tired. Terribly tired, Mina, and I sleep all night and wake worn out. The marks on my throat sting a little. I must have scratched myself on the pin, you know. You were so very good to pin my shawl.

speaker: player
text: Let me see. [Look at her throat]

speaker: player
text: You must rest. I will not leave you.

speaker: Mina
text: Two tiny punctures, white-edged and red-rimmed, such as I would not give to a pin. They are very small. I do not like the look of them, or of how pale she is.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Mina, dear, there is a draught, I'm certain. Lucy takes such risks with her health, you know, and her father's death, and my heart... We must keep her quiet.

speaker: player
text: Does Lucy have a habit of walking in her sleep?

speaker: player
text: Where do you keep the spare key to Lucy's door?

speaker: player
text: Mr. Holmwood has proposed, I hear.

speaker: player
text: I'll mind the draughts.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: As a child, indeed. It left her after her father died. But please don't speak of it to her; she is so sensitive. And Mina, you are such a comfort.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: The spare? Lock it up in the drawer, or the basket, or the old bookcase. I always put things where I shall remember them and then I don't. Look about the sitting-room, dear.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Arthur Holmwood! His poor father is so very ill. She does not know how ill, and I will not tell her until it is quite necessary. Her happiness comes first.

speaker: Housemaid
text: Beg pardon, miss. Cook says the sea-fret will be in by tea, and she's boiled up garlic broth, as her mother taught her for fever.

speaker: player
text: May I have a head of that garlic?

speaker: player
text: Is there news of the town?

speaker: player
text: Thank you.

speaker: Housemaid
text: Cook says take two, miss, if you'll swear not to tell the mistress how much she puts in.

speaker: Housemaid
text: The new searchlight on the East Cliff, miss, they're to try it out. Folks say a storm's brewing, the fishermen's wives won't have the washing out. And there's an old lady at the Abbey sees the White Lady every dusk.

speaker: Postman
text: Letter for Miss Murray, miss. From foreign parts, the stamp says Buda-Pesth. A convent's seal on the back, if you don't mind me noticing.

speaker: player
text: Give it here, quickly.

speaker: player
text: Thank you.

speaker: Mina
text: My hand trembles as I break the seal. At last, at last, news of Jonathan.

speaker: Mina
text: My trunk. The Sister's letter says Jonathan is in the hospital of St. Joseph and St. Mary, Buda-Pesth, broken down with brain fever, and has asked for me. I must go to him. But Lucy...

speaker: player
text: Pack and go. Jonathan needs me, and Lucy has her mother and Arthur.

speaker: player
text: I need to read the Sister's letter and see how Lucy is first.

speaker: Mina
text: I will write to Dr. Seward as I leave and ask him to look at her. He is the one man I can think of. And I will pray, if there is any praying that will serve.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mina goes to Buda-Pesth, to Jonathan. Lucy grows paler every day. Arthur, from his father's deathbed, writes to Dr. Seward: 'Come, for God's sake.'

speaker: Mina
text: I cannot go until I know both: the Sister's news for Jonathan, and how Lucy truly is.

speaker: Mina
text: The glass has fallen two-tenths since morning. Mr. Swales told me he can smell the storm in his bad knee, and the sunsets have been blood-red.

speaker: player
text: Take Lucy's arm and go to the East Cliff to watch the sky.

speaker: Mina
text: The whole town is up on the cliff to see the new searchlight tried, and a hush has fallen over the sea.

speaker: Narrator
text: 6 August, near midnight. The sea-fret rolls in and the wind rises.

speaker: Hennessey
text: Evening, doctor. Number 12 is in good spirits tonight, which is to say, in his usual spirits.

speaker: player
text: What exactly does Renfield do all day?

speaker: player
text: Has anyone else been able to manage him?

speaker: player
text: Thank you, Hennessey.

speaker: Hennessey
text: Collects flies, doctor. Sugar on the window-sill and the flies come. Then he eats them. Last month it was spiders; he fed the flies to the spiders. Then he found a sparrow...

speaker: Hennessey
text: Only me, sir, and only when he wants. He's polite to a man who doesn't argue. He asked me yesterday whether I knew the difference between a flea and a cat.

speaker: Renfield
text: Doctor, you must excuse me; the flies are very busy this evening and I should not like to neglect them. I have a purpose, you see.

speaker: player
text: Why do you eat flies, Mr. Renfield?

speaker: player
text: I would like to see your notes on the spiders.

speaker: player
text: Do you wish for anything, Mr. Renfield?

speaker: Renfield
text: The blood is the life, doctor, as the Scripture tells us. Flies are small lives; spiders eat flies; sparrows eat spiders; a cat would eat sparrows, and a man... a man would eat many lives and grow strong. It is the life that matters.

speaker: player
text: That is a remarkable theory.

speaker: Renfield
text: They are all numbered in a book, doctor. Each fed from the one before, and each given a place in the account. Would you not call that mathematics? You, who work with numbers of the soul?

speaker: Renfield
text: A kitten, doctor. A little one. I would be very good to it. And a great deal of sugar. No, I did not say that. Please forget it. You are a good man, doctor, and I should be sorry to see you hurt.

speaker: Seward
text: The cylinder is ready, the needle trimmed. Lucy's refusal is still raw, but work heals more than sympathy.

speaker: player
text: Record today's entry on R. M. Renfield.

speaker: player
text: Close the lid and think of Whitby.

speaker: Seward
text: Patient, R. M. Renfield, aetat 59. Sanguine temperament, great physical strength, morbidly excitable. Periods of gloom ending in some fixed idea which I cannot make out. I fancy he is himself a dangerous man, and I think...

speaker: Seward
text: And there, for tonight, is that. I will go on with my rounds, and think kindly of Miss Westenra, who has made a good choice, and of her chosen friend who writes such letters.

speaker: Narrator
text: Whitby. Mina Murray's Journal, 24 July.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Ah, 'tis the young leddy. Sit ye down, miss, and I'll tell ye the truth, which is more than the parson will. I've sat here since afore your mother was born.

speaker: player
text: May I sit and hear you talk?

speaker: player
text: What do you mean, the stones lie?

speaker: player
text: Tell me about the Abbey and the legends.

speaker: player
text: Will the weather hold, Mr. Swales?

speaker: player
text: You are known to every officer on the quay. Would you vouch for me if I need to see something there?

speaker: player
text: Good day, Mr. Swales.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Ye're a nice lass. Now these stones, they're all lies, every one. There's folk lying under 'em as ne'er were 'drowned', as ne'er were 'beloved', as ne'er did a dozen things the stone says. 'Tis the Judgement Day I fear for the carver more than the dead.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Aye. Look at 'em! 'Sacred to the memory.' Tchah. But there's one big lie in this yard that's a rare comfort, miss: the mother's stone, the widow's, for the lad that fell at Kettleness. 'Only son.' Aye, so it said. I'd not be surprised if a clever man who knew that lie hid something where nobody'd think to lift it.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Old Hilda's Abbey. There's the White Lady in the window at sunset, and the Barguest dog that walks before a death. And them that took their own lives lie yonder, where your seat is, though the parson says nowt. I sat on that stone as a lad.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Mares'-tails and a sun like blood. There's a storm in 'em, miss. Afore the week's out ye'll see the sea come up and swallow the piers. And God help any ship at sea.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Aye, miss, I'll say a word. The constable's my nephew's lad, and he'll mind his granddad. Ye need only say: Swales sent me.

speaker: Lady from Leeds
text: My dear, did you know that this very churchyard inspired the author of that famous ballad? The guide-book says so. Or the guide-book says something. And that Abbey, would you credit it, is the only ruin in England with its own ghost.

speaker: player
text: Have you seen the ghost?

speaker: player
text: Excuse me, I'm looking for old Mr. Swales.

speaker: player
text: Good afternoon.

speaker: Lady from Leeds
text: No, but the cab-driver has, twice, and the second time he was sober. The guide-book has a footnote on it.

speaker: Lady from Leeds
text: The old man by the bench? Oh, my dear, he says the most shocking things about the stones. Quite refreshing, in a churchyard.

speaker: Mrs. Pinder
text: Morning, miss. Rope, twine, tar and tallow, and the best garlic for sailors' wives. What'll it be?

speaker: player
text: A length of good rope, if you please.

speaker: player
text: A second head of garlic, for a friend.

speaker: player
text: What are the sailors saying about the weather?

speaker: player
text: Just looking, thank you.

speaker: Mrs. Pinder
text: There y'are, six fathoms of the tarred hemp. No charge for a young lady who looks like she'll make good use of it.

speaker: Mrs. Pinder
text: Two heads, then, tied with a bit of twine. Sailors swear it keeps off the ague. The old women say it keeps off worse.

speaker: Mrs. Pinder
text: That's not for me to say. But look at the gulls, miss; they've all come in off the sea, and not a one flying out. They're no fools.

speaker: Old fisherman
text: Mind the nets, miss. Aye, the sky wants watching. I've seen mares'-tails like that but twice, and both times someone died.

speaker: player
text: Is the coastguard about?

speaker: player
text: What's your opinion of old Swales?

speaker: player
text: I'll mind the nets.

speaker: Old fisherman
text: Dunn? He keeps the hut locked, miss; he's careful. But he's a forgetful man; he leaves his spare in the churchyard, under one of them lying stones, for safety. I'd not tell you where, but I know the stone is for a widow's son. Off you go.

speaker: Old fisherman
text: Swales? He's older than the pier. He says the dead are all liars, and the living are worse. Not a bad man to sit beside.

speaker: Constable
text: Back, miss, if you please. The ship's under guard till the Board of Trade man comes. The dead captain's still aboard.

speaker: player
text: Mr. Swales sent me.

speaker: player
text: Mr. Billington said I might look.

speaker: player
text: Please, constable. It is an extraordinary thing, and I'd like to see it.

speaker: player
text: I'll wait.

speaker: Constable
text: Old Swales? My grandfather's friend? Why, he'd have my hide. Go on, miss, but mind your skirts, and don't touch anything you don't have to.

speaker: Constable
text: From Mr. Billington, the solicitor? He said that? Go on, miss, but touch nothing that's evidence.

speaker: Constable
text: I'm sorry, miss, but I can't let anyone aboard on a feeling. Come with the owner's solicitor, or someone I know.

speaker: Mr. Billington
text: Madam, I am Samuel F. Billington, of 7 The Crescent. The wretched ship is consigned to me, and I assure you I know nothing of what is in it.

speaker: player
text: May I look at the vessel? I should like to describe it for friends.

speaker: player
text: Where were the boxes to go, Mr. Billington?

speaker: player
text: I have seen the consignment note. Who is Count Dracula?

speaker: player
text: Good day.

speaker: Mr. Billington
text: Eh? I suppose so; it is not as if the Board of Trade will let anyone else near it. Tell the constable I said so. My clerk is distraught as it is.

speaker: Mr. Billington
text: Ah! That note. Fifty boxes of clay to be taken to Carfax, an estate at Purfleet, bought through Mr. Hawkins of Exeter. Carter, Paterson and Co. are to cart them. It is quite regular, and quite incomprehensible.

speaker: Mr. Billington
text: A foreign nobleman, a client of Mr. Hawkins. Beyond that, madam, I know only that he bought a house in England and sent his earth ahead of him. The ways of the gentry are strange.

speaker: Mina
text: A notice-board, thick with pins. Among the tide-tables and warnings, a hand-written note: 'In case of lock-out, spare key kept with the stone of the widow's only son. Do not tell the boys. - Dunn.'

speaker: Officer Dunn
text: Miss Murray, is it not? Come in, and mind the oil. I've been sixteen years on this coast and never seen a glass drop like that.

speaker: player
text: What do you think is coming?

speaker: player
text: Might I borrow a little brandy for Lucy's nerves?

speaker: player
text: I have read the log of the Demeter. What do you make of it?

speaker: player
text: I'll leave you to it.

speaker: Officer Dunn
text: A big blow out of the north-east, if I'm any judge. And I'm judge of nothing else. If a ship's caught outside the piers tonight, God help her.

speaker: Officer Dunn
text: Ay, here, take a nip's worth in this flask. Mind, I'd not give it to every lady.

speaker: Officer Dunn
text: I read it, miss, in the coroner's office. A man who kept a log in a gale, and a mate who went for a knife at a ghost. I've no explanation, and neither has the coroner. He said 'open verdict.' I say a devil rode that ship.

speaker: Mina
text: A bare desk, ink-stained. If I had the leaves of the ship's log, I could lay them in order here, and read what happened. I should need all four.

speaker: player
text: Lay out the four leaves of the log.

speaker: player
text: The log is already read.

speaker: Mina
text: I have read it three times, and it has not changed.

speaker: Mina
text: Four leaves, all of different sizes, all dated. Which comes first?

speaker: player
text: The leaf dated 4 August, in a shaky hand.

speaker: player
text: The leaf dated 29 July to 3 August, with the mate's name.

speaker: player
text: The leaf dated 17 to 28 July, about the stranger.

speaker: player
text: The leaf headed Varna, 6 July to 16 July.

speaker: Mina
text: No. That speaks of men already missing. Something must come before it.

speaker: Mina
text: Varna: the cargo of silver sand and boxes of earth, the Bosphorus, the Dardanelles, a man gone off the watch off Cape Matapan. And next?

speaker: player
text: The leaf dated 4 August.

speaker: player
text: The leaf dated 29 July to 3 August.

speaker: player
text: The leaf dated 17 to 28 July, about the stranger.

speaker: Mina
text: That cannot be next; it assumes the stranger, and no one has yet seen him.

speaker: Mina
text: Olgaren saw the tall thin man. The crew searched the ship, found nothing. Then Biscay and the fog, and the second mate gone. And now?

speaker: player
text: The leaf dated 4 August.

speaker: player
text: The leaf dated 29 July to 3 August, with the mate.

speaker: Mina
text: He is alone in that one. The mate must still be alive in the one before.

speaker: Mina
text: The mate stabs the pale figure, and the knife passes through. He opens a box with a tool-chest, screams, and leaps into the sea. That leaves the last leaf.

speaker: player
text: Read the last leaf: 4 August.

speaker: Captain's log
text: 4 August. Alone, with the thing aboard. I am lashing my hands and a crucifix to the wheel. If we go down, bury me with this where my body is found, so that He may not have my soul. Whatever comes, I have done my duty as captain and as a Christian. The knots I tie with my teeth.

speaker: Mina
text: A tall, pale thing came out of a box in the hold and killed the crew one by one, until the captain alone remained to bring the ship to harbour. That man, and the dog that leaped ashore, were no creatures I know. Fifty boxes. Mr. Hawkins. Jonathan's firm. I feel quite cold.

speaker: Sexton
text: Afternoon, miss. Mind the old slabs; one of 'em tilts. They say an abbot lies under it.

speaker: player
text: The White Lady, sexton, have you seen her?

speaker: player
text: Is there anything of value in the Abbey?

speaker: player
text: Lucy loves the seat on the cliff. Do you know it?

speaker: player
text: Good day.

speaker: Sexton
text: At sunset, in the east window, the figure of a woman in white. 'Tis only the light, and the stones, and the Westerley wind on the glass. But I'd not be the one to stand there after dark.

speaker: Sexton
text: Digging a drain last spring, I turned up a little coin: silver, worn smooth, a sailor's penny maybe. You may have it, miss, if you promise not to throw it in the sea.

speaker: Sexton
text: That's on a suicide's grave. The parson says it matters not. I say a seat is a seat, but I'd not sleep there. There's folk have seen things at it, in the dark.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: I told 'ee so, miss! There's a hollow sound in the sea, like a giant beating on the Judgement. And a ship is out there tonight, mark my words, with her sails afire.

speaker: player
text: You are a prophet, Mr. Swales.

speaker: player
text: I'm frightened.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: I'm an old fool, miss, who's watched the sea sixty year. The wind was the Lord's, but the warning was mine.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Aye, and so ye should be. But fear's honest, miss. 'Tis the folk that aren't afraid I worry for.

speaker: Officer
text: Stand back! Miss, you must keep clear of the searchlight. She's untried, and the sea is a madman tonight. A schooner is making for the piers.

speaker: player
text: Can she make it?

speaker: player
text: What flag does she fly?

speaker: player
text: I'll stay clear.

speaker: Officer
text: Not by seamanship. By fool's luck, or the Devil's. The searchlight shows her sails, then loses her. She has no crew on deck that I can see.

speaker: Officer
text: Russian, by her cut. From Varna, I'd stake my pension. She's trying for the entrance, but the wind is dead on shore.

speaker: Onlooker
text: Ye gods, did you see that wave? Over the piers, it was, as high as the church! And the fog like hands, miss, like the wet hands of the drowned, touching everyone.

speaker: player
text: Is anyone out in a boat?

speaker: player
text: It is a terrible sight.

speaker: Onlooker
text: Not on the Lord's life. The lifeboat crew's gathered, waiting. There's a ship, though. Look! She's making straight for the harbour mouth, and no one at her helm.

speaker: Mina
text: The wind tears at my hair. The sea below is white and black, and the fog rolls in like a wall. The searchlight swings out over the water, and stops.

speaker: player
text: Look where the light has stopped.

speaker: Mina
text: A schooner! Every sail set, plunging between the piers, with a gale behind her and no hand on the sheets. 'She will be dashed to pieces,' someone cries. The searchlight lights her helm: a man stands there, bowed, quite still.

speaker: Mina
text: She runs full tilt on the sand of Tate Hill Pier. And from below her decks an enormous dog, the size of a mastiff, leaps out upon the shore and bounds straight up the cliff, toward the churchyard, into the dark.

speaker: Mina
text: The crowd cries out. Men run for the pier. The fog is thick as milk. I cling to the railing and see nothing more.

speaker: player
text: Go home to Lucy, shaken and soaked.

speaker: player
text: Stay a moment longer.

speaker: Mina
text: Lucy is sound asleep when I return. She has been out of bed twice, Mother says, and had to be coaxed back. We shall talk in the morning.

speaker: Narrator
text: Next morning. The wreck lies at Tate Hill Pier.

speaker: Mina
text: Lucy sleeps. It is past eleven. I remember how she walked in her sleep as a girl, and what Mother said. I should make sure of the door, the window, a warm shawl and a pin laid by me, in case the worst comes.

speaker: player
text: Lie down and sleep, everything being in order.

speaker: player
text: Lie down and sleep.

speaker: Mina
text: I lie down but cannot rest. The door is not locked with the key in my keeping, or the window is not fastened, or the shawl and pin are not laid ready. And is the ship's log read? Something is wrong.

speaker: Mina
text: I lock the door, put the key under my pillow, and sleep. Some hours later, I wake to a sound like a sigh. The moon is in the room.

speaker: Narrator
text: Night of 10-11 August. 1 a.m.

speaker: Mina
text: Lucy's bed is empty. The door is still locked, with the key under my pillow. The window, which I bolted, is open on the night. She cannot have gone by the door. I take the shawl, the pin and the key, and go.

speaker: Mina
text: She is lovely, asleep. I should not like to wake her. But her hands are cold, and I tuck the quilt about her as I would for a child.

speaker: Watchman
text: Out late, miss, and in a nightdress under that coat? Looking for someone? A girl in white went by an hour since, walking like in a dream, up to the churchyard.

speaker: player
text: Which way? Did she say anything?

speaker: player
text: Thank you!

speaker: Watchman
text: Up the steps, miss, quick and quiet. Barefoot. I called, but she never turned her head. And, begging your pardon, I saw something black behind her in the fog.

speaker: Street boy
text: Yer lookin' for a white lady, miss? She went down to the quay, she did, I seen her. Ghost, mebbe.

speaker: player
text: Are you sure it was the quay?

speaker: player
text: Thank you.

speaker: Street boy
text: Pretty sure, miss. It was dark. Or she might 'ave gone t'other way. But the watchman 'ud know, 'e saw 'er, 'e did.

speaker: Mina
text: I run up the last steps, calling her name. Something long and black stoops over the white shape on the seat, bent low, as if to whisper.

speaker: player
text: Rush forward, crying out.

speaker: player
text: Call her name as loudly as I can.

speaker: Mina
text: The thing raises its head. In the moonlight I see a white face, and red eyes, such as Lucy described in her dream. Then a flapping of dark wings; a great bat wheels up out of the churchyard and is gone. All is quiet.

speaker: Mina
text: Lucy sits upright on the seat, her eyes half shut and her head thrown back. She breathes in long, heavy sighs. Her lips are parted. At her throat... I can scarcely see for the shadows.

speaker: player
text: Wrap her in the shawl and fasten it with the safety-pin.

speaker: player
text: Look at her throat.

speaker: player
text: Wake her gently.

speaker: player
text: Lead her home.

speaker: Mina
text: I wrap the shawl about her and fasten it at the throat with the pin, but my hands are shaking, and I fear I must have pricked her, for she gives a little cry and puts her hand to her neck.

speaker: Mina
text: Beneath the shawl, on her white throat, two small red spots. I think the pin has marked her. But the marks are far apart, and I know in my heart that the pin does not make such marks.

speaker: Lucy
text: Mina? Where am I? Oh, I was dreaming. There was a sea, and a voice calling, and I walked on air. Why is my throat sore? And why are my feet wet? Did I walk in my sleep again?

speaker: Mina
text: She leans heavily on my arm. We go down the steps together in the grey light, I praying under my breath, she silent and dreamy.

speaker: Narrator
text: 12 August. Mina's journal: 'Lucy is not herself. She is very pale. I do not like it.'

speaker: Dr. Seward (phonograph)
text: I turn the crank and the cylinder begins to speak in my own tired voice. 'Patient: R. M. Renfield, aged fifty-nine. Sanguine temperament, great physical strength, morbidly excitable, periods of gloom ending in some fixed idea. Fixed idea: that he must absorb life. I note that he has begun to make a ladder of it.'

speaker: Dr. Seward (phonograph)
text: 'Also noted: two letters from Arthur Holmwood, three from Lucy, none from Quincey. Lucy writes of Whitby, of sleepwalking, of a pale and anxious friend, Mina. I do not like what I read between the lines. Practical matters: the dispensary key is mislaid again; Renfield's dose will need to be weighed correctly, for he is not what he was; and Hennessey will be wanting me.'

speaker: Case ledger
text: The asylum ledger lies open. Each patient has his column: weight, temper, treatment, notes.

speaker: player
text: Turn to the dosage page.

speaker: player
text: Read Renfield's entry.

speaker: Case ledger
text: In my own hand, in pencil in the margin: 'Chloral hydrate, ten grains for a man of nine stone; fifteen for twelve stone; thirty for a bull. Never above his weight, and never when he is already dosed.' I underline 'nine stone' and the word 'never'.

speaker: Case ledger
text: 'R. M. Renfield. Wt 9 st 4 lb, wasting. Eats little at table. Hoards sugar. Keeps a jar of flies, a box of spiders, and a sparrow. Asked this week whether he might have a kitten. Refused.' Beneath, in a different ink: 'Count the sugar.'

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: I spread what I have found across the table. Sugar in his pillow, a jar of flies, a box of spiders, his notebook of figures. I need all four before I trust my own deduction. 'What', I ask the room, 'does this man do?'

speaker: player
text: He is a harmless naturalist who loves small things.

speaker: player
text: He hoards sugar because he has a sweet tooth, and keeps the rest as pets.

speaker: player
text: Sugar draws flies; flies feed spiders; spiders feed sparrows. He is building a ladder of lives to feed on, and he wants a cat for the next rung.

speaker: player
text: I have not gathered enough yet.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: A naturalist keeps what he studies. He does not count them every night, and does not look at the sparrow like that. No.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: A sweet tooth does not hide sugar under a pillow and keep a ledger of insects. No.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: It is not a hobby; it is a method. He is feeding life into life, link by link, and believes the strength gathers in him. I wrote 'zoophagous mania' on his sheet this morning without understanding what I was writing. He is a maniac, and the maniac has a plan.

speaker: Dr. Hennessey
text: Morning, Doctor. Renfield was at it all night, counting out loud, sometimes in a whisper and sometimes not. I wouldn't go in without a sedative. He's been like a man listening for something.

speaker: player
text: What does he eat?

speaker: player
text: Has he tried to get out?

speaker: player
text: Where is the dispensary key?

speaker: player
text: I will take a pull from that flask of yours, if you can spare it.

speaker: Dr. Hennessey
text: Nothing at table, hardly. But Dobbs found sugar hidden in his pillow, and he lives on bluebottles, I swear it. He swallowed a spider in front of me. He said it was 'a very fine one'.

speaker: Dr. Hennessey
text: Twice since June, once at night, and Pocock found him in the Carfax garden at dawn. How he gets from his cell to the wall I don't know; but the wall, now, is another matter. Ask Pocock about the fence.

speaker: Dr. Hennessey
text: You always put it somewhere clever, Doctor. Last time it was behind Lombroso. The time before, the mantel clock. If I were you, I'd look in your own study before you look anywhere else.

speaker: Dr. Hennessey
text: Take what you need. You've earned it. Between us, if the old fellow's quiet at last, I'd drink to that myself.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Scales, a graduated glass, a brass measure. Chloral crystals dissolved in water: but how many grains? The ledger has the rule; the weighing table has the weight. A mistake here is a mistake in a man's body, not a ledger.

speaker: player
text: Five grains: a mild draught, in case he is already tired.

speaker: player
text: Ten grains: right for nine stone.

speaker: player
text: Fifteen grains, to be certain.

speaker: player
text: Thirty grains. Make a certainty of it.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Five would make him drowsy and furious. A furious Renfield does not stay drowsy. No.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Ten grains in a measure of clean water: not a grain more than his nine stone can carry. I stopper it and put it in my pocket.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Fifteen is for a man of twelve stone, and Renfield is nine and wasting. He would sleep all night and wake raving with a bad heart. No.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Thirty is a bull's dose. It would stop his heart. I put the measure down with a shaking hand.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Rainwater, clean enough, and a tin dipper hanging on its chain.

speaker: player
text: Fill a measuring-glass with water.

speaker: Dobbs
text: Evening, Doctor. I'd not go in alone, if I were you, not unless he's had his draught. He bit Mr Hennessey's glove in half last week, and wasn't sorry.

speaker: player
text: How is he tonight?

speaker: player
text: Anything unusual?

speaker: Dobbs
text: Like a clock wound too tight, sir. He's been talking to the window. Not praying, sir, just talking, as if someone were out there answering.

speaker: Dobbs
text: The sparrow, sir. He's tamed one, and it sits on his shoulder. And last night he asked me, very civil, whether the 'Master' had come. I said I didn't know any master in the building, only you. He laughed at that. Laughed for a quarter of an hour.

speaker: Renfield
text: Ah, Doctor Seward. How very good of you to call. I have had the strangest sort of calm. I was wondering whether we might speak as gentlemen.

speaker: player
text: Why do you keep flies, Renfield?

speaker: player
text: Is it true you asked for a kitten?

speaker: player
text: Who is the Master?

speaker: player
text: What do you see from the window?

speaker: player
text: Do you know a lady called Lucy Westenra?

speaker: Renfield
text: They are lives, Doctor. Each is a little, glittering life, and it takes so many to make one great one. A spider eats a hundred flies. A sparrow eats a hundred spiders. And a cat... a cat has the lives of the whole garden in her.

speaker: Renfield
text: A kitten. A nice little sleek playful kitten, that I can teach and feed and feed, and feed. I should not hurt it. Not until it was grown.

speaker: player
text: No, Renfield. You may not have one.

speaker: player
text: Perhaps. If you are good.

speaker: Renfield
text: (He is not angry; he is quiet. He says, softly:) Then you will regret it, Doctor. Not me. I shall not.

speaker: Renfield
text: (He brightens horribly.) You will? Oh, Doctor, then you are a friend! (I wish I had not said it. I shall not repeat it.)

speaker: Renfield
text: He is coming, Doctor. Not yet, not tonight, but he is near. He promises me lives, and more lives, a world of flies... I only want to be ready. I was a poor mad creature, and he has said that I shall be honoured. (He looks at the window and weeps.)

speaker: Renfield
text: Carfax. There are lights in it now, at night. Boxes. Great boxes, carried by men who sweat and swear in a foreign tongue. Mr Hawkins's clients, perhaps. Whoever it is, he has more patience than I.

speaker: Renfield
text: Lucy? A sweet name for a sweet creature. I believe I have seen a letter. Sweet things go to waste, Doctor, in a house with an open window. Do you know, you should be very careful, very careful indeed. (He is not mocking me. He is frightened.)

speaker: Pocock
text: Doctor. Fine day for the fruit trees. You're not here for the fruit trees.

speaker: player
text: Mr Hennessey says someone has been through the wall.

speaker: player
text: I need a hammer.

speaker: player
text: Carfax. What do you know of it?

speaker: Pocock
text: Aye. Slat by the elms, hangin' by one nail. There's a track through the long grass to Carfax's garden, worn like a sheep-path, and the grass bent the wrong way, sir; towards the house. I told Mr Hennessey. Told 'im last month.

speaker: Pocock
text: Toolbox in the shed, sir. Don't leave any nails about. They find them.

speaker: Pocock
text: Sold in the spring. Men have been carrying boxes in at night, like coffins. I don't ask, sir. The fruit doesn't ask me.

speaker: Telegraph boy
text: Telegram for Dr. Seward, sir! Came at four, sir, by Hampstead. The sender looked proper upset.

speaker: player
text: Take the telegram.

speaker: player
text: Nothing to send in return.

speaker: Telegraph boy
text: No reply paid, sir. Thank you, sir!

speaker: Mr. Bilder
text: Berserker? Lord love you, sir, the gentlest great beast in the Gardens. Dog-gentle. Would let the Missus scratch him through the bars. Yet that night, sir. That night.

speaker: player
text: What happened the night he went?

speaker: player
text: Was anyone about?

speaker: player
text: May I have the newspaper cutting?

speaker: Mr. Bilder
text: Storm, sir, thunder and lightning. He began to howl before it started. I was in the cottage when I heard iron bend. Went out with a lantern, and the bars were wrenched. He was gone by morning, and not a track in the mud, not a sign of him over the wall.

speaker: Mr. Bilder
text: Aye. A tall, thin man, hooked nose, black moustache and a pointed beard with a few white hairs. A tight-lipped gent, with red in his eyes under the lamp. He'd been standing at Berserker's cage the evening before, and Berserker, who never so much as shifted for visitors, put his head on the bars and looked at him. Nothing more. They knew each other, I'd swear.

speaker: Mr. Bilder
text: It's on the table, sir. A reporter wrote it down as I said it, and he got one thing right and nine things wrong. Take it. The Missus reads it aloud and I can't abide it.

speaker: Mrs. Bilder
text: Mr. Bilder says it was a storm, sir. I say a wolf in a storm would stay in his cage and howl. This one went where he was wanted. Mark me.

speaker: player
text: What do you mean, 'wanted'?

speaker: Mrs. Bilder
text: He was a pet, sir, a great soft dog of a thing, till somebody whistled. Don't ask me who. I only say there are things that go when they are called.

speaker: Berserker
text: The wolf stops pacing and looks at you. For a moment you are sure he is about to speak, and then he drops his head, and begins again, back and forth, back and forth, with his eyes on the north.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: You are Miss Murray. I wrote to you. He has been calling for you in his sleep, and sometimes in his waking. The doctors say it was a brain fever, brought on by some great shock. What shock, he will not say.

speaker: player
text: How is he, Sister?

speaker: player
text: Where is his journal? I have heard of it.

speaker: player
text: Sister, may we be married here, today?

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: Weak, and very quiet. He wakes sometimes in the night and asks whether the windows are barred. I tell him they are not, and he is comforted. I have watched men who fought on battlefields. He has seen something worse.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: Under his pillow, Miss. He asked me to keep it from him, then asked for it back. He says he cannot bear to read it, but that you may, if some solemn duty ever demands it. Ask him gently. It is his to give.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: I would be proud to witness it, child. I will arrange a priest, and the chapel. Bring a ring, bring your husband's consent, and let that journal be sealed first, so neither of you is tempted. Black ribbon is in the basket, wax on the desk. Some promises are better kept by a seal than by a vow.

speaker: Jonathan
text: Mina? Is it really you? I had been afraid... I thought it was another dream, with a kind face on it.

speaker: player
text: Rest, Jonathan. I am here, and I shall not leave you.

speaker: player
text: Sister Agatha says there is a journal, Jonathan.

speaker: player
text: Jonathan, will you marry me, here, today?

speaker: Jonathan
text: (He takes my hand with both his. His fingers feel like twigs.) The Count... no, I shall not say it. Not now. Only that when I walked out of the Castle, I walked out of every door I had ever believed in.

speaker: Jonathan
text: Here, take it. I wrote it all, every night. Read it if you must, never if you needn't, and do not ask me to confirm one line. I want to be married before I remember what is in it. (He pushes the little black book across the blanket.)

speaker: Jonathan
text: Yes. Oh, yes. There is a ring in my coat, I think, in the waistcoat pocket. I bought it in London the week before I left, and could not bring myself to throw it away. Mina, if you will have a broken man...

speaker: Sister Maria
text: He is a very good patient, Miss. He eats everything. But he sleeps with the light on, and the Sisters say he talks of wolves. We do not mention wolves.

speaker: Mina
text: A table by the window, and good light. If I could close Jonathan's journal so that it can only be opened by our decision... black ribbon, wax, and the book itself.

speaker: player
text: Tie the journal with the ribbon and seal it with wax.

speaker: Mina
text: I tie the ribbon in a bow and let the red wax fall, a drop, a seal. It is nothing, a book and a ribbon, and I feel as though I have closed a door in my own house. Whatever is in it is safe from us until we need it.

speaker: Father Hermann
text: My child, Sister Agatha says you wish to be married. It is not the usual hour, and not the usual reason. Tell me.

speaker: player
text: We are ready, Father: the ring, his consent, and the journal sealed.

speaker: player
text: What must we bring, Father?

speaker: Father Hermann
text: A ring, my child, and the bridegroom's consent, which he must give freely and in his right mind. Sister Agatha mentions something about a journal that must be sealed first; I confess I do not ask. And a witness, which she is.

speaker: Father Hermann
text: Wilhelmina Murray, wilt thou have this man to be thy wedded husband, to live together after God's ordinance? Wilt thou love him, comfort him, honour and keep him in sickness and in health?

speaker: Mina
text: 'I will.' (My voice is not mine. It is smaller, and certain.) 'I will, in sickness and in health, and I think the sickness is the part that matters.'

speaker: Jonathan
text: 'I will. I, Jonathan, take thee, Wilhelmina, to my wedded wife. To have and to hold, from this day forward... and I will not let go.' (His fingers are shaking. He puts the ring on, and it does not slip.)

speaker: Father Hermann
text: Those whom God hath joined together let no man put asunder. Go in peace, Mrs Harker.

speaker: Narrator
text: Hillingham, 7 September.  The wire from Dr. Seward was answered, in the end. Van Helsing is on the step.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I can stand if you hold my arm. If I could ask one more thing, Mina: that we never talk of the Castle unless we must. I want to remember being happy before I remember anything else.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: I have put my hand to many a bedside, child. This is the first altar I have been asked to stand at in sixteen years. Go on. The priest is waiting, and the candles do not last.

speaker: Bradshaw's Guide
text: The Continental pages are open, and someone has underlined a line in pencil. Amsterdam: the Hook of Holland boat leaves at night for Harwich, the boat-train for Liverpool Street. The day services by Calais and Dover take half as long again, with two changes.

speaker: player
text: Note the night boat times.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Night boat from the Hook; boat-train reaches Liverpool Street at five minutes past six. And the telegraph at Hampstead closes at eight, with a boy who must be paid before then. If I want Van Helsing here by breakfast, my wire must name the night boat.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: A box of garlic flowers from Haarlem, with the Professor's own scrawl on the lid. 'Not for the kitchen.'

speaker: player
text: Take a handful of the flowers.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: The fire is low. The house is silent. The wire is gone; there is nothing to do but wait for morning, and the train.

speaker: player
text: Sit by the fire until morning.

speaker: player
text: Not yet. There is more to do first.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: I sit in the armchair, and the fire gutters, and Lucy's breathing comes down the stairs like a clock. Somewhere, Jonathan Harker is lying in a foreign bed, and Mina has gone to find him. I have not even had time to think of them.

speaker: Narrator
text: Meanwhile, in Buda-Pesth, a fortnight earlier.  24 August.  Mina Murray crosses Europe to find a man she is not yet married to.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Dr. Seward! How good of you. Lucy is so very much better, I think. She only wants her window open and a little air. Girls will make such a fuss about the stuffiness of a sickroom.

speaker: player
text: How is Lucy, Mrs Westenra?

speaker: player
text: And you, Mrs Westenra? Your own heart?

speaker: player
text: I should like her room kept quiet and undisturbed tonight.

speaker: player
text: About the garlic in Lucy's room, madam...

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: She sleeps so much. She was never so languid at Whitby, and those sea airs were supposed to have done her such good. She cries out in her sleep sometimes, poor child. I have thought of sending for Dr. Hargreaves, but Arthur says to wait for you. You may go up. She is sleeping, I think.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Oh, a little fluttering. It is nothing. I have it every evening. Dr. Hargreaves says I must not be startled. I tell him I am never startled; nothing ever happens in Hampstead.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Of course, Doctor. I shall not so much as put my head round the door. Although I do think the poor child is too much alone at night; the house is so large, and the maids are so far.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Those dreadful flowers! I confess I threw them out, and opened the window. A girl cannot get well in a room that smells like a kitchen drain. Dr. Seward, it is my house and my child.

speaker: player
text: They are a fashionable Dutch remedy, madam, nothing more.

speaker: player
text: Professor Van Helsing has many degrees. He prescribes it.

speaker: player
text: Madam, they are as real a medicine as digitalis. If they are moved again, I fear Lucy may not wake. I beg you to trust a physician who has seen this before.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: A fashionable remedy! Then it will be out of fashion by Sunday. No, Doctor, I think not.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Degrees! Dr. Hargreaves has several, and he does not tell me to hang a vegetable round my daughter's neck.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: (Her hand has gone to her heart.) Oh, my dear Doctor. Put like that... I would never forgive myself. I promise, on my honour. Touch nothing in that room. I shall not even pass the door.

speaker: Maid
text: Oh, sir, begging your pardon. I've worked here nine years, and I never saw Miss Lucy like this. She isn't herself in the mornings, sir, and she never was a one to walk about.

speaker: player
text: Does she walk in her sleep?

speaker: player
text: Where is the key to Miss Lucy's room kept?

speaker: Maid
text: At Whitby, Mrs W. says, sir. But here, I found her slippers wet one morning, standing by the window. I thought: she's been walking on the dew. Then I thought: no, I'm being silly.

speaker: Maid
text: On the rack in the hall, sir, with all the other keys. Miss L.'s room, in the housekeeper's hand. We keep them all there. Mrs Westenra says it makes the house feel safe, sir.

speaker: Maid
text: (She mumbles, 'The port, the port... the gentleman said it was for the mistress.' Her head rolls. She is as insensible as a log.)

speaker: player
text: Try to rouse her.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: I shake her, slap her wrists, call her name. Her eyes roll open, and shut. Whatever she took has her fast. Smelling salts might do what shaking cannot; Mrs Westenra has a bottle in her dressing-case upstairs.

speaker: Arthur
text: Jack! Thank God. Is she... how bad is it? They would not let me stay at the Hall, with my father as he is, and I have been going out of my mind.

speaker: player
text: Arthur, Van Helsing says she needs a man's blood tonight. Will you give it?

speaker: player
text: Arthur, there is something I must tell you about the transfusions.

speaker: player
text: She is sleeping, Arthur. Be patient a little.

speaker: Arthur
text: Take what you want, Jack. Take all of it. I'd give my last drop and think it cheap. (He is already rolling his sleeve.)

speaker: Arthur
text: Patient. Yes. I have been told to be patient since June.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: (The Professor has told me, bluntly, that Arthur must never know another man's blood has gone into her. A lover has jealousies even for gifts.) Arthur... I mean to tell you the truth about this.

speaker: player
text: I gave her blood too, Arthur.

speaker: player
text: Nothing. Only that you saved her life.

speaker: Arthur
text: You gave... then in a manner of speaking, she is... (He is white.) No. No, Jack, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. You saved her too. I am the lowest kind of fool to be jealous of a doctor's arm.

speaker: Arthur
text: Then I am the happiest man in London tonight, and I would not have it otherwise.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: Jack. I came on the first train after your wire. Arthur said to come quick and not to ask questions, and I never do. Looks to me as if you fellows have been through a stampede.

speaker: player
text: Quincey, Lucy needs blood, and the Professor says yours is the best we have.

speaker: player
text: Tell me about the bat on the Pampas.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: A brave man's blood is the best thing on this earth when a woman's in trouble. I'm your man, Jack. And here, take my flask. Texan brandy. It will put a fire in anyone's veins.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: Out on the Pampas, my mare, the best in the world, was found dead one morning with two little punctures in her throat and not a drop in her. One of those big bats that they call vampires had been at her. I've been thinking of her all night.

speaker: Telegraph boy
text: You want to send a wire, sir? I take 'em to the office at Hampstead. Office shuts at eight, sir, and the last Amsterdam collect goes out at half past seven. What's the message?

speaker: player
text: 'Come tomorrow morning if convenient. Lucy unwell.'

speaker: player
text: 'Come by the day train through Calais and Dover; two changes.'

speaker: player
text: 'Come by the night boat from the Hook; boat-train reaches Liverpool Street 6.05; urgent, a matter of life.'

speaker: player
text: I am not ready to send it yet.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: 'Tomorrow morning if convenient' is no message to send to a man who runs a hospital. Lucy may not have the day to spare. I tear it up.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Two changes and a long day. He would arrive tomorrow evening, if the Channel is kind. No. The night boat, surely.

speaker: Telegraph boy
text: 'Night boat, 6.05, urgent, a matter of life.' That'll fetch him, sir. Never saw a wire to Amsterdam with so few words. I'll run.

speaker: Lucy
text: Dr. Seward. How kind of you to come all this way. I hope you don't think I'm ill. I'm so sleepy, that's all. And Arthur's poor father... I wish he were here.

speaker: player
text: How are you feeling, Lucy?

speaker: player
text: May I look at your throat, Lucy?

speaker: player
text: Do you walk in your sleep?

speaker: player
text: Do you remember the flowers last night?

speaker: player
text: Lucy, Arthur is here. He has come to see you.

speaker: Lucy
text: Weak, and rather faint, and hungry for a thing I don't know the name of. I dream so vividly, Doctor. There is a flapping at the window, and a long thin shadow, and sometimes a pair of red eyes that I can't bring myself to dislike.

speaker: Lucy
text: If you must. (She lifts the lace at her collar, and I see them.) Two little punctures, white-edged, not deep, not angry. They will not heal. She says she must have pricked herself on a safety-pin.

speaker: Lucy
text: Mamma says I did at Whitby. I woke on the East Cliff once, with Mina beside me, and I was freezing. But I haven't, here. I'm sure I haven't.

speaker: Lucy
text: Flowers? I never liked garlic before, but last night it was delightful. I slept as I have not slept in weeks. In the morning... it was all gone from my neck? I don't remember. I don't remember taking it off.

speaker: Lucy
text: (Her eyes open, blue and clear, and a little flush has come into her cheeks.) Arthur. Dear Arthur. Is it really you? I dreamed you'd come, and now I can't tell the dream from the room.

speaker: Arthur
text: (He kneels by the bed and takes her hand. He cannot speak for a moment.) Lucy. My Lucy. I am here, and I shall not leave you.

speaker: Lucy
text: (Very softly, to him alone.) Kiss me, Arthur.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: (He is across the room before I can speak, and his hand is on Arthur's shoulder.) No! Not on your life! Not for your life, nor hers!  Arthur... the forehead, only the forehead, I implore you.

speaker: Arthur
text: (He kisses her on the forehead, and she smiles, and closes her eyes, and the smile does not change.) Lucy? Lucy?

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: She does not answer. The colour that fed her cheek stays there, and her lips are red and soft in the candle, and she looks more beautiful than I have ever seen her. I put my fingers to her wrist. Nothing. Van Helsing takes Arthur out gently; Quincey follows. I stay with her.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Friend John. You have the face of a man who has not slept, which is correct. You may speak.

speaker: player
text: Professor, what do you make of her?

speaker: player
text: What must be done tonight?

speaker: player
text: Show me again how to ward the room.

speaker: player
text: Professor, look at the petals and the slippers.

speaker: player
text: Mrs Westenra threw out the garlic and opened the window.

speaker: player
text: Professor, the wolf. What is it? Where did it come from?

speaker: Van Helsing
text: I have looked, friend John, but you have looked first. Tell me what you saw. Three questions, as a surgeon answers before a student. Where are the marks?

speaker: player
text: On her wrist, like a bad vaccination.

speaker: player
text: On her throat, two small punctures, white-edged and torn.

speaker: player
text: On her ankle, where a bat might alight.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: No, friend John. Think. Look again with the candle. You are a physician and you have an eye. Use it.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Good. And what does she do, in the evenings? What happens to her, in the night, that does not happen to other sick girls?

speaker: player
text: She sleeps badly from nerves, nothing more.

speaker: player
text: She sleeps with the window open, walks in her sleep, and wakes weaker each morning.

speaker: player
text: She has consumption; the pallor shows it.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: No. A phthisis does not shift with the window. Think about her nights.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Good. And now the hardest question. She has lost, I judge, a great deal of blood. We cannot do the most simple thing, give it back, with a single man. Whose blood first?

speaker: player
text: Her mother's: she is of the same blood.

speaker: player
text: Arthur's: her betrothed, who loves her.

speaker: player
text: A stranger's from the hospital.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: No. Her mother's heart would stop. A stranger's... it is not wrong, but he is not the man whose blood is a gift. Think again, friend John. The man she loves.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Exactly. Arthur's. And then yours, and then mine, and, when God sends him, a fourth. Fetch Arthur. And you shall prepare: the black bag with the tubing, the brandy, the chloral for her sleep; I will bring the flowers.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Four things tonight. First, the black bag, your silver tubing and lancets. Second, brandy, for the donor, afterwards, and for you when you faint. Third, a sleeping draught, chloral; she must not be awake or the sight will frighten her. Fourth, her room: garlic at the window, at the door, in the chimney, and a wreath for her neck. And then, we pray.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Window, door, chimney, neck. A chimney is a door to what is thin enough. And the neck: a wreath tied with white ribbon, so it does not fall. Rub the flowers, press them into the cracks. Leave nothing out, friend John. A ward with one hole is no ward at all.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: You have seen the petals. You have seen the slippers. They are a story. Tell me what happened in this room, in the night.

speaker: player
text: Mrs Westenra came in meaning well, and took the garlic away.

speaker: player
text: The maid came in and cleared the room.

speaker: player
text: Lucy herself rose in her sleep, took off the wreath, swept the window, and lay down again.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: No. Her mother did not come near. The trail begins at the bed and ends at the window, and no hand but hers made it. Think again.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: The maid is here for the daylight, not the night. Her footprints do not wander. No.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Yes. Asleep, walking, drawn by something that is not her, she undid what we did, and does not remember. The thing that hunts her has found a will that is weaker than the flowers. So: we lock her door and keep the key. We pin her window shut with iron. And we wake her, friend John, if we must. Find the key on the hall rack. The pin is in the garden somewhere; a cottage garden always has an iron pin.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: (He sits down on the edge of the bed with his hands between his knees. His shoulders shake, and he laughs, and it is not laughter.) Oh, God. God forgive me; I am a fool. That good, kind woman has killed her daughter, and she believes she was kind. Friend John, there is only one thing left. You are strong, and so is Arthur; I am older, but I am here. The third transfusion shall be mine. Speak to Mrs Westenra. Persuade her.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: A wolf from the Gardens, friend John. Escaped, by every account in the paper. That is the plain explanation, and I have not the heart to give you the other. Go. See to the servants. Something has gone through this house tonight that wanted all its doors open.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Lucy lies white on the pillow, her breath no louder than a moth's. The black bag, the tubing, the lancets are ready, if I am; and a donor, and brandy for afterwards, and chloral to keep her from seeing what is done.

speaker: player
text: First transfusion: Arthur's blood.

speaker: player
text: Second transfusion: my own blood.

speaker: player
text: Third transfusion: Van Helsing's blood.

speaker: player
text: Fourth transfusion: Quincey Morris.

speaker: player
text: Use Mrs Westenra's blood. She is her mother.

speaker: player
text: Ask Arthur to give again so soon.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: No! Her heart is a thing that will stop at a loud word. The blood would do no good, and the shock would be worse than the loss. Another donor, friend John.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: A man may give a little, once. Not twice in a day. We shall have to find other donors, and lose no time about it.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Chloral in water, a cup, drink. Good, she sleeps. Now, Arthur, your arm. (He lays the cut vein to the silver tube; the blood goes in, and the colour comes to her cheek like dawn.) Good. Brandy for Arthur. Not a word to him of what we shall do hereafter, friend John. A lover is jealous of everything, even the gift.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: You, friend John. Roll the sleeve. (I lie back and he opens the vein. It does not hurt; it is merely cold. The room goes grey, then white; the brandy brings it back.) She has colour. Say nothing to Arthur. It is our secret, and a good one.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Mine, then. (He is shaking, though not with fear.) I am not young. Do not stare, friend John; it is my arm, not yours, that I am wasting. (The tube is warm. His face is grey and his jaw is set. He says, quietly, 'We fight him all the same.')

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: (He peels off his coat, rolls his sleeve, and lies down on the sofa-bed with his boots on.) Do it quick, Doc. I never had a tooth drawn easier. (The tube hums. His colour holds. Van Helsing, white at the mouth, injects morphia under Lucy's skin to keep her still.) A brave man's blood is the best thing on earth.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: The chair by the bed. The candle. The ticking. A man can sit here and keep time against the dark. But only if everything else has been done first.

speaker: player
text: Keep watch through the first night.

speaker: player
text: Keep watch through the second night.

speaker: player
text: Keep watch for the days that follow.

speaker: player
text: Keep watch through the seventeenth night.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: I sit, and doze, and nod, and the candle sinks. Towards dawn something wakes me; I cannot say what. The wreath is on the floor, the garlic has been swept off the sill, and the window is ajar. Lucy has not moved. She is white as paper.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: I slept at the Professor's order, in the next room, and for the first time in days I slept. When I woke, Mrs Westenra was in Lucy's room opening the shutters and singing, with a handful of garlic flowers in her apron. She had meant it kindly. The room was cold.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Four days. Every morning a box from Haarlem, and every evening the same quiet. Lucy eats a little and laughs a little, and Mrs Westenra, true to her promise, will not so much as touch the door. At night something taps, and flaps, and Van Helsing says it is a bat, and does not say it with a smile. On the fifth night the wind rises.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Outside, a long howl, and a thin one answering it, and the whole house cowers.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: She lies so quietly. The candles are lit at head and foot, and Van Helsing is standing at the window with his back to me, very straight.

speaker: player
text: Look closely at her mouth.

speaker: player
text: Search for the paper Van Helsing noticed at her breast.

speaker: player
text: Ask Van Helsing what we must do now.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: (He draws her lip back with a finger. The canine teeth are longer and sharper than any I have seen in a living mouth.) You have eyes, friend John. You see them? Remember this, and tell no one. I shall explain later, and you will not believe me, and that is as it should be.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: It is folded small, in the fold of her nightgown over her heart. 'Hillingham, 12 September. Arthur, if you read this, forgive me; I am not myself. There is something in the night that is not a dream. I am so frightened of what I am becoming...' The handwriting fails near the end.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: The funeral, friend John. The undertaker comes in the morning. You will say nothing to Arthur of the teeth, nothing of the paper. We shall bury her as a Christian woman, in her own vault, and we shall watch, afterwards. The hearse is at the garden gate. Come.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Friend John. The others have gone to the carriages. Stay a moment. Look at the vault, and tell me what you see.

speaker: player
text: What did you mean, 'it is not finished'?

speaker: player
text: Professor, the garlic.

speaker: player
text: The memorandum. 'There is something in the night.' What is it?

speaker: player
text: I am ready to go back to Purfleet.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: I mean that you will see, friend John. In a week, in a fortnight, there will be news in the papers that you will read with a clear head. When it comes, remember that I was not mad. Remember her teeth.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: You have some garlic still? Lay it on the coffin, and across the door. It is a custom of the country where I was born. I ask you to do it for her sake, not for mine, and not to laugh.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: It is the voice of a girl who was not alone in her room. Keep it. If Arthur ever asks, you will tell him that she wrote of him with love, which is the truth. The rest, we shall see.

speaker: Arthur
text: I cannot believe it, Jack. A month ago she was laughing on the lawn. A month. And I was there at the end, and I did not know what I was seeing. You and the Professor knew, I think. I don't ask. I am not able to ask.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: Funeral. Never could abide funerals. Never could stay away from one, either. Look after Art, Jack. He'll want somebody to hold on to, and he'll pretend he doesn't.

speaker: Sexton
text: Forty years, sir, I've been putting 'em in, and never once buried a young lady with so many gentlemen in a row. Quiet, they were. Real quiet. Four of 'em, and the foreign one.

speaker: player
text: Did you notice anything unusual?

speaker: Sexton
text: No, sir. Only that the Professor made us bring the coffin up a second time to look at the lid. And he wanted the key, and wouldn't let it go. And the dog won't come near the yew. Might be nothing.

speaker: Newsboy
text: Westminster Gazette! 'A Hampstead Mystery', the Bloofer Lady, sir! Tuppence the copy.

speaker: player
text: Buy a copy (tuppence).

speaker: player
text: What do you know of this lady?

speaker: Newsboy
text: Thank you, sir. They say she is a pretty lady in white who takes the wee ones to see the swans. Not a swan on the Heath, mind.

speaker: Newsboy
text: Seven nights, sir. Seven children. Always a little after dark, always on the north side by Shooter's Hill. The coppers say it's a woman wanting a baby; the old ones say it's a witch. Me, I stay on the road.

speaker: Nursemaid
text: Is it a doctor you are? My master's boy was out two hours on Tuesday last, and I thought I should die.

speaker: player
text: What did the child say when he came back?

speaker: player
text: Was he marked?

speaker: Nursemaid
text: That a pretty lady with white teeth had played with him under the thorn. Smiled at him. Then she kissed him on the neck, like. He was quite happy.

speaker: Nursemaid
text: A scratch, sir. Two little pricks, both sore. The doctor said it was a bramble. There are not many brambles on the Heath, and there is nothing in them like that.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: She is frightened, and she is hiding it for the child's sake. It does not read like the tale of a lunatic.

speaker: A small girl
text: I'm the Bloofer Lady! You must lie down and shut your eyes, and I'll take you to see the swans!

speaker: player
text: Where does the real lady live?

speaker: player
text: Does she sing?

speaker: A small girl
text: In the big white house with the high door, past the church. She's hungry, so she's thin. She always goes back before it's light.

speaker: A small girl
text: She sings very low, and her hair is the colour of a guinea. She had a long white dress with mud on the hem.

speaker: Constable
text: Seven this week, sir. Four at the hospital, two home, one I'd rather not say.

speaker: player
text: Where was the last found?

speaker: player
text: What hour?

speaker: Constable
text: On the grass by Shooter's Hill, laid out neat as a doll. No sign of a struggle. The lady must have put her down.

speaker: Constable
text: Four in the morning, near enough. Whoever she is, she keeps good time. And I never see her. I see the wet grass, and the child.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Look at the ground, friend John. The grass tells more than the newspaper, if we are patient. A shoe, a thread, a footprint: three witnesses.

speaker: player
text: What are we looking for?

speaker: player
text: The shoe, the thread and the prints all lead north, toward Kingstead.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Whatever walked here does not mind the cold. Find me anything left by the one who takes the children: cloth, a trail, a shoe. And ask the children who is the lady. A child does not invent.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Kingstead. Yes. A white house, a high door, bare feet on the grass. Let us go to the hospital and see the child. I have had enough of theory; it is time you saw the wound.

speaker: Dr. Vincent
text: Dr. Seward? I know your name. The Professor wrote ahead. Mind, the child is mine; I cannot have the dressing changed for a stranger's curiosity.

speaker: player
text: I am a physician of the same kind. Here is my card; I should be glad of your opinion on the wound.

speaker: player
text: Your scruples will not matter if more children disappear.

speaker: Dr. Vincent
text: Very well. Matron saw the same marks on a boy last week. If you can name them, I will thank you. Mind, the girl is nervous; do not frighten her.

speaker: Dr. Vincent
text: I resent that, sir. Come back when you can ask civilly.

speaker: The child
text: Are you the doctor? Mother said the doctor would bring me a sweet.

speaker: player
text: May I see your neck, little one?

speaker: player
text: Who was the pretty lady?

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Two punctures on the throat, small and neat, a finger-breadth apart. The edges are white and ragged, as if the vein had been drawn by suction. I have seen their likeness before, on Lucy's neck.

speaker: The child
text: She smiled at me. She said she was thirsty and would I give her a kiss. Her teeth were long.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: You see, friend John? The same as Lucy. Not the same hand, perhaps; the same mouth.

speaker: Ward sister
text: I have never seen a child so pale with so little hurt. Dr. Vincent says anaemia. I say there has been something at her.

speaker: player
text: Might I trouble you for some clean linen?

speaker: player
text: Do any of the children speak of the lady?

speaker: Ward sister
text: Take it, sir. We have plenty. Will you put it to good use?

speaker: Ward sister
text: All of them. They call her kind. That's what frightens me.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: You are angry, friend John. Good. Anger shows a mind that is working. Now will you let it work?

speaker: player
text: This is madness, Professor. Lucy is dead. I saw her buried.

speaker: player
text: Where is the proof you promise?

speaker: player
text: I have read Mrs Harker's pages and your wound notes. Convince me, if you can.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: You have heard of bats that drink the blood of cattle in Brazil. Of the fakirs who are buried alive for months and come back. Of the tree that eats flies. Do you believe in these because you can explain them, or because you have seen them? I ask only that you believe what you have not seen.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: There is a woman in Paddington, Mrs Harker, who has typed a document that will do what my arguments cannot. Fetch it, and bring her husband's word that he did not dream. I trust the paper; you trust paper.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: The wound in the child's neck and the wound in Lucy's: the same. A foreign nobleman who leaves not a reflection, who crawls down a wall, who is dead by day and alive by night. A man who seeks London. I cannot say I believe it. I cannot say I do not.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: That is enough, friend John. It is the beginning of belief. Now we go to Hillingham, for Lucy's papers, and to prepare. Tonight we shall see what is in the Westenra tomb.

speaker: Mina Harker
text: Professor, I have been waiting. Jonathan is awake, but he is not himself. I have your letter, and I have his journal.

speaker: player
text: Madam, I have a great need of your shorthand and your typewriter.

speaker: player
text: Tell me of Lucy's last weeks, as you saw them.

speaker: player
text: How shall I get back to London?

speaker: Mina Harker
text: Jonathan's shorthand is a private matter. But if it will help Lucy, I will let you have it. My machine wants a new ribbon; there is a spare in my workbasket, I think. I will wait.

speaker: Mina Harker
text: She was sleep-walking. I found her on the seat at Whitby churchyard with something dark at her throat. It looked like a ribbon. It was not.

speaker: Mina Harker
text: The quick 3.34 from Exeter, with a change at Reading. I have marked it in the timetable.

speaker: Jonathan Harker
text: Professor? Mina says I wrote it all down in Buda-Pesth. I do not know whether to believe my own hand.

speaker: player
text: Your journal is not a dream, Mr Harker. I have read it, and I know where the Count has gone.

speaker: player
text: What do you remember of London?

speaker: Jonathan Harker
text: You... believe me? Then the castle was real? The three women, the Count in the box?

speaker: player
text: Every word. And your wife has typed it, God bless her.

speaker: player
text: I believe what I find in the evidence. That is enough.

speaker: Jonathan Harker
text: I am cured, Professor. If I am a madman, then a madman can swing an axe. Tell me what to do.

speaker: Jonathan Harker
text: I saw him in Piccadilly. Younger by twenty years, outside Guiliano's, watching a girl. My heart stopped. I walked away because I could not stand it any more.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: The Professor's bag clinks and rattles. He asked me to take what is needed.

speaker: player
text: Take the turnscrew, the fret-saw and the candle-end.

speaker: player
text: Leave it. It is not my bag.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: A turnscrew for coffin-screws, a tiny fret-saw for lead, and a candle-end. The tools of a respectable burglar.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: The bench is cluttered with files and wards. I can cut a key if I know the lock.

speaker: player
text: Cut a six-lever key, to be safe.

speaker: player
text: Cut a spring-latch key, simple and quick.

speaker: player
text: Cut a four-lever key for a falling-bolt lock, as the undertaker's invoice describes.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Six levers is more than the lock has. The key would not drop the bolt. I abandon that and think again.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: A spring latch is not a falling lock. That is a cheap house-door pattern. The key would be useless in a tomb.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Four levers at the depths the invoice gives, a plain bit, the shoulder cut for a falling bolt. I file for an hour. At the end the key turns smooth in my hand.

speaker: Mr. Marquand
text: Dr. Seward. A sad business. Lord Godalming inherits everything, and has bidden me give Professor Van Helsing every liberty with Miss Lucy's papers. There is a good deal of correspondence.

speaker: player
text: Please sort the legal papers from the private ones. I shall take the private ones.

speaker: player
text: Tell me about the tomb. Who has the key?

speaker: Mr. Marquand
text: Of course. The deeds, the will and the bills are to remain with me. Her private letters and her sleep-walking notes are yours. The desk is open. Do be careful of the undertaker's account; there is an item about the vault lock that has taken my fancy.

speaker: Mr. Marquand
text: The undertaker holds one key, and the family another, held at Ring. I should not trouble either of them in this season of grief.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Three stacks of paper on Lucy's desk: deeds and the will, the undertaker's accounts, and her private letters.

speaker: player
text: The undertaker's account.

speaker: player
text: Her private letters and diary leaves.

speaker: player
text: The deeds and the will.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: 'To Messrs. Chubb, one four-lever falling-bolt lock for the Westenra vault, fixed to the iron-banded door, and two keys.' I fold the bill into my pocket book.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: A few lines, in Lucy's hand: 'I walk in my sleep, I think. Mina found me on the churchyard seat; my throat is sore and I am so tired.' I will let the Professor see this.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Legal. It stays with Mr. Marquand. It is not for us.

speaker: Hannah
text: Oh, sir. I did not know it was you. Is there anything you need?

speaker: player
text: A small gold crucifix is missing from the room where Miss Lucy lay.

speaker: player
text: I have the pawn ticket for a crucifix that was pawned yesterday.

speaker: Hannah
text: I never saw such a thing, sir! I did not! You will not blame me, for I am an honest girl...

speaker: Hannah
text: Oh sir, I only meant to borrow it. It's gold; my mother is ill. I put it in pawn on the corner. I am so ashamed. Here, this is the ticket for it and my own wage for the redemption.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: No punishment, Hannah. I have been poor too. But hear me: the cross is there for a reason. Pray that you never know it.

speaker: Landlord
text: Doctors, gentlemen. You'll want your dinner. Is it a long walk you have tonight?

speaker: player
text: We go to Kingstead churchyard. Is the road watched?

speaker: player
text: Anything strange on the Heath of late?

speaker: Landlord
text: The horse patrol goes by the high road at half-past ten, sir; they have been on edge with all the children. The Heath path along Hampstead Lane is dark, but there is no one on it after eleven.

speaker: Landlord
text: Dogs howl in the evening for no reason. Cows go dry. And the nurses all say the same lady with a smile. Shut up, Mr. Carter, we are not all frightened.

speaker: Carter
text: You gentlemen are doctors? Then tell me what takes the kiddies. My own nipper was out two nights ago and came back chuckling about a lady.

speaker: player
text: Keep him indoors after dusk, and tell the others.

speaker: Carter
text: I'd do that. Aye. And leave a crucifix by the door, as the old woman says. It can't hurt, can it?

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Eat, friend John. A man who tomb-robs on an empty stomach makes mistakes.

speaker: player
text: Tell me the plan again.

speaker: player
text: Which road shall we take to Kingstead?

speaker: player
text: I am ready. Let us go.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: A falling lock, a coffin, a lead case. We shall open it and see. If Lucy is within, I am wrong and you may call me a fool for the rest of my days. If she is not, you will have no more excuses. We need the key, the turnscrew, the fret-saw, the candle and the matches, and a crucifix, since I do not want to meet her unarmed.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Three ways, John. Choose carefully, for a detective in the dark has no second chance.

speaker: player
text: The high road, past the Spaniards, where the lamps are.

speaker: player
text: The Heath path by Hampstead Lane, after eleven.

speaker: player
text: A hansom straight to the church gate.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: The horse patrol will stop us on the high road, and a hansom would be marked by every dog from here to the church. No.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Good. The dark path, after the patrol has passed. You are an apt pupil.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: We go. And if anything within seems to move, friend John, trust the crucifix more than your eyes.

speaker: Sexton
text: Evening, gentlemen. I lock up at dusk. We've had folk wandering about. Not a good place for the likes of you after dark.

speaker: player
text: A silver coin, good sexton, for a doctor's quiet visit to a grave.

speaker: player
text: Where is the Westenra vault?

speaker: player
text: We shall wait until you have locked the gate, then take our chance.

speaker: Sexton
text: Ah. Well, the wicket does lift from the inside. I'll leave the latch easy. Mind you don't leave anything behind, gentlemen.

speaker: Sexton
text: Head of the yew avenue, sir, up the church path, past the junipers. A fine grand vault, that; they say the young lady was beautiful.

speaker: Sexton
text: As you please, sir. I'll lock the gate, but the wicket opens from the inside. I never saw you.

speaker: Cabman
