text: The brougham will go as soon as you say, sir. Only the Lord gave me orders. No one goes to Hillingham without a word of his blessing, and a letter from him to carry.

speaker: player
text: I will have both before I go.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Mr. Holmwood. Lucy has told me nothing, which means she has told me everything. Have you anything for me, from your father?

speaker: player
text: Only my respects, madam.

speaker: player
text: Thank you for your kindness, madam.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Respects are very nice, but a mother likes a signature.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Go on. Lucy is waiting. I have never seen her so fond of a lawn.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: I see. He writes beautifully. But a mother must ask what a letter cannot say. Is the Ring in good heart? I do not ask about money. Only whether it will keep my daughter warm.

speaker: player
text: It is sound, madam. Entirely sound.

speaker: player
text: It is burdened, madam. My father's illness has cost us dear. But my honour is not for sale.

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Splendid. I am so glad. (She says it too quickly, as if she had made up her mind first and asked afterward.)

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: Thank you. That is the first plain answer a gentleman has given me in thirty years. I shall not hold your father's debts against you; I shall hold your honesty for you. Go and find my daughter.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: Say, Art. I had a speech ready. Three fine paragraphs. I reckon I'll keep it for the next wedding. Go on. She's by the roses.

speaker: player
text: You are a better man than I, Quincey.

speaker: player
text: Thank you, old fellow.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: Hell, no. I'm a worse shot at the heart. You hit it dead centre without even aiming. I'd call that luck, but I'd rather call it honest.

speaker: Lucy
text: Arthur! You have come after all. Mamma has been unbearable about it. She says you shall decide to like us on a full stomach.

speaker: player
text: I have something to ask you, but I am not ready.

speaker: player
text: I am so glad to see you.

speaker: Lucy
text: Then I shall wait. A girl who has had three proposals in a day knows the smell of a fourth. (She smiles.) Mamma must approve of the thing first, and the rose arbour is so lovely this month.

speaker: Lucy
text: And I of you. Go and sit in the summer-house, we are expected for tea.

speaker: Arthur
text: Lucy, my father is dying. The house I shall inherit is old and tired and heavy with duty. I have nothing to offer you but the whole of myself and my mother's ring. Will you take it?

speaker: Lucy
text: Oh, Arthur. Yes. I have been saying yes for six weeks; you were simply not listening. (She laughs, and takes the rose, and puts the ring on, and wipes her eyes with her wrist.)

speaker: Lucy
text: Sit by me, Arthur. No one has the right to look so solemn in a summer-house.

speaker: player
text: Tell me what you would do with the Ring.

speaker: player
text: I want to remember every hour of this.

speaker: Lucy
text: Open all the windows. And invite the whole village to tea. I am quite certain nobody has ever done it.

speaker: Lucy
text: Then look about you. The mallets, the music-box, the poems. They are all here, and they will keep.

speaker: Footman
text: A telegram, Mr. Holmwood. From the Ring. I am sorry to bring it.

speaker: Arthur
text: 'LORD GODALMING SINKING. COME AT ONCE. BATES.' Lucy turns her face into my shoulder, and does not speak, and does not need to.

speaker: Narrator
text: Hillingham stood on its lawn in the last of the light. By the time the train reached the Ring, the Lord had died.

speaker: Mr. Pennefather
text: My lord. I mean, the title is yours, as of this morning. I am obliged to tell you the estate is encumbered. I am not at liberty to tell you how. Mr. Wilkes can; the muniment room can; I should rather not.

speaker: player
text: Who holds the key to the muniment room?

speaker: player
text: And the seal?

speaker: Mr. Pennefather
text: The steward holds the key, and, I fancy, an oath to the late Lord not to give it up. You will have to persuade him, my lord. With the ledger, I should think.

speaker: Mr. Pennefather
text: Your father's signet. It lies with him, in the vault, as is the custom. A custom, my lord, is only a rule you have not been asked to break.

speaker: Mr. Crowle
text: My lord. My deepest sympathy. Business can wait a day, but only a day. May I speak plainly?

speaker: player
text: Please do.

speaker: player
text: What are your terms?

speaker: player
text: I have read the deed, Mr. Crowle.

speaker: Mr. Crowle
text: Your father borrowed against the Ring. It is no scandal; half the peerage does. But the debt is large, and the interest is hungry. Sell the Home Wood and the Green to a syndicate I know, say nothing to the village, and the whole matter dissolves by Michaelmas. No one need ever know.

speaker: Mr. Crowle
text: As I said, my lord. A comfortable arrangement. Bring me the deed when you have read it, and I shall draw it up.

speaker: Mr. Crowle
text: Then you know. Now, my lord: your father's way was a lie, and mine is a quiet sale. What will you do?

speaker: Mr. Crowle
text: My lord, you do not have the tenants with you. A truth with nobody behind it is only a confession.

speaker: Mr. Crowle
text: A wise young man. The Wood will be down by spring. Nobody will say your name unkindly; nobody will say it at all.

speaker: Narrator
text: Arthur signed. The Home Wood was sold by Michaelmas. The Ring was saved, and the village never knew what it had been spared or what it had lost. He wore the signet for the rest of his life and never quite got used to its weight.

speaker: Mr. Crowle
text: I see. Then you are your father's son after all, in the way that matters. I shall extend the term. I would rather lend to a man who tells me how it stands.

speaker: Narrator
text: Arthur read his father's letter aloud on the village green, with the deed in his hand and Gideon Marsh at his side. The Ring was mortgaged for twenty years more; the tenants gave what they could; the Home Wood stood. In the autumn he stood at Lucy's side in Hillingham church, and was, for an hour, only a man.

speaker: Mr. Wilkes
text: My lord. Condolences. The funeral was well attended. The estate is... in its customary order.

speaker: player
text: Show him the ledger of arrears.

speaker: player
text: Tell me the truth about the estate.

speaker: player
text: Thank you for your thirty years, Mr. Wilkes.

speaker: Mr. Wilkes
text: The estate is... as it has been. I am sworn to say no more, my lord. You must look in the ledger on my desk yourself, if you want proof.

speaker: Mr. Wilkes
text: It was a privilege, my lord. I hope I have not cost you more than I saved.

speaker: Mr. Wilkes
text: ...Where did you find it? Never mind. It is on the page. There is no sense hiding what you can read. The Lord made me swear. I have served him thirty years and I will say it plainly: he borrowed to keep every cottage warm. And I let him.

speaker: player
text: You did right, Mr. Wilkes. Give me the key to the muniment room.

speaker: player
text: You lied to me for four years.

speaker: Mr. Wilkes
text: I did, my lord. Dismiss me if you like. But the Lord asked, and I owed him more than I owed you. I do not know whether that was loyalty or cowardice. Perhaps they are the same.

speaker: player
text: Forgive me. Give me the key, and stay.

speaker: Mr. Wilkes
text: Here, my lord. It opens the muniment room, but the lock has a recess for the seal, and the seal is your father's signet. It lies with him in the vault.

speaker: Gideon Marsh
text: Lord Godalming. We're sorry for your loss. We're sorrier, I'll not lie, for our own. A new Lord is a new landlord.

speaker: player
text: What do the tenants fear?

speaker: player
text: I want to help.

speaker: player
text: Hobbs says there are men in the Home Wood.

speaker: player
text: The Home Wood is clear, Mr. Marsh.

speaker: Gideon Marsh
text: That the rent goes up, that the Wood goes down, that the Green goes to a railway. Your father kept it all as it was. We never asked how.

speaker: Gideon Marsh
text: Words. Fine words. Show us. There's men in the Home Wood, snaring the Lord's hinds and worse, and no one's gone in. If the new Lord will walk in his own wood by night, we'll listen to what he says by day.

speaker: Gideon Marsh
text: Aye. Go and see to them yourself. Not Hobbs. You.

speaker: Gideon Marsh
text: Hobbs has told us. You went in yourself. That's something none of your family's done since the old Sir Hugh. Now tell us the rest, my lord. The whole of it.

speaker: player
text: The estate is mortgaged to its roof, but not a cottage will be sold.

speaker: player
text: The estate is entirely sound, Mr. Marsh.

speaker: Gideon Marsh
text: ...Sound. Is that so. The miller's rent was paid by a bank, my lord, and every one of us knows it. Come back when you can look at us and tell it straight.

speaker: Gideon Marsh
text: ...Well. That's a new thing to hear from a Lord. (He takes his hat off, and the miller does the same.) We've a petition. Thirty names. We'll stand surety for the interest, if you'll stand surety for the cottages.

speaker: Mrs. Marsh
text: Gideon speaks for all of us. I only speak for the one who'd rather you didn't pretend. Your father pretended beautifully, and never fooled any of us.

speaker: player
text: What would you have me do?

speaker: Mrs. Marsh
text: Tell us the truth. Even a bad truth. People can build a house on it.

speaker: The miller
text: The mill-race was your father's loan, my lord, and I'll be paying it till I'm dead. I never knew who he borrowed from. I thought it came from the Lord's own pocket.

speaker: player
text: It came from a bank. I am sorry.

speaker: The miller
text: A bank! Well. I'd rather have known. A man likes to know whose bread he's eating.

speaker: Hobbs
text: My lord! Don't come further. There are three of them by the old beech, and I swear one is a wolf, or something wolfish. There hasn't been a wolf in England since the Stuarts.

speaker: player
text: I will deal with them myself.

speaker: player
text: Where did the hind come from?

speaker: Hobbs
text: God bless you, my lord. Aim for the dog first. The men will run when the dog does.

speaker: Hobbs
text: Dead by the log, my lord. Throat torn, not cut. I thought the poachers killed it. Now I think the poachers are as frightened of it as we are.

speaker: Pike
text: My lord. The Wood gate was open last night, though I locked it myself. Hobbs says there's trouble in there.

speaker: player
text: I shall see to it.

speaker: The kneeling woman
text: Hush, Master Arthur. It's only old Nan, who nursed you and your mother. I come when the bell tells me there's a Holmwood in grief. I thought you would find the vault.

speaker: player
text: The bell rang by itself.

speaker: player
text: How does one open the vault, Nan?

speaker: Nan
text: It rings for the family. It rang for your mother, and for your father this morning. The sexton says it's the wind. Wind or not, I answer.

speaker: Nan
text: It's a lock of years, dear. The first Lord's 'resting', the old brass says. Read the brasses. Not when he fell, my dear. When he came home.

speaker: The vault lock
text: A dial of years. 'HERE HE RESTS.' Which year is that?

speaker: The vault lock
text: The dial turns. Nothing. Not that year.

speaker: The vault lock
text: The dial clicks. The black door sags inward onto a stair that has not been used since Mother's funeral.

speaker: The vault lock
text: [You descend the steps]

speaker: Arthur
text: My father is in there. The signet lies on his folded hands, as the custom is.

speaker: Arthur
text: His fingers are cold. The ring slips off the way it does when a man has grown thin. I whisper that I shall wear it better than I have worn the weeks.

speaker: Arthur
text: Our father, who art in heaven. I cannot get past 'forgive us our debts', and I stand there for a long time.

speaker: Clerk
text: Captain! The bill of lading, signed and sealed as Herr Hildesheim promised. Fifty boxes, silver sand and earth, consigned to Mr. S. F. Billington of Whitby. A very odd cargo for July, but the freight is paid in full.

speaker: player
text: Who orders earth by the shipload?

speaker: player
text: Why Whitby?

speaker: Clerk
text: Take care of it, Captain. The customs officer will want to see it, and the officer is not a man who forgets. Nor does he stamp for nothing.

speaker: Clerk
text: A foreign nobleman, Captain. He did not come himself. Everything was by letter and by agents, and the earth came down from the mountains on Szgany carts. He paid in gold. I did not ask questions.

speaker: Clerk
text: A quiet harbour, little watched, with deep water by the pier. That is what the gentleman's letter said. I thought it a strange thing for a gentleman to know.

speaker: Customs officer
text: Papers.

speaker: Customs officer
text: Fifty boxes of earth. Irregular. Extremely irregular. For a small consideration, however, a ship may be regular in everything.

speaker: Customs officer
text: Everything is in order, Captain. A good voyage. I shall never see that ship again, I think, and I do not mind it.

speaker: Customs officer
text: A stamp costs silver, Captain. The paper first; the coin second. That is how the law is read in Varna.

speaker: Candle-seller
text: A beeswax candle for the icon, Captain? One silver. It has been blessed in St. Constantine's and will burn all night, whatever the wind does.

speaker: player
text: What do the sailors say about this ship?

speaker: Candle-seller
text: Light it before the icon on the quay. Father Nikolai will say the words. A ship that has not been blessed is a ship with no mother.

speaker: Candle-seller
text: That the Slovaks who loaded her would not look at the boxes. That they crossed themselves each time they put one down. That the last one was warm.

speaker: Father Nikolai
text: A ship may sail without a blessing, my son. Sailors may not.

speaker: player
text: What is in the boxes, Father?

speaker: Father Nikolai
text: Lord, who rebuked the winds and the sea, keep this ship and every soul aboard her. Here is water from the font, Captain; use it where you must. And keep a cross about you. A cross is better than a pilot.

speaker: Father Nikolai
text: I do not know. I know that the Szgany kissed the ground before they would touch them, and I know that the earth has a smell I have smelled once before, in a vault where a man was buried who should not have been.

speaker: Slovak foreman
text: Fifty. Not one more, not one fewer. We counted them twice.

speaker: player
text: Who carried them to the quay?

speaker: player
text: Was anything wrong with them?

speaker: Slovak foreman
text: Szgany. They came down in the night, with their carts and their dogs, and they would not take payment from us. They took it from the clerk and rode away.

speaker: Slovak foreman
text: The last box was warm, Captain. In July that is nothing. But it was warm through the night, and not from the sun.

speaker: Amramoff
text: Captain. The ship is stowed. The tide is turning. If you want to sail, we can sail.

speaker: player
text: About the hold key...

speaker: Amramoff
text: At noon, then. East wind, fresh. She will go like a bird.

speaker: Narrator
text: 6 July. Varna. At noon the Demeter set sail, east wind, fresh. Crew: five hands, two mates, the cook, and myself, the captain. Cargo: silver sand and fifty boxes of earth, for Whitby.

speaker: Amramoff
text: The papers must be stamped by the customs officer, and the men will not cast off without a priest's blessing. They are Russians, Captain. You know what that is.

speaker: Amramoff
text: I locked the hold when the boxes were stowed. The key I hung where a captain keeps keys: near where he sleeps, or where the cook keeps his spoons, or in the locker where we keep our tools. If it is not there, the carpenter's crowbar will do the same work.

speaker: Amramoff
text: Captain. What are your orders?

speaker: player
text: How are the men?

speaker: player
text: I want the whole ship searched.

speaker: player
text: The men want a double watch. I mean to grant it.

speaker: player
text: Do you believe there is a man aboard?

speaker: Amramoff
text: Frightened women, Captain. A handspike will cure it. A man who is afraid of a deck-house is a man who needs more work.

speaker: Amramoff
text: A fool's errand. Sixty feet of boxes, and no man can hide in a box. I shall take the helm, and let the men search. But it is folly, and it will demoralise them.

speaker: Amramoff
text: Then give me the dark watch, Captain. The men will not stand with me, and I will not stand with them. I will stand with you, with a handspike and a lantern, and between us we shall keep the middle watch.

speaker: Amramoff
text: There is no man aboard. There is what comes of men who sleep too little and think too much. I will find the cause. I shall find it if I have to open every box.

speaker: Amramoff
text: It is here. I know it now. On the watch last night I saw It, like a man, tall and thin and ghastly pale. It was in the bows, looking out. I crept behind It and gave It my knife, but the knife went through It, empty as the air.

speaker: player
text: Mr. Amramoff, go to your bunk.

speaker: player
text: What will you do?

speaker: Amramoff
text: It is in the hold, perhaps in one of those boxes. I shall unscrew them one by one and see. You work the helm.

speaker: Narrator
text: Then a sudden startled scream, and he comes up the hatchway as though shot from a gun, with his eyes rolling and his face convulsed with fear. 'Save me! Save me!' He looks round on the fog, and his horror turns to despair.

speaker: Amramoff
text: You had better come too, Captain, before it is too late. He is there. I know the secret now. The sea will save me from Him, and it is all that is left!

speaker: Narrator
text: 3 August. He sprang on the bulwark and threw himself into the sea. I suppose I know the secret too, now. Lord, help me. How am I to account for all these horrors when I get to port? When I get to port! Will that ever be?

speaker: Petrofsky
text: Captain. Good watch.

speaker: player
text: You look tired, Petrofsky.

speaker: player
text: Anything strange on your watch?

speaker: Petrofsky
text: I sleep with my boots on, Captain. The floor has begun to feel cold. Cold the way a cellar is cold, not a sea.

speaker: Petrofsky
text: No. Nothing. Only that I take the larboard watch tonight, and Abramoff relieves me at eight bells, and I would rather he came early.

speaker: Dmitri
text: Captain. It is cold on deck.

speaker: player
text: What are the men saying?

speaker: Dmitri
text: That Petrofsky did not drown. A man who drowns makes a noise. They say he walked forward and the fog took him. Do not laugh, Captain. I will go and stand by the lantern.

speaker: Ivan
text: At the wheel, Captain. Steady as a rock.

speaker: player
text: Would you stand a watch alone?

speaker: Ivan
text: No. Not alone, Captain. If I stand it, Bolotin stands it with me. He is my kinsman, my mother's cousin's boy. He does not leave my side, and I do not leave his.

speaker: Olgaren
text: Captain.

speaker: player
text: Something is on your mind, Olgaren.

speaker: player
text: You are afraid of something.

speaker: Olgaren
text: No, Captain. A little uneasy. I will tell you more tomorrow.

speaker: Olgaren
text: In my watch, Captain, I was sheltering behind the deck-house from the rain, when I saw a tall, thin man come up the companion-way, who was not like any of the crew. He walked forward along the deck and disappeared. I followed softly, but when I got to the bows, there was no one, and the hatchways were all closed.

speaker: Stepan
text: Captain. Soup in a quarter-hour. It will be hot, whatever else is not.

speaker: player
text: Have you any garlic?

speaker: player
text: The gulls and the weather...

speaker: player
text: What do you make of all this?

speaker: Stepan
text: Garlic? There is a string over the stove. My grandmother hung it over the cradle, against what, she never said. Take it. A man should have something in his pockets besides his hands.

speaker: Stepan
text: The gulls have all gone inland, Captain, and the porpoises are running to the west. A cook knows when to put the fire out. Weather, and soon, from the south-west. I have not seen it so since Odessa.

speaker: Stepan
text: They say there is a stranger aboard, Captain. I say there are fifty strangers aboard and I have been feeding them for a week. Fifty boxes. A man who eats little and sleeps all day. That is no stranger. That is a passenger.

speaker: Abramoff
text: Captain. Mending.

speaker: player
text: Who stands which watch?

speaker: player
text: You relieved Petrofsky that night.

speaker: Abramoff
text: Olgaren and I sail together, Captain, or we do not sail at all. He is my friend. If he goes on deck alone, I go; if I go alone, he goes. That is understood in the forecastle.

speaker: Abramoff
text: At eight bells, as arranged. I came up and found the deck empty and the lantern burning. I looked in the bows. I did not look in the hold.

speaker: Bolotin
text: Captain. The wheel is steady.

speaker: player
text: Will you take a watch with Ivan?

speaker: Bolotin
text: With Ivan? Gladly. He is my kinsman; I would stand with him on a burning ship. I will steer and watch, sir, if you let me. Let the others sleep.

speaker: Slate
text: In three different hands the men have chalked: 'We ask for double watch. We do not go on deck alone. Not one of us.' Under it, in a fourth, a note: 'Not with the mate.'

speaker: Captain
text: A round robin, in the sailors' way: names in a ring, so that no one signs first. I will keep it, and I will grant what it asks. Double watches. It is the least I can do.

speaker: Captain
text: The sail-plan. What do I know about the weather, and what will I do about it?

speaker: player
text: Carry all sail: the sky is clear and the wind is fair.

speaker: player
text: Take in sail: weather from the south-west by morning.

speaker: player
text: Run for the nearest port.

speaker: Captain
text: Let me count the signs. The glass:

speaker: Captain
text: falling long and slow, if I have read it (the barometer by the wheel). The sky: mares'-tails from the north-west, if I have looked at it (from the deck). The birds and fish: the cook's own word (galley). Three signs; they must agree.

speaker: Captain
text: No. I do not trust a clear sky with a falling glass. Let me think again.

speaker: Captain
text: A harbour in this wind is a reef with a name. We hold our course; we only shorten sail.

speaker: Captain
text: Glass falling, mares'-tails to the north-west, gulls inland, porpoises running west. That is a south-westerly gale before the next forenoon. We reef down, secure the boats, and get everything lashed. I give the orders.

speaker: Captain
text: The watch bill. Three watches, three pairs, and no man alone. I must match them by what the men have told me.

speaker: Captain
text: Abramoff says Olgaren stands only with him. Ivan and Bolotin are kin and will not be parted. The mate says the men won't stand with him and he will stand the dark watch with me. And the round robin: nobody alone. I need to hear all of it first.

speaker: Captain
text: The bill is chalked up: First watch, Ivan and Bolotin. Middle watch, the mate and myself, armed. Morning watch, Olgaren and Abramoff.

speaker: Captain
text: The first watch, eight bells to midnight. Who?

speaker: player
text: Ivan and Bolotin (kin, they won't be parted).

speaker: player
text: Olgaren and the mate.

speaker: player
text: Stepan the cook, alone, by the stove.

speaker: Captain
text: No. The men have said they will not stand with the mate. It would be better to have no watch at all.

speaker: Captain
text: Alone? The round robin says not one man alone. No.

speaker: Captain
text: The middle watch, midnight to four, the darkest. Who?

speaker: player
text: The mate and myself, armed.

speaker: player
text: Olgaren and Ivan.

speaker: player
text: Abramoff and Olgaren.

speaker: Captain
text: No. Ivan is already on the first watch with Bolotin and Olgaren will only stand with Abramoff.

speaker: Captain
text: No. They belong on the morning watch, a pair for the grey hours, and the middle watch needs the strongest.

speaker: Captain
text: The morning watch, four to eight. And the last pair?

speaker: player
text: Olgaren and Abramoff.

speaker: player
text: Bolotin and the mate.

speaker: player
text: The cook, alone.

speaker: Captain
text: No. Bolotin is on the first watch with Ivan, and the mate is with me.

speaker: Captain
text: No, no one alone.

speaker: Captain
text: There. A ship has never been better watched, and there is not a single man alone. If anything can be done by arithmetic, I have done it.

speaker: Captain
text: The ship's log lies open. A log is not a diary; it must say only what is true, in the right order, in a steady hand.

speaker: Captain
text: I read the log back. It is short and honest, and every line of it frightens me more than the one before.

speaker: Captain
text: What do I write of the cargo?

speaker: player
text: Fifty boxes of Carpathian clay for Hamburg.

speaker: player
text: Silver sand and fifty boxes of earth, consigned to Mr. Billington, Whitby; customs stamped, Varna.

speaker: player
text: No cargo worth the ink.

speaker: Captain
text: That is not what the bill of lading says. A log that lies is not a log. I strike it out.

speaker: Captain
text: The cargo is the whole point of the voyage. I strike it out.

speaker: Captain
text: And the weather I have read?

speaker: player
text: Fair and settled.

speaker: player
text: Glass falling, mares'-tails NW, weather from SW by morning; reefed down.

speaker: Captain
text: No. I did not read it so, and I will not write it.

speaker: Captain
text: Written, and signed, and sanded. The cargo and the weather.

speaker: Captain
text: What did the search find?

speaker: player
text: Searched stem to stern, found nothing at all; crew's fears are folly.

speaker: player
text: Searched stem to stern with lanterns: no man; but earth spilled from box thirteen to the bows, and Petrofsky's cap.

speaker: player
text: Found a stowaway and put him in irons.

speaker: Captain
text: That is what the mate would write. It is not what I found.

speaker: Captain
text: There is no stowaway in irons. I would have remembered.

speaker: Captain
text: A strange entry, but a true one.

speaker: Captain
text: How many men have I lost since Varna?

speaker: player
text: Three: Petrofsky, Dmitri and the second mate.

speaker: player
text: Two: Petrofsky and Dmitri.

speaker: player
text: None; they have deserted.

speaker: Captain
text: Bolotin is alive; I saw him at the wheel. Let me count again.

speaker: Captain
text: A man does not desert a ship in the middle of the Atlantic. No.

speaker: Captain
text: Two men. Both off watch, neither seen again. I write it exactly so.

speaker: Captain
text: The final entry. What do I tell the people who find this bottle?

speaker: player
text: The mate murdered the crew and then himself.

speaker: player
text: The mate saw It: tall, thin, pale. The knife went through It. He leapt overboard. I know the secret now, and I will lash my hands to the wheel with the cross.

speaker: player
text: Pirates.

speaker: Captain
text: No. That is what the inquest will say, and it would be convenient. It is not what I saw.

speaker: Captain
text: I will not make up a pirate for the Board of Trade.

speaker: Captain
text: I write it as steadily as I can, and I seal it in the bottle with wax from the lamp, so that those who find it may understand. If not, all men shall know that I was true to my trust.

speaker: Captain
text: A few hours of sleep, if the ship allows it. But every night that I lie down, the ship is a man short in the morning.

speaker: Captain
text: Let me count what is wanted.

speaker: Captain
text: In general: read the weather, count the hold, write the log (July 6th to 16th); search every corner and find the trail (17th); set the watch and gather garlic (22nd to 29th); open the box and deal with it (2 August).

speaker: Captain
text: Black earth, damp, the shape of a man pressed into it. There is a smell I knew in a vault, once. This is where It lies by day. What shall I do?

speaker: Captain
text: The water hisses where it touches the earth, like water on a hot stove. The black soil blisters and goes grey; the smell changes from the grave to something that is only a smell. Whatever lay here has lost its bed.

speaker: Captain
text: The oil takes, and the torch with it. The flame is low, blue at the heart and does not like the earth. Smoke rolls along the hold. The box burns badly and the others do not burn at all; and across the boxes, in the dark, something is awake.

speaker: Captain
text: The wheel. The fog. The night coming on. The hands are the ship's, now; they must be tied to it.

speaker: Captain
text: A rope for my hands. The crucifix and my mother's beads, which He dare not touch. The log, sealed in the bottle, in my pocket, with the cabin key. The mate gone, and the last entry written. When all is ready, I shall tie myself to the wheel.

speaker: Captain
text: I lash my hands to the spokes with the manila, wind the rosary through my fingers, and set the crucifix between them. Come good wind or foul, I shall save my soul and my honour as a captain. I am growing weaker, and the night is coming on. God, the Blessed Virgin and the saints help a poor ignorant soul trying to do his duty.

speaker: Narrator
text: 6 August. In the great storm the Demeter ran before the wind into Whitby harbour, all sails set, and struck the sands under the East Cliff. As she struck, a great dog sprang from the deck to the shore and ran up the cliff path into the dusk; no trace of it was ever found. The captain was found lashed to the wheel, dead, his hands bound over a crucifix and a string of beads, a corked bottle and a cabin key in his pocket. The folk of Whitby buried him as a hero, on the cliff, near the seat where a girl and her friend sat watching the sea.

speaker: Stanciu
text: My lord. Severin has been under siege six weeks. Boyar Vlaicu says we cannot afford the grain to relieve it. I say we cannot afford not to. The council waits for your word, and your father's seat.

speaker: player
text: What is the state of the border?

speaker: player
text: Tell me of the Order of the Dragon.

speaker: player
text: What must be done before I march?

speaker: Stanciu
text: The Turk comes at us across the Danube every spring, my lord, as the tide comes up the beach. We are the beach. Your father held it for twenty years with a fist; you will have to hold it with a head.

speaker: Stanciu
text: Your father's collar: the Dragon. The lock on the chest in your chamber bears the Order's year, not your father's. Do not mix them. The founding was in the king's reign, at the very beginning of this century, in 1408, when the Turk was still a rumour. Your father was merely accepted into it much later.

speaker: Stanciu
text: The order sent to the camp must be written, sealed with the Voivode's ring, and carried. The signal on the tower should be fired to call the ridge garrison. And your brother Radu has been seen in the corridors at odd hours; I do not like corridors at odd hours. Bring your father's hammer, my lord: the men follow what they remember.

speaker: Stanciu
text: Then to the matter. Two hundred starving villagers are camped in the courtyard. They want the granary opened. Boyar Vlaicu says the granary is the army's, and will be needed for the siege. A prince must choose, my lord, between a kindness that may cost a battle and a hardness that may cost a conscience.

speaker: player
text: Open the granary to the villagers. The army will march lighter.

speaker: player
text: Close the gates. The army eats first, and the weak must bear it.

speaker: Stanciu
text: (He bows, very slowly.) It is the harder choice, my lord, and perhaps the wrong one. But I will see it done, and I think you will remember it. They will.

speaker: Stanciu
text: (A long silence.) As you command. The gates will be shut. Some of the villagers will walk away at dawn. Some will not walk. I shall see to it that none of this is said in the Voivode's name.

speaker: Vlaicu
text: My lord. Three hundred spears at your service, naturally. At my own expense, naturally. One only asks that the boyars be consulted in the matter of the spoils. Of the matter of the spoils, I have a great many thoughts.

speaker: player
text: The spoils are for the soldiers who bleed, Vlaicu.

speaker: player
text: You shall have your share when Severin is relieved.

speaker: Vlaicu
text: A noble sentiment, my lord. Admirably young. I trust you will find your army grows lighter in the night when it hears it.

speaker: Vlaicu
text: Then we understand each other. And may I say how like your father you are, in the matter of understanding.

speaker: Radu
text: Brother. Prince. Voivode. I never know which to use first. It is a strange thing to come home and find that everyone defers to the boy who used to cheat at dice.

speaker: player
text: You returned from the Sultan's court. How was it?

speaker: Radu
text: Very warm, very civilised, and quite unlike what the priests say of it. They gave me a horse. I did not have to cut off anyone's head to be given a horse. I commend the arrangement.

speaker: Radu
text: (He reads. He does not blush. He sets it down, very exactly.) Yes. I wrote it. 'The ford at the new moon, the boyars divided, the Voivode young.' I wrote it, brother, because the Sultan's hand is longer than ours, and I wanted to be on the right end of it. I did not think it would be you who read it.

speaker: player
text: You will leave this castle tonight. I do not want to see a Turkish banner in your wake. Go with your life.

speaker: player
text: Take him to the cells. He will answer for treason.

speaker: Radu
text: (Quiet.) You are very like father at his best, Vlad. It is not a compliment. I shall be at the Sultan's court. I shall not forget your mercy, and I think it will not be quite enough.

speaker: Radu
text: (He smiles, with a sort of tenderness.) That, too, is like father. Do as you will. When I scream, remember who taught you to put a man in a hole.

speaker: The Order chest
text: The dial is a ring of years, the iron cold under the thumb. 'The year the Dragon was founded.' Which year?

speaker: The Order chest
text: The dial turns. Nothing. A year, but not that year.

speaker: The Order chest
text: The dial clicks over. The lid breathes up an inch on a smell of cedar and old wax.

speaker: The Order chest
text: Under a folded cloak lie my father's collar, an Order medal, and his signet, a dragon coiled round a cross. I put the ring on, and the room seems a little smaller.

speaker: The seal-press
text: Wax, a candle and the brass press, waiting for a ring.

speaker: player
text: What do I need?

speaker: The seal-press
text: The wax is green. The dragon stands up out of it, tail in its teeth. For the first time in its history, the order is real.

speaker: The seal-press
text: A written order, and the Voivode's signet. The first is on the clerk's table. The second is, I think, somewhere my father hid it.

speaker: Petru
text: My lord, I can carry anything to the camp in a day and a night. But the captains won't take my word and I won't bring them a word they cannot read.

speaker: player
text: Ride well.

speaker: Petru
text: The levy will be at the camp below the Reed ford by the third night, my lord. God keep you.

speaker: Ileana
text: You have your father's chair and your father's frown. Both look better on him. Are you going to speak to me, or only to your counsellors?

speaker: player
text: I am afraid, Ileana.

speaker: player
text: What do you think of Radu?

speaker: player
text: I will come back.

speaker: Ileana
text: Of course you are. If you were not, I would marry Radu instead. (She smiles, and it hurts.) Fear is not the enemy. Not knowing what to do with it is.

speaker: Ileana
text: He comes into this room when you are away. He looks at your desk, not at me. A man who looks at a desk is a man deciding what to do with the room.

speaker: Ileana
text: Say it again when you are in the doorway, Vlad, with the army behind you. I will believe it then. (She presses a ribbon of grey silk into his palm.) For a ring, until you have time to buy another.

speaker: Dan
text: The ridge answers if we fire the beacon, my lord. There's a platoon on the far crag, forty spears. But the beacon's dry as a priest's sermon. It wants lamp-oil, and a torch to set it going. The oil is down in the hall: the garrison barrel. The torch is in the bracket by the stair-door; the others are burned out.

speaker: player
text: Thank you, Dan.

speaker: The grandmother
text: You are the new Voivode. You have your father's eyes, and your father's chin. Your father left the villages out of his reckoning. I hope you will count us in.

speaker: player
text: Where have you come from?

speaker: player
text: Take what you need from my pack.

speaker: The grandmother
text: From beyond Severin, where the Turk has been burning the barns. We walked ten days. The wolves have followed us for three. They are patient, my lord. Wolves usually are.

speaker: The grandmother
text: Then God bless you, young lord. It is the first kind word I have had from a man in armour.

speaker: Mircea
text: My lord. The scouts say the Turk will raid across the river before dawn, in the dark of the moon. They cannot cross at the Stone Ford, nor the Wolf's Ford. We should know which. You will find the map on the table.

speaker: player
text: What do you remember of Kossova, Captain?

speaker: player
text: What do the men say of me?

speaker: Mircea
text: Don't ask. I was a boy. Three days in the heat, and on the third the Hungarian king ran, and the Crescent stood in the field where we had been. Your father said afterwards that the shame was not that we had lost but that we had not been trusted to lead.

speaker: Mircea
text: They say you are your father's son. Some say it to praise you. Some say it as a warning.

speaker: player
text: Then I will be both.

speaker: Cristea
text: My lord. I lay in the reeds two nights. They are coming down the old creek bed in the dark, from the north-east. They walk their horses, they wrap the hooves in felt: no clatter on stone, no splash. It must be a place with reeds to hide in and soft mud to cross; not a rocky ford.

speaker: player
text: And Wolf's Ford?

speaker: player
text: And the Stone Ford?

speaker: Cristea
text: Four hours upstream, past the old mill, west of the hills. They would have to march round the whole army to reach it. No, my lord.

speaker: Cristea
text: A causeway of slabs, a quarter-mile of echoes. A felt-wrapped horse is still a horse. They would not choose it. It is too proud a crossing for a night raid.

speaker: The Akinji
text: (He speaks a little Wallachian, with the care of a man spelling a word he hates.) I will not talk. I am of the Sultan's household. You may do what you please.

speaker: The Akinji
text: ...I did not expect it. (He drinks.) We cross at the Reed Ford, where the river is slow, before dawn. Do not harm the reeds. My cousins are in them. If you must kill, kill quickly. That is all I ask.

speaker: The Akinji
text: (He talks, white-faced, for a quarter of an hour. When he is finished he does not look at me, and I do not look at him.) The Reed Ford. The reed-ford. Before dawn. I have told you everything. Cut my cords.

speaker: The map
text: Three fords marked in red wax. The scout says the Turks are coming down the old creek from the north-east, with felt on their hooves, to a place with reeds and soft mud. Where do I put the army?

speaker: player
text: The Stone Ford.

speaker: player
text: Wolf's Ford.

speaker: player
text: The Reed Ford.

speaker: The map
text: A causeway of slabs. A quarter-mile of echoes. They would not choose a ford where every hoof rings.

speaker: The map
text: Four hours upstream, far from the north-east creek. The Turks would have to round the whole army to reach it.

speaker: The map
text: The wax shows a broad slow river, reed-banks on both shores. A creek runs in from the north-east. It is the one place where felt-wrapped horses would make no sound. I move the stones.

speaker: The map
text: [You take the track to the river]

speaker: The scholar
text: A quick sword, Voivode. A quicker mind. A pity both are in service of a throne which has just been sold. Do you know that? The ford was told to the enemy by one of your own. You were meant to lose tonight.

speaker: player
text: Who are you?

speaker: player
text: Who sold the ford?

speaker: player
text: What do you want of me?

speaker: The scholar
text: A man who collects those who do not wish to end. I keep a school, under a mountain, by a lake in Hermannstadt. A small school, ten places at a time. The tenth is the Devil's. Everyone is told that. Nobody believes it until the end of term.

speaker: The scholar
text: I could tell you. But a prince should learn to read faces himself. You will read your brother's face long before you read my school-books.

speaker: The scholar
text: To teach you to be a king who is not beaten, Voivode. Not by Turks. Not by brothers. Not by time. The price is a winter of your life and a risk you will be told about in plain language. Come, if you dare.

speaker: The scholar
text: Then take this token. It will open the ferry to those who carry it. Nine days' ride, and we shall begin.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Voivode held the ford that night, and the Turks went home across the water with fewer men than they came with. But the betrayal at Severin was done, and the border fortress fell on the third day. It was the first victory he could not enjoy. He went with the pale scholar the next dawn, without a word to any of his captains, to the school under the mountain that takes every tenth of its sons.

speaker: The ferryman
text: (No sound. A long, pale finger points at the open palm. Then, in a voice like water in a cistern:) The toll. One silver, from a scholar's own hand.

speaker: The ferryman
text: (The coin vanishes. The gull on his shoulder does not stir.) Board, scholar. Do not look at the water.

speaker: The ferryman
text: Nine fall short; the tenth pays more. A coin lies in the cairn, with the drowned scholar's cross. He kept it. He kept it badly.

speaker: The ferryman
text: Board.

speaker: The Master
text: Voivode. You came. I remember very few who come. The winter is long and the lessons are plain. First, the lesson of names: every thing has a name that is not its name. Learn to speak to a thing in the voice it hears itself in.

speaker: player
text: What is the rite I must learn?

speaker: player
text: I want to read your library.

speaker: player
text: What is the tithe?

speaker: The Master
text: Three vessels, three acts, and an order that matters more than any of them. It is written in the Clavis Minor, in the library. A scholar who cannot read it will not be able to perform it, and a scholar who cannot perform it will not earn the stair.

speaker: The Master
text: The key is Vasile's. I give nothing away; the school teaches by taking. You must get it from him as best you can. Princes are used to getting things from men.

speaker: The Master
text: When the winter ends, ten scholars sit in a ring. One is the Devil's. He pays the tuition of all of us. Don't look so grave, Voivode. It is only a custom. The roll in the library says whose turn it is.

speaker: Vasile
text: The new boy. A prince in a scholar's gown. I have the key to the library, you know. The Master gave it to me because I do not want what is in it. You do. That makes you very interesting.

speaker: player
text: What are you running from, Vasile?

speaker: Vasile
text: (He laughs, a surprised, boyish laugh.) You are very strange, Vlad. All right. A share. But the first thing you learn, you'll teach me. (He lifts the cord over his head.) Do not lose it. And do not lose me.

speaker: Vasile
text: (He goes quite white, and does not move.) You would not. (A long breath.) Take it. Take it. I'll remember this when I'm Master.

speaker: Vasile
text: From a town that taught me my place and then did not give me one. My father drank, my mother prayed and nobody did either well. I came here to be taken seriously.

speaker: Teodor
text: They say one of us goes down the stair at the end of the winter, my lord. They say it is chosen by the roll. They say the roll can be read by anyone with the key, and altered by anyone with ink. I have not said any of this.

speaker: player
text: Where is the ink kept?

speaker: Teodor
text: Everywhere, and nowhere. The Master leaves a pot out for the beginners and moves it every night. Look where a clerk would put it, and where a child would hide it.

speaker: Maria
text: I have learned to call the weather. It takes about three hundred hours and the loss of one's eyebrows. Do not look at me like that, prince. Do not look at any of us like that. We are all here for the same reason: nobody at home was going to teach us anything.

speaker: player
text: What is the third lesson?

speaker: Maria
text: The Wolf-Tongue. In the spring the Master takes us out on the heath and teaches us to call the beasts of the wood. A wolf-tooth is the pledge. If you have ever fought wolves, they may remember you.

speaker: The rite-altar
text: Three hollows: a bowl, a disc, a lamp. Water, silver, flame. In what order do I begin?

speaker: The rite-altar
text: The hollow cracks with cold and the stone spits. The order is wrong. I must start again.

speaker: The rite-altar
text: Water in the bowl. The hollow drinks. What next?

speaker: The rite-altar
text: The disc settles. The stone hums. And last?

speaker: The rite-altar
text: The lamp lights without a match. The three hollows glow, and a cold calm falls on the room. I feel, for a moment, that I have been heard.

speaker: The Roll
text: A scroll as tall as a man. Ten names for this winter, in this order: Nicolae. Gheorghe. Vasile Cernat. Maria. Teodor. Anca. Bogdan. Lupu. Cosmin. And, last, in ink still wet: Vlad, Voivode of the Wallachians. The tenth to enter is the Devil's.

speaker: The Roll
text: The quill scratches. I have made a name that was Vlad's into one that is not. I have made a tenth out of a man who did nothing but tell me the truth. The ink dries at once, and does not look wet or recent. The roll accepts it, as paper accepts anything.

speaker: The Roll
text: The last line is wet and sullen. A change would need ink, and I have none.

speaker: The Master
text: The winter is over. Ten stand in the ring. The roll is read. (He turns the scroll in the green light.)

speaker: The Master
text: The tenth to enter is the tenth to pay. It is you, Voivode: Vlad, son of Vlad, of the House of the Dragon. It is an honour of a kind. It is not an easy one.

speaker: player
text: I will pay. It was my choice to come.

speaker: player
text: Take Vasile Cernat. He is the better scholar, and the weaker man.

speaker: The Master
text: (A long, slow smile.) Good. Hold my hand. Below the grate a sound like a great beast breathing grows loud, and then it gathers itself, and rises. When it reaches you, I think you will not scream. You will never scream again.

speaker: The Master
text: (Interested.) A prince's choice, quick and cold. Very well. The name, spoken in the ring, becomes the debt. Vasile, come. Do not weep: you have been a good scholar.

speaker: The Master
text: (He reads, and stops. His eyes, for a moment, flick to mine.) The tenth to enter is Vasile Cernat. (A pause.) Strange. I had remembered it otherwise. But the roll says what the roll says, and the debt follows the ink. A prince's art, Voivode. I should have guessed.

speaker: The Master
text: The term is ended. Whatever comes up that stair belongs to the Devil and the one he leaves behind. Take this book, Voivode. It teaches the speech of wolves and the weather. It is a poor payment for what you have just seen, and it is the one I give. Go home. Rule. You will not need to wait for death to find a kind of eternity.

speaker: Narrator
text: He left the school with a book of black leather, a ring of pale grey rime that never melted from his hand, and a voice that wolves came to when he spoke. Some years later, the Turk crossed the river again and the Voivode rode out to meet him, and did not ride home. The boyars carried him back by night in a closed bier, and Father Dragomir said the office over him in a hurry, and sealed the vault with lead. They were wrong to think that this was the end of it.

speaker: Ileana's tomb
text: 'Ileana Corvin, who waited.' The ring on the stone is the silver ring I never gave her, which she must have had made herself.

speaker: Ileana's tomb
text: It is very small. I can close my fist around it. I do not know why that is the thing that finally does it.

speaker: Ileana's tomb
text: 'Say it again when you are in the doorway, Vlad,' she said. I am in the doorway. She is not here. I say it anyway.

speaker: Father Dragomir
text: (He tries to rise, and fails.) My lord. You are... You are cold. I sealed you myself. I said the office. And yet you stand there, and the candle does not move when you breathe. (He is quite still.) Forgive me. Are you my Voivode, or something he has become?

speaker: player
text: I am your Voivode, Father. Tell me what has happened.

speaker: player
text: What of the Turks?

speaker: player
text: What of Ileana?

speaker: Father Dragomir
text: The Turks took the gate the night you were laid in the vault. The boyars have gone; Vlaicu to the Sultan, they say. I stayed. Someone had to. I took a spear in the side defending the door I ought to have barred, and I think, my lord, that I will not see the morning.

speaker: Father Dragomir
text: They have the courtyard and the gate, and the boyars have gone, Vlaicu to the Sultan, they say.

speaker: player
text: And Radu?

speaker: player
text: And Radu?

speaker: Father Dragomir
text: He rides with them, under the Sultan's green banner. You gave him his life, my lord, and he has used it to take yours.

speaker: Father Dragomir
text: He died in the cells, in the first cold. The village has not forgiven you, and does not mean to.

speaker: Father Dragomir
text: She waited, my lord. She came every morning to the tower. When the news came, she walked into the lake and the people found her ring on the shore. I buried her under the stone. You will see it. She said you would come back. She said it quite crossly.

speaker: The altar
text: I am standing at the altar of my own chapel, a hundred paces from where I was laid. A priest who may die by dawn lies against a pew. A wolf is howling in the hills; I understand it. I understand every word. And I am more thirsty than I have ever been. Nobody is here to tell me what to do. That, I think, is the whole point.

speaker: The Voivode
text: He does not scream, which is the worst of it. He puts out one hand, as if to bless me, and then it falls. I think he understood. I think he forgave me. I cannot be sure which is the greater sin.

speaker: The Voivode
text: I open the doors and call, in a tongue taught under a mountain. They come out of the dark with their breath steaming, and I choose the weakest, an old one, whose time was nearly done. It is not what I wanted. It will keep a priest alive. It will keep the chapel's door unbarred.

speaker: The Voivode
text: I kneel by her stone with her ring in my fist and ask whatever I have become to wait for the sun. The sun rises. It does not kill me: it only turns the whole world to glass, and the priest, who is still alive, sees that I am weeping, and says my name, and dies.

speaker: The Voivode
text: I remember Radu.

speaker: The Voivode
text: A brother sent away alive, with a green banner at his back.

speaker: Narrator
text: His brother Radu, whom he had spared, returned with the Sultan's army and was given the throne of Wallachia as a prize. He ruled it quietly, and was loved by nobody and feared by nobody. He died in bed. It was, in its way, the cruellest outcome.

speaker: The Voivode
text: A brother left to rot in a cell, and the village that watched me do it.

speaker: Narrator
text: His brother Radu, whom he had chained, died in the cells within the winter, and his name was struck from the family roll. The castle's servants learned the new Voivode's justice and did not forget it. When the Turks came, nobody manned the walls with any enthusiasm.

speaker: The Voivode
text: I remember the school.

speaker: The Voivode
text: I paid what I owed, in the coin I chose.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the school, the Voivode had stood in the ring and taken the tithe upon himself. The Master was fascinated by this. Vasile Cernat, who lived and was a scholar to the end of his days, taught for a time at the Scholomance and left behind a book of lessons that Van Helsing would later read with a chill.

speaker: The Voivode
text: I paid what I owed with another man's life.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the school, a name in wet ink had moved the tithe from one scholar to another. Vasile Cernat went down the stair and was not seen again. The Master never reproached the Voivode for it. It was a very princely art, and he set it among his best lessons.

speaker: The Voivode
text: The thirst, the choice, the debt. Seven hundred years, and not one day of them without the memory.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Voivode rose at dusk, and fed on the only warm thing in the chapel. It was the first death for which he was, in the strictest sense, responsible. It would not be the last. By the time the Turks left the castle, he had gone into the hills, and the village learned to leave a door unbarred for the lord who no longer slept. Seven hundred years passed. The hunger did not.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Voivode rose at dusk, and learned that the beasts of the hills would keep his secret. He fed on the old and the dying, and left the living to their hearths. The shepherds called him the Wolf-Lord, and their children's children told it to strangers, and in time Harker heard it. In the strictest sense, he never took a man's life. It was a very thin sense, and he knew it. Seven hundred years passed.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Voivode rose with the sun and was not destroyed. He was something worse: the same man, with the same thirst, in a different world. At dusk he took Ileana's ring and went out. He did not feed that night, nor the next, nor for a long time, and he grew very strange and very sorrowful. Eventually he did, and the bell in the village was never rung for it. Seven hundred years passed.

speaker: Cabman
text: Morning, Mr. Harker. Where to? Your Mr. Hawkins has the cab-rank in his pocket, so I take it you are going somewhere dear.

speaker: player
text: To the station - for the London train and the Museum.

speaker: player
text: To the station - and then, God willing, the East.

speaker: player
text: Not yet. I have a few things to finish.

speaker: Cabman
text: Paddington by the 9.15, then. The Museum is a step from the Underground. Mind the pickpockets in the Reading Room: they read, too.

speaker: Narrator
text: By the morning train to London.

speaker: Cabman
text: The Great Western to town, sir, and the boat-train after that. You are the first man from this street who ever went so far. I'll tell your landlady you looked cheerful.

speaker: Narrator
text:
THE SOLICITOR'S ROAD

By rail and river, through Munich and Vienna, to Bistritz and the Borgo Pass...

A month later: the castle.

speaker: Cabman
text: I am here until four, then the horse insists on his oats.

speaker: Flower-seller
text: Violets, sir? Penny a bunch. For Miss Murray, is it? She was by this morning for geraniums and told me you were off to a great foreign place.

speaker: player
text: Is it that obvious?

speaker: player
text: What do the violets mean?

speaker: player
text: Not today, thank you.

speaker: Flower-seller
text: You walk like a man counting his steps to a station, sir. I've seen soldiers go to war with less spring.

speaker: Flower-seller
text: Modesty. And faithfulness. A gentleman about to go abroad could do worse than both.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: Ah, Jonathan. Come in, come in. You look as though you had not slept. Are the Count's letters still on my desk? I should like you to master them before you go.

speaker: player
text: Tell me again about the Count's commission.

speaker: player
text: I have the surveys, sir. Let me tell you which house will suit the Count.

speaker: player
text: The Count wants nothing but Carfax, I think. May I have my instructions?

speaker: player
text: Do you think I shall like Transylvania, sir?

speaker: player
text: Is there anything else I should know before I go?

speaker: player
text: Excuse me, sir.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: A foreign nobleman, Count Dracula, has bought a house in England through us. He wants it large, old and solitary, with a chapel, a high wall, and no neighbours who can overlook him. The surveys are in the deed-box in the muniment room, but Pell has the key, and he will give it up only for good reasons.

speaker: player
text: The Count's letters, sir - may I take them?

speaker: player
text: I shall see to it.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: They are on the desk. Take them. Show them to Pell; he will not move without papers.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: I am all attention. Which of the three would you recommend? He is a man of wealth and old habits, and he does not care to be watched.

speaker: player
text: The Hampstead villa: handsome, but near a good deal of neighbours.

speaker: player
text: The house at Whitby: quiet, and by the sea.

speaker: player
text: Carfax at Purfleet: old, walled, with a chapel, a pond and only a madhouse for neighbour.

speaker: player
text: I need a little more time to study them.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: Hampstead? The Count asks for seclusion; the villa has fourteen neighbours, a vicar and a bandstand. Look again at the surveys.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: Whitby is a fine place, but it has no chapel, and a villa on the cliff is overlooked by half the town. Look again at the surveys.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: Carfax. Yes. Ancient, enclosed by high stone, with the old chapel and a pond like a well. And the nearest house is Dr. Seward's asylum. A quiet neighbour, as the Count remarks. I think we have our man the house.

speaker: player
text: Then I must go and see him in person, sir.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: Quite right. The Count is no common client, and I am too old to travel. You are to go to Castle Dracula, find his house of business, and have the deed signed. Take these - a letter of credit and the particulars - and visit the British Museum before you leave: learn what you can of the country. And, Jonathan - say goodbye to Miss Murray.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: A country of beauty and ignorance, I am told. Be careful what you eat, and keep your own counsel. The Count writes in a very good English, but the English of a man who has read much and spoken little.

speaker: Mr. Hawkins
text: Only this, my boy: when you are ready to marry that girl, do it quickly. I am old; I like to see good things done in good time. I shall give you a partnership when you return.

speaker: Mr. Pell
text: Mr. Harker. The muniment room is not a public thoroughfare. May I ask what business takes you there?

speaker: player
text: Mr. Hawkins wants the Transylvanian surveys. Here are the Count's letters.

speaker: player
text: Why do you keep the key so close, Mr. Pell?

speaker: player
text: What do you think of the Count's letters?

speaker: player
text: Never mind.

speaker: Mr. Pell
text: Letters. Hmm. A good hand, a foreign seal, and a request in four pages. Yes, I see you are expected. Here. Lock up after you, and put the box key back where you found it; I hide it in the room itself.

speaker: Mr. Pell
text: In thirty-one years, Mr. Harker, nothing has been lost from that room. That is not luck; that is a chain.

speaker: Mr. Pell
text: A well-bred hand, and a seal with a wolf on it. I dislike a seal with a wolf on it. I have no reason. The ink is very black, and the paper very cold.

speaker: Copy-book
text: Nine letters of the firm's side of the correspondence, in Mr. Hawkins's own pressed copy. Which would you like?

speaker: player
text: The first: the Count's enquiry.

speaker: player
text: The seventh: Carfax.

speaker: player
text: The ninth: the Count's summons.

speaker: player
text: Close the book.

speaker: Letter 1
text: 'My dear Sir: I am a foreigner who desires a house in England, near London, of ancient build, with ample grounds and a chapel. My friend Mr. Hawkins is recommended to me as a gentleman of probity. I am, Sir, yours truly, Dracula.'

speaker: Letter 7
text: 'The house must be large, secluded, well walled, old, and not overlooked. I care little for the comforts of modern life, but a pond or well, and a chapel are required. I am not young, and I have habits.'

speaker: Letter 9
text: 'I expect Mr. Harker at the Borgo Pass on the 5th of May. A carriage will await him. I trust he will not mind the journey, which is long; the people are simple, and their superstitions many. Be assured, I shall be a good host.'

speaker: Mina
text: Jonathan! You came, and in school hours. The headmistress has gone to the dentist, so we may talk, if we are quick and a little bit improper.

speaker: player
text: I am going to Transylvania, Mina. A month, perhaps more.

speaker: player
text: Mina, I have something of my mother's to give you.

speaker: player
text: Mina, will you wait for me?

speaker: player
text: Shall we practise the shorthand?

speaker: player
text: I should go. I just wished to see you.

speaker: Mina
text: I knew it, Jonathan. Mr. Hawkins told the whole parish. You will write to me. You will write to me every day, even if you cannot post it. Promise.

speaker: player
text: I promise.

speaker: player
text: I shall try, Mina.

speaker: Mina
text: A ring? It was your mother's? Oh, Jonathan. Put it on, then - quickly, before I lose my nerve. No: keep it safe, Jonathan, for the day itself. I shall wear it on my finger then, and no sooner.

speaker: player
text: There. I feel taller already.

speaker: Mina
text: Wait? I should wait for a Pasha's decision, Jonathan, but for you I'll do it gladly. Take this. It is the ribbon from my hair; tie your diary with it, and write to me in shorthand, and I shall learn to read it faster than a clerk.

speaker: Mina
text: Look at the board. I wrote you a line in Pitman's: 'Come back safe.' It is quite the shortest sentence in the world, and the hardest to keep.

speaker: Small pupil
text: Are you Miss Murray's gentleman? She cries when she looks at the map. She says it is the chalk dust.

speaker: player
text: Does she, indeed?

speaker: player
text: Run along, child.

speaker: Small pupil
text: And she draws your name in the margin and rubs it out. I can read it, though. It begins with a J. Is it Jonah?

speaker: Mrs. Dunmore
text: Mr. Harker! The trunk has stood there since the day you came, and I shall be glad to see something done with it. A man should not live with a locked box in his bedroom. It is not healthy.

speaker: player
text: Do you know where the combination might be?

speaker: player
text: I shall pack tonight.

speaker: player
text: What shall I do about the dreams, Mrs. Dunmore?

speaker: player
text: Thank you, Mrs. Dunmore.

speaker: Mrs. Dunmore
text: Combination? Your father had it from the Admiralty, I was told, and he used it for the year he stopped sailing. A man puts the saddest year of his life in a lock like that. Ask the verger at St. Petroc's; he buried him.

speaker: Mrs. Dunmore
text: Then pack with what's in the trunk and what's on the table: your diary, the Count's papers and the notes from the Museum. I'll have the cab ready for the morning.

speaker: Mrs. Dunmore
text: Dreams? I never remember mine. I find it saves a deal of explaining at breakfast.

speaker: Father's trunk
text: A brass-bound trunk with a four-wheel lock. The wheels read 18-- . You must set the last two digits. What year did your father die?

speaker: player
text: I do not remember. I shall find out.

speaker: player
text: (The trunk is open.) Look inside again.

speaker: Father's trunk
text: The wheels click, but the lock does not yield. It is not the right year. Somewhere there is a stone with the date on it.

speaker: Father's trunk
text: The wheels fall into place, and the hasp springs free. Inside: my mother's ring in a twist of tissue, my father's last letter to me, and a small crucifix. The smell of camphor and thirty years.

speaker: Father's trunk
text: The trunk is empty but for tissue and lavender. My mother's ring and my father's letter are in my pocket now.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I lie down for an hour. In the half-sleep I see a long road winding up into mountains, and a lit window high on a rock. Somebody is standing in it, waiting. I do not know why that should make me afraid.

speaker: player
text: (Get up.)

speaker: Verger
text: Harker, is it? I knew your father. A decent, tired man, and the fever took him in a week.

speaker: player
text: What year did he die, Mr. Pascoe?

speaker: player
text: Who tends the graves?

speaker: player
text: Thank you.

speaker: Verger
text: Read it from the stone, young sir; I'm not a clerk. It's the Harker stone by the yew. But I'll tell you this: it was the winter of the great frost, and the Exe froze to the bridge.

speaker: Verger
text: I do. And the one who leaves the snowdrops, I won't say, though I know. She has nice handwriting.

speaker: Reading-table
text: A heap of folios and one reader's lamp. What do you look up?

speaker: player
text: Consult Bradshaw's Guide.

speaker: player
text: Leave the table.

speaker: Bradshaw
text: Bradshaw's Continental Guide: Munich to Vienna, thence to Klausenburg and Bistritz. There is a ten-hour delay at Klausenburg. 'Passengers are advised to take their own provisions.' I mark the page.

speaker: Superintendent
text: Slip, pen, and a press-mark? We do not retrieve books by hope, sir.

speaker: player
text: Press-mark K.7: Geography and Ethnology of the Carpathians.

speaker: player
text: Press-mark H.2.

speaker: player
text: Press-mark Z.19.

speaker: player
text: I have no slip.

speaker: player
text: Never mind.

speaker: Superintendent
text: That press-mark belongs to a treatise on cattle-breeding, sir. I recommend you consult the catalogue: the entry on Transylvania has a red ticket.

speaker: Superintendent
text: The tray of slips is by the catalogue. We are a library, sir, not a mind-reader.

speaker: Superintendent
text: K.7. Yes. A rare work, and a good one. I shall have it brought. You will find a table prepared.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I read for three hours. The country lies in the horseshoe of the Carpathians; it is a whirlpool of races, Saxon, Wallach, Magyar and Szekely; and the Szgany, who are its gypsies. The people believe in the Evil Eye. I copy what I can. I note a mention of the Borgo Pass, and a name, Dracula, which means 'son of the dragon' and 'devil'.

speaker: Elderly reader
text: You are reading the Carpathians, sir. Go no farther than the facts. The superstitions of that country are so numerous that every bridge has a ghost and every ghost a recipe.

speaker: player
text: What superstitions?

speaker: player
text: Do you know the Dracula family?

speaker: player
text: I'll leave you to your Hungarian wills.

speaker: Elderly reader
text: The Evil Eye, for one. At midnight on St. George's Eve every evil thing in the land is abroad. The peasants hang garlic over their doors, and leave wild roses at the cross.

speaker: Elderly reader
text: A voivode's line. One of them held the Danube against the Turk, and was either a hero or a devil according to which shore you lived on. The name means 'dragon'. I should not ask about it in the village.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I lean from the sill and look down. A drop of three hundred feet, and a ledge. The Count went down this wall like a lizard, head first, with his cloak spread out. If I am to follow, I must know the way. What can I use?

speaker: player
text: Try the handholds, starting with the ivy.

speaker: player
text: Try the handholds, starting with the iron ring.

speaker: player
text: Try the handholds, starting with the loose stone.

speaker: player
text: (Climbed.) Continue to the window.

speaker: player
text: Wait. I must study the wall.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I catch the ivy and lower my weight. It holds, and I let myself down a foot at a time to the first anchor. Now: the iron ring, or the stone?

speaker: player
text: The iron ring.

speaker: player
text: The loose stone.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I try the ring first. My hand slips; the rust is smooth and I cannot reach the ivy. My fingers fail, and I scramble back to the sill, shaking.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I put my foot on the stone. It shifts, and a block falls into the dark, a long time before it strikes. I scramble back with my heart in my mouth.

speaker: Jonathan
text: The ring takes my weight. It is bright where a hand has used it. Now I can reach the stone with my toe.

speaker: player
text: The loose stone.

speaker: player
text: Back to the ivy.

speaker: Jonathan
text: The stone, which is loose only on the outside, takes my foot as it must. From there, the eastern corner is within reach. I cross the face on my belly, a foot at a time, and drop through the open window into the Count's room.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I put a hand wrong and lose my grip. For a moment I hang by one arm over the abyss before I scramble back to the sill. I will try again, in a better order: ivy first, then iron, then stone.

speaker: Jonathan
text: The window is waiting. I drop through into the room.

speaker: Jonathan
text: The Count lies in the box, looking younger than I have ever seen him. His eyes are open and stony; there is a bloated look about him; his lips are red as if with blood. A key should be on him, but I do not find one.

speaker: player
text: Search his pockets for the key.

speaker: player
text: Strike him with the spade.

speaker: player
text: Back away.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I search him as one searches a dead man. No key. No watch, no purse; a few gold coins loose in a pocket, and nothing else. He does not move. I cannot bring myself to look at his face again.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I raise the spade, and his eyes turn toward me. The face is a mask of hate. I cannot do it. The spade slips from my hand and strikes the box, and I run.

speaker: Footbridge
text: The middle plank is gone, and the gully below is a black throat of water. A single plank, if you had one, might bridge it.

speaker: player
text: Lay the plank across and cross.

speaker: player
text: Go back and look for something.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I lay the plank across and take it step by step with the roar of the water below. On the far side a track runs down toward a valley that is, God willing, the road to civilisation. My legs give way beneath me; I rest against a boulder and the dark comes down.

speaker: Narrator
text:
Who can say how long, or by what road?

The next that Jonathan Harker knows is the smell of linen and the sound of a woman's voice, praying in German.

speaker: Szgany woman
text: Ah, the English gentleman, who walks on the mountain at night and is white as milk. Sit. Eat. The Count's people do not eat with us, but you are not one of his.

speaker: player
text: Can you sell me food?

speaker: player
text: May I ask about the Count?

speaker: player
text: Will you help me?

speaker: player
text: I'll go on.

speaker: Szgany woman
text: Gold of the old kings! That has not been seen in these hills for three hundred years. Take the bread and the goat-cheese, and a flask. I'll not ask where you found it, for I do not wish to know.

speaker: Szgany woman
text: We carry his boxes. We take his coin. We do not ask what is in them, nor why they are filled with earth. Our grandfathers bowed to his grandfathers, and we have kept the habit.

speaker: Szgany woman
text: I cannot take you down the mountain; the men will say I betrayed the master. But the herdsman by the woodpile may take you to the footbridge. He is not afraid of the old man.

speaker: Slovak herdsman
text: Dobry vecer, pan. You have the look of a man who has seen something in the castle. Hush! I do not need to hear what.

speaker: player
text: Which way to the valley?

speaker: player
text: Is there a way over the gully?

speaker: player
text: Thank you, old man.

speaker: Slovak herdsman
text: Down the path, left at the cross, and over the gully by the old bridge. The plank is gone, but there is wood by the pile. You'll find a plank long enough.

speaker: Slovak herdsman
text: Plank, rope, courage. Courage you have, or you wouldn't be here. Plank is at the woodpile.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: Sh, sh. Do not try to rise. You have been very ill, mein Herr, a brain fever, and you spoke much in your sleep, in English, of wolves and women and a wall. I was afraid.

speaker: player
text: Where am I?

speaker: player
text: What day is it? What month?

speaker: player
text: My name is Jonathan Harker. I am an English solicitor.

speaker: player
text: Sister, I must write to a lady in England.

speaker: player
text: Sister, may I have my pocket-book and diary?

speaker: player
text: Sister, I want to seal my diary. I do not want to know what is in it.

speaker: player
text: Thank you, Sister.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: In the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary, in Buda-Pesth. A herd-boy found you on the road to Bistritz, weeks ago, and the doctors say you came by wagon and cart and charity. You are among friends.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: It is the second week of September, mein Herr. You were brought in at the end of August. We counted every day.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: Harker. Yes, the name was in your pocket-book, but you spoke it in your sleep, so I knew it was true. Rest. The doctor will see you at noon.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: I will tell you what to write: the date, the place, that you are alive, and nothing more. Your friend must hear you are safe before she hears anything else. Use the writing-desk, mein Herr.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: Your coat is torn. Your diary is in the lining. I have not read it; it is in shorthand, and I'm only a Sister. Take it from the patient's chest.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: You give it to me to seal? No - to your friend. That is better. I shall pour the wax, if you will say the words. Give me the ribbon and the book.

speaker: player
text: I'll do it myself, Sister.

speaker: player
text: Do it for me. I cannot bear to touch it.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: There. The ribbon is Miss Murray's, I think? Red-white. The wax is the chapel's. Now say it, mein Herr: why do you not want to read it?

speaker: player
text: Because I do not know whether it was a dream, or whether I went mad. I will not know unless some solemn duty come upon me.

speaker: Sister Agatha
text: That is the vow, then. Not to read it, and not to doubt it, unless duty. Hold the book. I shall say a prayer.

speaker: Dr. Hartenstein
text: Ah, you are awake and sane. Good. I will tell you plainly: it was brain fever of the severest. You will not remember the first three weeks, and I advise you not to try.

speaker: player
text: What did I say?

speaker: player
text: May I write to England?

speaker: player
text: When may I leave?

speaker: player
text: Thank you, Doctor.

speaker: Dr. Hartenstein
text: You spoke of a castle in the mountains, of wolves, of women with red lips, and of a man who walks down a wall. I took it for delirium. Sister Agatha did not.

speaker: Dr. Hartenstein
text: By all means. Here, you may keep my pen. A letter soothes the mind better than any bromide.

speaker: Dr. Hartenstein
text: When the lady arrives, and we have married you, and not before. I shall not release an unmarried man in your condition.

speaker: Magyar patient
text: You are the Englishman. You shouted in the night. In German, in English, and once in what I think was Latin. Do you remember?

speaker: player
text: I remember a castle.

speaker: player
text: I remember nothing.

speaker: player
text: Go back to sleep, old man.

speaker: Magyar patient
text: There are many castles. Only one of them you should not name. Do not name it. It has ears.

speaker: Magyar patient
text: Then you are fortunate. I broke my leg falling from a cart, and I remember every pain.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I lie down on the clean linen and close my eyes. The ward is quiet. At the edge of sleep I hear a soft laughter, like silver bells, and three women are in the moonlight: two dark, with hooked noses like the Count, one fair as the sun with great wavy hair. I feel a wicked, burning desire that they would kiss me with those red lips.

speaker: player
text: (Wake. Cross myself.)

speaker: player
text: (Sleep on.)

speaker: player
text: (Lie quiet.)

speaker: Jonathan
text: I wake with the sheet in my fists, drenched in sweat. A hand cools my forehead: Sister Agatha. 'You said the word again,' she says. 'It was a woman's name. Not a good one.' I hold her hand until the fear passes.

speaker: Jonathan
text: This time the women stand back. One of them turns her head, and for a moment she has Mina's eyes, then no eyes at all. I wake knowing that I shall never again be quite at ease in sleep. A cab-wheel sounds in the courtyard. It is morning, and a woman is on the stairs.

speaker: Narrator
text: Three days later.

speaker: Writing-desk
text: A sheet of hospital paper and the doctor's pen. What shall I write to Mina?

speaker: player
text: 'I am safe, in Buda-Pesth, in the care of the Sisters. I am ill, but mending. I love you.'

speaker: player
text: 'I have terrible things to tell you.'

speaker: player
text: Step away.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I fold the letter, and Sister Agatha writes under mine: 'He is well, but weak, and he asks that you come.' She seals it herself. 'Mr. Hawkins will be told,' she says. 'And your friend will not read a word that frightens her.'

speaker: Jonathan
text: I stare at the page, and the pen shakes. I cannot say it; she must not read it. I cross it out, and begin again.

speaker: Mina
text: Jonathan. Oh, Jonathan. Sister Agatha has told me everything; she has also told me nothing that matters. I am here. I am not going away.

speaker: player
text: Mina, I have something to ask.

speaker: player
text: Mina, I have my diary. I cannot read it. Will you keep it?

speaker: player
text: Mina, a Sister says the chaplain can marry us tomorrow.

speaker: player
text: Rest, my dear.

speaker: Mina
text: Ask, then. I have come across the sea, and I have six hours of train in my bones.

speaker: player
text: Will you marry me, here, as soon as you are rested?

speaker: Mina
text: I will marry you tomorrow. Today if the chaplain could be found. But one condition: that you let me take care of you. And that you tell me, one day, what it was that frightened you.

speaker: Mina
text: A sealed book? You wish me to keep it, unread, and to give it back only if some solemn duty comes upon us? I will, Jonathan. I do not need to know what is in it. I know what is in you.

speaker: Mina
text: Then let us be married. I will find Sister Agatha and the white roses.

speaker: Old gardener
