text: The Herr Englishman. I have seen you in your chair on the third bench every afternoon this week. You look better. The cherry-trees are better than the roses; roses are tricky.

speaker: player
text: May I cut a rose for my fiancee?

speaker: player
text: What flowers do the Sisters prefer?

speaker: player
text: Thank you.

speaker: Old gardener
text: A white one. White for a wedding, and white for a funeral, but never red; red is for the bold.

speaker: Old gardener
text: Lilies for Our Lady. Roses for St. Joseph, who never asked for any. Sage for the kitchen, rue for the fever.

speaker: Young convalescent
text: You are the English one. They say you came with your hair white and your coat in ribbons.

speaker: player
text: White?

speaker: player
text: I'd rather not say.

speaker: Young convalescent
text: A white streak, Sister Agatha says. She calls it a mark of grace. I think you look like a pirate.

speaker: Altar
text: The altar is bare but for a vase of white roses and two brass candlesticks. A prayer-book lies open.

speaker: player
text: Write a letter to my parents.

speaker: player
text: Kneel for a moment.

speaker: player
text: Leave.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I write at the altar-rail: 'Father, Mother: I have been far from home, and nearly did not come back. I found your letter again - you never said that you were proud of me, but I knew. I am to be married. I wish you could see her. I wish you could see me now, and not the boy who ran along the Exe with a kite.' I fold it, and my hand is steadier than it has been in weeks.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I kneel. I do not pray in words; I only think of the long road that brought me here, and of the chain of kindly hands: a herdsman, a carter, a Sister. I am not yet quite sane, but I am nearer.

speaker: English chaplain
text: You are the young man from Exeter. I have been sent a letter by your Mr. Hawkins, who writes, I may say, a very fine hand.

speaker: player
text: Will you marry us, sir?

speaker: player
text: Is it permitted, in a hospital chapel?

speaker: player
text: I'll come back later.

speaker: English chaplain
text: With the Sisters' leave, and the doctor's, and the Bishop's lack of objection, which I have in writing. It is not usual, but it is not forbidden. Come back when the lady is ready.

speaker: English chaplain
text: Gladly. Is there a ring? A bride must have a ring.

speaker: player
text: I have my mother's ring, sir.

speaker: player
text: I lost it.

speaker: English chaplain
text: Then we wait.

speaker: English chaplain
text: Then let us begin.

speaker: English chaplain
text: Dearly beloved. We are gathered together in the sight of God, in a little white chapel in a foreign city, to join together this man and this woman. If any man can show just cause...

speaker: player
text: (Take Mina's hand and answer.)

speaker: player
text: (Step back.)

speaker: English chaplain
text: Jonathan, wilt thou have this woman to thy wedded wife, to live together after God's ordinance?

speaker: player
text: I will.

speaker: Mina
text: I will. For better, for worse, and for the unspoken things in the sealed book.

speaker: Jonathan
text: I slip my mother's ring on her hand. It fits. Sister Agatha weeps openly into her veil. The chaplain says the final words; the white roses breathe in the candlelight; and the world, which has been a nightmare for so long, is only a room full of people who love us.

speaker: Mina
text: Now we are husband and wife, Jonathan. Whatever comes. Whatever you saw, we shall face it together, and perhaps the sealed book can stay sealed for ever. 'Unless some solemn duty come upon us.'

speaker: Hannah
text: Miss Lucy! Mrs. Westenra says there are to be gentlemen to tea and the parlour vase is to be a credit to the house. And the flowers want doing properly, if I may say so.

speaker: player
text: How do you arrange a vase properly, Hannah?

speaker: player
text: What do you think of my gentlemen, Hannah?

speaker: Hannah
text: Mrs. Westenra's rule, miss, and her mother's before her: height at the back, then the middle, then the shortest in front, so the eye can walk in. Lilies behind, rose between, little blue things before.

speaker: Hannah
text: I think the doctor will bring a book, and the American will bring a horse, and Mr. Holmwood will bring his whole heart in his two hands and not know where to put it. I'd say that last is the one for you, miss, but it's not for the likes of me to say.

speaker: Mamma
text: Lucy, there is a tea at four and a vase that looks as though it has been in a fight. I want a bouquet in this room before the doctor comes, and I shall not be put off with half the garden in a jam-jar.

speaker: player
text: What do you want in the vase, Mamma?

speaker: player
text: Mamma, may we speak of Whitby?

speaker: player
text: I am very tired today, Mamma.

speaker: Mamma
text: Flowers, child. White lilies, a wild rose from the arbour, and the forget-me-nots Mina sent seed for. Arrange them yourself; you have the best eye in Hillingham and the worst patience.

speaker: Mamma
text: You have been tired all spring, my darling, and rosy with it. It is the gentlemen. When they are settled you will sleep like a log. (She pats my cheek, and her hand is trembling a little.)

speaker: Mamma
text: Oh, Lucy. It is exactly right. The lilies stand up, the rose looks out, and the little blue things hold hands in front. I could weep. Take Mina's key; I have been keeping it from you since Tuesday for no reason except that I like to be asked.

speaker: Mamma
text: Whitby! Mina has been scribbling about it for weeks, and the sea air will do you good, and so shall poor Mrs. Murray's gossip. Pack your trunk, Lucy. The Crescent is taken, and I shall travel with you.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the summer Lucy went to Whitby, with her mother and her best friend, and a trunk full of white frocks. She took a bright laugh with her, and the sea took notice.

speaker: Lucy
text: A green jar, empty. I have the stalks to fill it, if I have the flowers.

speaker: player
text: I haven't all I need.

speaker: player
text: I haven't all I need.

speaker: player
text: I haven't all I need.

speaker: Lucy
text: I need three things: white lilies, a wild rose and forget-me-nots. All in the garden, if I know the garden.

speaker: Lucy
text: Which flowers go at the back of the jar, to stand highest?

speaker: player
text: The lilies.

speaker: player
text: The wild rose.

speaker: player
text: The forget-me-nots.

speaker: Lucy
text: I put it there, and it sinks. The jar looks lopsided and apologetic. The tallest should be at the back, I think, so the others can lean on it.

speaker: Lucy
text: And in the middle, standing between the lilies and the front?

speaker: player
text: The wild rose.

speaker: player
text: The forget-me-nots.

speaker: Lucy
text: The forget-me-nots flop forward like little blue sleepers and the rose is left behind them. I take them out. The middle is the rose's.

speaker: Lucy
text: And last, the front?

speaker: player
text: The forget-me-nots, in a fringe at the front.

speaker: player
text: Nothing; leave it with its lilies and its rose.

speaker: Lucy
text: It looks bare. There is a rule against bare vases, and I am married to rules at the moment. The blue ones go in front.

speaker: Lucy
text: I stand back and look. The tall lilies stand and the wild rose looks out between them, and the small blue things hold hands in the front. It is the first thing I have done well all spring.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Miss Westenra... Lucy. I came to speak to you. I have a note somewhere, but I think I had better say it myself. I have thought of nothing else. I should like very much to ask for your hand.

speaker: Lucy
text: He is the dearest man, and I cannot marry him. But what shall I say?

speaker: player
text: Not yet, John. Ask me again in a year, and I'll see how I feel.

speaker: player
text: Dr. Seward, I like you better than almost anyone, and I cannot marry you. I will not keep you hoping.

speaker: player
text: You are far too grave for me, John! You would bury me in your casebooks.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: A year. Yes. Of course. I shall wait. I am a patient man, you know; it is the whole of my profession. (He smiles, and my heart sinks, because I have given him a hook to hang a year on.)

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: ...I see. I beg your pardon. (He turns his hat in his hands, and says nothing, and I am ashamed of myself for the rest of the day.)

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Thank you. That was kind, and it was plain, and I would rather have it so than the other way. I knew, I think, before I asked. May I still be your friend?

speaker: player
text: Always. You will be Jack to me as long as you like.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Then I shall go and be of use to someone. Good day, Lucy. Be happy; it is a medical prescription.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: Miss Lucy. I'll be as brief as a Texan can. I've ridden a long way and shot a few things and I'd like to ask if you'd take me on as a husband. That's the whole speech. The rest is for you.

speaker: Lucy
text: I must not make him sit through a speech. But I must not be too short either.

speaker: player
text: Mr. Morris, one cannot speak so quickly of such things, and one must consider the whole situation, and the position, and one's dear Mamma, and the prospects, and...

speaker: player
text: No, Mr. Morris. I am sorry. I am proud you asked, and I should like us to be friends.

speaker: player
text: Perhaps, if you were to stay in England a few more months, I might think of it.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: That's a heap of words, ma'am, for what I reckon is a no. I'd have gone easier with the plain article. (He takes off his hat, and puts it on again.)

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: More months? Hell, Miss Lucy, I'd stay years. I'd stay till the Thames froze over. (He is smiling. I have just made a very kind, very stupid mistake.)

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: No hard feelings, ma'am. A man gets to say it, and a woman gets to say the other, and neither of us gets to be sorry for the saying. But if you ever want a man to ride out in the rain for you, you whistle.

speaker: player
text: I shall whistle badly, Quincey, but I shall whistle.

speaker: Quincey Morris
text: That's the girl. Now, I reckon there's a gentleman waiting for you behind that rose-bush who's been standing there for half an hour. Good luck, Miss Lucy.

speaker: Arthur Holmwood
text: Lucy... I had a long speech and I've dropped it somewhere in the lilies. I only want to ask whether you could be happy with me. If you could, I should be the most fortunate man in England. If you couldn't, I should try to deserve it.

speaker: Lucy
text: I do not need a speech either. I only need to be myself for once, and plain.

speaker: player
text: I must ask Mamma, Arthur, and then I shall tell you, at some convenient time next week.

speaker: player
text: Yes, Arthur. Plainly, and you shall not have to ask a second time.

speaker: player
text: Ask me tomorrow. I shall think it over.

speaker: Arthur Holmwood
text: Of course. Mrs. Westenra. Next week. (His face is a perfect picture of a man who has been ordered to stand in the rain.)

speaker: Arthur Holmwood
text: Tomorrow. Yes. I shall be at the Station Hotel and I shall not sleep. (And I know, watching him go white, that I have done wrong, and I want to run after him.)

speaker: Arthur Holmwood
text: Lucy! ...Lucy. (He takes my hand, and discovers the rose in his buttonhole, and puts it in my hair, and I laugh until I cry.) My mother's ring is in my pocket. May I?

speaker: Lucy
text: It is a small old ring with a pale stone, and it fits. I wish, oh I wish one girl could marry all three of them. Jack, who sees what is wrong; Quincey, who is the one you want in a storm; Arthur, who is the one you want at home. But there is only one of me, and I have said yes to the one I love.

speaker: Lucy
text: A desk, a window and the best light in the house. Mina's letters are always so careful. Mine always have the postscript first.

speaker: player
text: I have nothing to tell her yet.

speaker: player
text: I need ink, paper and Mina's last letter first.

text: I need ink, paper and Mina's last letter first.

speaker: player
text: I need ink, paper and Mina's last letter first.

speaker: Lucy
text: I have nothing settled to tell her. Not about the gentlemen, anyway. I shall come back when my heart has stopped changing its mind.

speaker: Lucy
text: The ink from my room, the paper from Mamma's escritoire, and Mina's own letter to answer. It is in the left-hand drawer.

speaker: Mina
text: 'Dearest Lucy, you must tell me everything, but not in the order it comes to you, for your letters are all middle. Begin with what you see out of the window; then the people in the house; then what you cannot tell anyone else; and last, your love, always your love. It makes a letter into a path.' - Mina.

speaker: Lucy
text: 'Dearest Mina.' How do I begin?

speaker: player
text: The window: 'The roses are out, the lawn is cut, and the whole house smells of tea.'

speaker: player
text: The secret: 'Mina, I have had THREE proposals in a single afternoon!'

speaker: player
text: My health: 'I am so very tired lately, Mina, and I cannot think why.'

speaker: Lucy
text: I cross it out. She would read no further than that and answer by return of post in alarm. Mina said to begin with the window.

speaker: Lucy
text: I cross it out. She worries too easily; I must give her something steady first.

speaker: Lucy
text: And next?

speaker: player
text: The people: 'Mamma is well, the doctor has been twice, and Hannah has opinions about everything.'

speaker: player
text: My love, quickly, so it is not forgotten.

speaker: player
text: The postscript: 'P.S. Please do not tell Jonathan anything.'

speaker: Lucy
text: Too soon. A path should have somewhere to go before it ends.

speaker: Lucy
text: I smile, because it is exactly my habit, and cross it out. Not yet; it is the middle of the letter, not the end.

speaker: Lucy
text: And then, the part I have been burning to write?

speaker: player
text: The secret: Jack, Quincey, Arthur, and why can't one girl marry all three?

speaker: player
text: Sign off now; she has enough.

speaker: player

speaker: Lucy
text: I cannot stop there. She would know there was something I was not telling her, and she would write me four pages of worry. The secret goes before the love.

speaker: Lucy
text: The roses have had their turn. The bit Mina wants is the bit I have been avoiding.

speaker: Lucy
text: And at the end?

speaker: player
text: 'My love, always, and come to Whitby if you can. I shall keep the other bed made up. - Lucy.'

speaker: player
text: 'Burn this when you have read it.'

speaker: Lucy
text: She would never burn it. She would put it in the blue ribbon with the rest. I write what I really mean.

speaker: Lucy
text: It is a good letter. I read it through, blot it, fold it, and give it to Hannah for the post. Mina will have the whole of it by Friday, in order, as she asked.

speaker: Mamma
text: Lucy, my pet, I have unpacked everything but your trunk. Your father's letter, the one with the forget-me-nots... I cannot find it anywhere. You took it out of the trunk at Hillingham, I remember, and you never let it out of your sight.

speaker: player
text: I have lost Papa's letter?

speaker: player
text: Where might I have left it, Mamma?

speaker: player
text: I found it, Mamma. It is safe.

speaker: Mamma
text: It has the pressed forget-me-nots, my dear, and your father's hand. If you left it anywhere, it was in your trunk, or the window-seat by the harbour, or on that wretched seat on the cliff where you and Mina sit.

speaker: Mamma
text: The trunk, the window-seat, the seat on the cliff. I have looked in none, because you are the only one who ever knows where she put things down.

speaker: Mamma
text: Thank heaven. Keep it safe, my darling; it is the one thing of his I have left you.

speaker: Mina
text: Lucy! There you are. I have been keeping the seat warm, which in this wind is like keeping a promise to a gull. How are you?

speaker: player
text: Mina, did I walk in my sleep last night?

speaker: player
text: Any news of Jonathan?

speaker: player
text: What do you make of Whitby?

speaker: Mina
text: I am afraid you did, dearest. I woke in the night and your bed was empty and the door was open. I found you at the window, in your nightgown, looking at the Abbey. I put you back to bed, and I have taken the key to our door and put it under my pillow.

speaker: Mina
text: Nothing since the letter from Buda-Pesth. I dare not hope and I dare not not hope. Let us not speak of it; you have enough to be going on with.

speaker: Mina
text: A town built like a staircase. Churchyard on the cliff, old graves, and tombstones for people who were buried at sea. It is the saddest place I have ever loved. Mr. Swales is the oldest man on the cliff, and the most disagreeable; he knows every story in it.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Eh, look who's come. T' lady wi' t' pretty frocks. Sit tha down. Nay, not on yon seat. It's a rare place for a lass to be lonely, that seat.

speaker: player
text: How many steps are there down to the town, Mr. Swales?

speaker: player
text: What do you know of the seat?

speaker: player
text: Why do they say there is a bell at night?

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: A hundred and ninety-nine, miss. I've counted 'em wi' coffins on my shoulder. Tha counts 'em right, tha's off the cliff in no time; get it wrong and tha's on the cliff all night, wi' no way down but the long one.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: Folk sit there to look at the sea. It's been there longer nor I. Sailors' wives sat there to watch for t' ships, and some of 'em sat so long they forgot to go home.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: There's no bell, lass. There's a bell on the sea, a buoy, that rings when t' water's rough. Other folk say it's the Abbey's old bell, rung by monks that never left. I say a bell's what you hear when tha wants to be called.

speaker: Lucy
text: My bed. It is evening, and Mina has taken the key. I am to sleep the sleep of the just, if only I knew what I am to be just about.

speaker: player
text: I cannot go to bed yet. Father's letter is lost.

speaker: player
text: I want to speak to Mina first.

speaker: player
text: I should like to speak to old Mr. Swales first.

speaker: player
text: Something about my slippers worries me.

speaker: Lucy
text: I am not going to bed without it. I want it under my pillow. I shall look in the trunk, the window-seat and on the cliff.

speaker: Lucy
text: Mina would know about last night. She was awake. She will be on the cliff.

speaker: Lucy
text: Mr. Swales knows the cliff and what is on it. I should like to ask him something first.

speaker: Lucy
text: My slippers are by the bed; I should look at them before I do anything else.

speaker: Lucy
text: I lie down with Papa's letter on the pillow beside me, and the window open on the sea, and Mina's key under her head. I count sheep, then waves, then steps. I do not remember falling asleep.

speaker: Narrator
text: That night Lucy slept. And at some hour of the night, the key stayed under Mina's pillow and the door stayed locked, and Lucy was not in her bed.

speaker: The tall dark figure
text: There you are, little one. I have waited. The sea has been calling you for weeks, and you have been such a good listener. Sit with me. Cold, are you? Come closer.

speaker: Lucy
text: I take one step toward the seat. My feet are wet. My head is full of waves. The bell is very close now, and very warm, and I want to lie down. I must hold on to something. I have something in my hands.

speaker: The tall dark figure
text: Yes, that's it. You see me now. No need to speak. Your pulse is lovely, did you know? Quick as a bird. Come.

speaker: Lucy
text: The red goes on forever. I think I am falling into it. There was a ring on my finger. There was a letter in my hand. There were people.

speaker: Lucy
text: Arthur. Arthur Holmwood. My ring is cold in my hand and Arthur's name is warm in my mouth. 'Arthur,' I say. He flinches, very slightly, as if I had thrown something.

speaker: Lucy
text: Mina. Mina Murray. Her letter is folded in four and I read the first line aloud, 'Begin with what you see out of the window.' I see a dark man, and a Moon, and a path home. 'Mina,' I say. He hisses.

speaker: Lucy
text: Papa. A man I barely remember, writing to a girl of ten with flowers pressed in every fold. I hold it against my heart. 'Papa,' I say. The forget-me-nots are stiff and dry and exactly real.

speaker: The tall dark figure
text: Stay. Stay, little one. You are mine. Not tonight, then. Not tonight.

speaker: Lucy
text: I am on the top of the steps, in my nightgown. The tolling follows me down. If I lose count, I shall be lost. How many steps are there from the cliff to the town?

speaker: player
text: One hundred and ninety-nine.

speaker: player
text: A hundred.

speaker: player
text: Two hundred.

speaker: player
text: A hundred and ninety.

speaker: Lucy
text: ...ninety-eight, ninety-nine, a hundred... no. I am not sure. The tolling swells and I lose the place and begin again from the top, my heart going like a bird in a net. Count again.

speaker: Lucy
text: I count them down, step by step, aloud, as I would count out Arthur's name. Ninety-seven, ninety-eight, ninety-nine. Eventually the cobbles. One hundred and ninety-nine. At the bottom, a lamp swings, and somebody is running.

speaker: Mina
text: Lucy! Oh, Lucy. I woke and the door was locked and you were gone and the key was still under my pillow. I ran all the way. Your feet. Your poor feet! Come, come, put this round you.

speaker: player
text: Mina, there was a man on the seat. A tall dark man with red eyes.

speaker: player
text: Take me home, Mina.

speaker: Mina
text: There is no one, dearest. Only the moon on the grave-stones. But I believe that you saw it. Come away. I shall keep the key under my pillow as long as you need me to.

speaker: Mina
text: Look at me. You are shivering and your cheeks are white, and you are alive, which is all that matters. Home, and warm milk, and in the morning we shall tell Mamma that we saw the sunrise.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lucy was found on the Abbey steps and put to bed. But the pallor stayed, and the dreams stayed, and by September she was at Hillingham again, and nothing that anyone could say was strong enough to make her well.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: (He stirs, but does not wake. His lips move: 'Lucy... a little more time.')

speaker: Lucy
text: Dear Jack. You asked me for one thing and I said no, and you have given me everything else. I shall not wake him; he has had so little sleep.

speaker: Lucy
text: Mamma is sleeping with a handkerchief in her hand, her heart as fragile as mine. I should like to say something to her, but there is nothing she could hear that would not frighten her. I shall leave her to dream I am well.

speaker: Lucy
text: Paper, a pen, ink. Dr. Van Helsing is somewhere in the house and Arthur is on his way. I have not much time. Two letters to write and one thing to leave: Papa's pressed-flower letter. Who shall have it?

speaker: Lucy
text: Arthur. Dear Arthur. What shall I tell him?

speaker: player
text: 'Do not be small with grief. Live, and love again, when you can. I shall not mind.'

speaker: player
text: 'Remember me in the garden, with the rose in my hair, and be the man I knew.'

speaker: Lucy
text: Mina. Dear Mina. What do I tell her?

speaker: player
text: 'Watch over Arthur for me; he does not know how to be alone.'

speaker: player
text: 'Keep writing, everything you see, in order, as you taught me. One day someone will need it.'

speaker: Lucy
text: Papa's letter, pressed with forget-me-nots, the one thing that held me back from the sea. Where shall it go?

speaker: Miss Hallam
text: 'Miss Murray. The Tennyson for Speech Day was in the cupboard at four last night. At eight this morning it was not. The cupboard was locked. Do you imagine, as I do, that books have no legs?'

speaker: player
text: Tell me exactly what was taken.

speaker: player
text: I think I can find out who did it.

speaker: player
text: Here is your Tennyson, Miss Hallam.

speaker: player
text: About the typewriting room...

speaker: Miss Hallam
text: 'Tennyson's poems, in green morocco, with a gilt edge. Worth four guineas, and worth more to the girl who is to receive it. The cupboard shows no scratch; I keep the only key on the staff-room hook. Look to the cupboard, the blotter, and the girls, in that order.'

speaker: Miss Hallam
text: 'You are a young woman of more sense than the rest of the staff together. Find it, and I shall give you the key to the typewriting room, which you have been looking at like a dog at a butcher's shop since Christmas.'

speaker: Miss Hallam
text: 'Green morocco, gilt edge, not a thumb-mark. Who...? No. I shall not ask.' She takes a small iron key from her chatelaine. 'The typewriting room is yours after lessons. Do not teach the girls to use it before they have learned to spell.'

speaker: Miss Hallam
text: 'The Remington is a temperamental animal. Old Miss Tuck sits with it on Thursdays and understands it better than anyone. She taps on the table, which I take to be encouragement.'

speaker: Edith
text: 'Miss Murray! I have seen nothing. I have only heard everything, which is not the same.'

speaker: player
text: Who was in the schoolroom yesterday evening?

speaker: player
text: Is anyone in the form having a difficult time?

speaker: player
text: You are a great help, Edith.

speaker: Edith
text: 'Dora stayed to dust the staff-room. She does it on Wednesdays for her penny. Her mother is poorly in Heavitree, you know. Dora sews at night to pay for the doctor, and she does not like anyone to say so.'

speaker: Edith
text: 'She has been writing letters in the dinner-hour. Always on the cheapest paper and always rubbing them out, as if the words were wrong. I should not tell, but you asked kindly.'

speaker: Edith
text: 'Then I shall expect to be Head Girl.' She writes something in her notebook. I should very much like to know what.

speaker: Dora
text: 'Good morning, Miss Murray. Is it about the book? I know nothing, truly.'

speaker: player
text: Show me your hands, Dora.

speaker: player
text: Dora. The red smear on the cupboard lock, the letter on the blotter: I know it was you.

speaker: player
text: I think you took the book, but I cannot prove it yet.

speaker: player
text: Thank you, Dora. [Leave]

speaker: Mina
text: She holds out her hands. They are clean. But the cuff of her sleeve has a mark on it, brick-red and shining, the shape of a thumb, and she keeps turning the mark inward as if she could hide it by looking away.

speaker: Dora
text: 'You cannot prove anything because there is nothing, miss. I swear it on my mother.' She looks at the floor; there is a great deal of floor in that look.

speaker: Dora
text: She says nothing for a long moment. Then her face crumples. 'I only wanted to copy out one poem. Mama has no books, and she cannot read much now, but I read to her, and she cried at the Tennyson when I read it from Edith's lesson. I meant to put it back on Friday. I used the red ink for the date, so I would remember when to return it. I never meant to keep it.'

speaker: player
text: Take the book back and tell no one how it was found.

speaker: player
text: You must tell Miss Hallam yourself, Dora. I shall stand beside you.

speaker: Dora
text: She puts the book in my hands as if it were hot. 'Thank you. I shall copy it out by hand this Sunday, and put a penny in the poor-box for each verse.' I think she will.

speaker: Dora
text: 'Yes, miss.' She trembles, but she gets the words out. When the three of us stand at Miss Hallam's desk, the headmistress looks at the girl for a long moment and says only, 'You have chosen the hard way, Dora Pike, which is the only honest one.' The Tennyson goes into my hands, and later, I believe, a second copy goes into Dora's.

speaker: Mina
text: I hold Miss Hallam's blotter up to the mirror by the window. A letter, backwards, in a round hand that makes its capital D with a loop: 'Dearest Mama, I have it safe and I will read you the part about the Lady of Shalott. Do not tell Dr. B. that I...' The rest is smudged. The hand is a girl's.

speaker: Mina
text: Red ink, which only the staff are supposed to use, for marking. The bottle is a quarter lower than it was last week. Someone has been dipping a pen where no pupil should.

speaker: Mina
text: The lock is unscratched, the hasp is whole: nobody forced it. On the brass escutcheon is a tiny smear of red ink, shining, a thumb-print. Whoever opened it had the key from the hook, and had been writing with the staff's red pen not an hour before.

speaker: Miss Tuck
text: 'You have the key! I thought you would, in the end. Sit down, child. The Remington is a good machine with a bad temper. Ask it what it wants.'

speaker: player
text: What is wrong with it?

speaker: player
text: How do I free a jammed type-bar?

speaker: player
text: The ribbon is dry as a leaf.

speaker: player
text: It squeals like a gate.

speaker: player
text: Tell me something about shorthand.

speaker: Miss Tuck
text: 'Three things, child, always three. The bars stick, the ribbon dries, the pivots rust. When a Remington is silent for a year, it has all three, like a bad marriage.'

speaker: Miss Tuck
text: 'Something thin, steel, and not your fingernail. Girls have been unjamming type-bars with hairpins since the machine came over from America.'

speaker: Miss Tuck
text: 'A new ribbon. They used to be kept in the stationery cupboard, or the shelf, or sometimes the waste-basket, when some careless girl had thrown away a perfectly good one. Look about.'

speaker: Miss Tuck
text: 'There is an oil-can on the table. Do not use it all at once. A drop on every pivot, no more.'

speaker: Miss Tuck
text: 'It is the quickest way to learn what people mean rather than what they say. You will be a great help to your young man with it. Is he fond of dictation?' 'He has never dictated to me in his life, Miss Tuck.' 'Then he is a fool or a gentleman. Probably both.'

speaker: Mina
text: The dictation sheet is in my own shorthand, from Mr. Hawkins's last letter to the school: 'Please confirm that the old house at Purfleet, called Carfax, with its chapel and twenty acres, is secured for the Count, and that the deeds go to Transylvania by the post of the ninth instant.' Twenty acres, the ninth instant, Carfax at Purfleet. I commit it to memory.

speaker: Mina
text: The Remington sits under its dust-sheet like a patient waiting to be seen.

speaker: player
text: Try the keys.

speaker: Mina
text: Three keys rise and refuse to come down; the type-bars have tangled in a little steel knot. Something thin would free them.

speaker: Mina
text: The bars move now, but the carriage squeals like a gate and the pivots grind. It wants oil.

speaker: Mina
text: The keys strike beautifully, and leave nothing behind. The ribbon is dry as a dead leaf. It wants a new one.

speaker: Mina
text: The Remington is mended. I feed in a sheet of foolscap, and the machine waits with a little ratchet-click for me to begin. What did the sheet say?

speaker: player
text: '... Carfax at Purfleet, with its chapel and twenty acres, the deeds to go by the post of the ninth instant.'

speaker: player
text: '... Carfax at Purfleet, with its chapel and twelve acres, the deeds by the ninth instant.'

speaker: player
text: '... Carfax at Whitby, with twenty acres, the deeds by the nineteenth instant.'

speaker: Mina
text: The page comes out clean and wrong. Miss Tuck, passing, taps the table. 'No, child. Read it again.' I rip it out, and feed in another sheet.

speaker: Mina
text: The keys go down like rain on a roof, and the carriage bell rings at every line. Eleven lines, no errors, and the margins as straight as a ruled slate. It is the most satisfying thing I have done since I learned my times-tables.

speaker: Mina
text: I fold the page, direct it to Mr. Hawkins's office, and drop it into the post-box in the passage, with a note: 'Miss W. Murray, if the Remington is spoken of at all.' It is the first thing I have sent that has not been written in my own hand. I expect nothing and hope for everything.

speaker: Mrs. Pym
text: 'Good day, Miss Murray. Nothing in the post for you today, I am afraid. Nothing, nothing.' She has a sad way of saying it, as though the letters were her own children kept from her.

speaker: player
text: Is there a reply from Mr. Hawkins's office?

speaker: player
text: Nothing from Mr. Harker at all?

speaker: player
text: Thank you for waiting up for me, Mrs. Pym.

speaker: Mrs. Pym
text: 'Not a line since he went abroad, my dear. And no one in the town knows where abroad is. I did hear Mr. Hawkins is quite uneasy himself.'

speaker: Mrs. Pym
text: 'This came by the afternoon delivery. Typed, so it must be important. A clerk wrote it for Mr. Hawkins. He says...' She hands me the envelope. 'You had better read it yourself, dear.'

speaker: Mrs. Pym
text: 'There, there. Go and be clever at the station, if it will make you feel better. Though I wish you would take a shawl.'

speaker: Lucy
text: 'Mina! Do not look at me like that. I am here for the whole night and I intend to sit up on your sofa and be miserable on principle. Have you heard from Jonathan?' 'Not a word, Lucy. But I have this.' I put the letter in her hand.

speaker: player
text: Read the letter aloud.

speaker: player
text: Lucy, tell me about the three men.

speaker: player
text: Lucy, I have a strange dream. I want to tell someone.

speaker: player
text: Good night, Lucy.

speaker: Mina
text: I read the letter, the one that took twelve days and a Taunton stationmaster to reach me: 'Beloved Mina, I write from the Golden Krone at Bistritz. The landlady pressed a little cross on me at parting and cried; I took it to be superstition and humoured her. Tomorrow I drive into the mountains, and I shall be among strangers for a month. I wish you were beside me, with your shorthand and your timetables. Wait for me, and do not be anxious. Your own Jonathan.' Lucy has her hand at her mouth. 'Oh, Mina.'

speaker: Lucy
text: 'Three of them, Mina! Dr. Seward, who looks at me as if I were an interesting case; Mr. Morris, who is a Texan and makes me laugh; and Arthur Holmwood, who is a gentleman, and kind, and very big and very blushing. I cannot decide. How does one decide?' 'I think,' I say, 'one doesn't. One finds that one has.' Lucy thinks this over. 'Why can't a girl marry all three?' 'I have absolutely no answer.'

speaker: Mina
text: 'I dream of water, Lucy. Always the same: lapping, very close, and then the creak of wood, as of a floor or a ship's side, and then I am not in my body at all, and something calls me by a name I cannot catch. In the morning I am perfectly well and perfectly tired.' Lucy, who tells me everything, is quiet. 'That would frighten me,' she says, at last. 'It frightens me too,' I say. 'But only in the way a locked door does: because I do not know what is behind it.'

speaker: Lucy
text: 'Mina, I mean to say this once.' She takes my hand. 'He will write. He is not the kind of man who forgets. And if he does not, I shall find him myself and shake him. Meanwhile, come to Whitby with Mother and me. The sea air will cure your dreams, or at least change them.' We lie awake until the rooks begin, talking in whispers about men and trains.

speaker: Mina
text: My travelling trunk stands open. Shorthand, a spare petticoat, a favourite novel, and a space where the hope goes.

speaker: player
text: Pack, and take the morning train to Whitby.

speaker: player
text: Not yet; there is still something to do in Exeter.

speaker: Mina
text: I cannot leave Exeter with the question of Jonathan's letter still open in my head.

speaker: Mina
text: I close the lid. The key turns, like a small decision.

speaker: Narrator
text: July. Whitby. The summer I would later call the happiest and the saddest of my life: and the one in which I first heard the sea call my name.

speaker: Mina
text: I know the book by heart, but I read it anyway, the way other people say their prayers. The pages for the Bristol line: 'Exeter St. David's, dep. 10.20, stops at Tiverton (10.55), Taunton 11.30. Dep. 10.50, express, non-stop, Taunton 11.40. Dep. 11.15, stops at Tiverton, Taunton 12.05.' A girl could live and die by a table like this.

speaker: Porter
text: 'Mornin', Miss. Lovely weather for trains.' He swallows. 'Mr. Pomfret's in a stew over a bag.'

speaker: player
text: What kind of bag?

speaker: Porter
text: 'Well, I heard the guard say as the train had blown clean through Tiverton, which as you know it never does. So it was not a stopper, Miss. That's all I know.'

speaker: Mr. Pomfret
text: 'Miss Murray. I know you; you are the young lady who corrects my timetable. I shall have you know it was a misprint.'

text: 'Ah. The Taunton bag. The sorter swears it went on the first train out after the half-past-ten sorting. The porter swears it did not stop at Tiverton, since the guard saw it on the van-floor when they roared through. I only know that it is somewhere between here and Bristol. Name me the train, and Hobbs will wire the right station-master.'

speaker: Mr. Pomfret
text: 'Which train, then? Think, Miss Murray. You have Bradshaw by heart.'

speaker: player

speaker: player

speaker: player

text: 'That train called at Tiverton, Miss Murray, or left before the half-past-ten sorting, or both. It could not have carried the bag. Think again.'

speaker: Mr. Pomfret
text: He consults his watch, then Bradshaw, then me. 'The ten-fifty. After the sorting, and clean through Tiverton. By George, Miss Murray, if you ever tire of teaching, I shall find you a place at the Great Western.' He snaps his fingers at Hobbs. 'Wire Taunton.'

speaker: Hobbs
text: 'The wire is warm, miss. Mr. Pomfret has had me tapping to Taunton since the clock struck.'

speaker: player
text: Is there any answer from Taunton?

speaker: Hobbs
text: 'The click before the click, miss. You can hear a man hesitate over a word. That is the thing no one writes in the books.'

speaker: Hobbs
text: He reads off the tape. '"Bag found under van seat, registered letter M. Murray, Exeter, intact. Forwarded by next down train." And here it is, miss, in the guard's own hand.' A thick envelope, soft at the corners, with a foreign stamp and Jonathan's handwriting. I have to sit on the bench.

speaker: Mina
text: My notebook of dreams, in shorthand, tucked behind the tide-tables where Lucy will never look. 'It always begins with the water, lapping, near enough to touch. Then the wood, a creak, then another. Then the darkness, a single point turning in it, and I forget my name. Water, wood, swing. Always in that order, and always before I wake.' I underline 'always'.

speaker: Lucy
text: 'Mina, you have been writing for two hours! Mother says you will ruin your eyes, and I say you have ruined your appetite. Come and see Mr. Swales this evening: he tells the most dreadful stories.'

speaker: player
text: What does he say about the tombs?

speaker: player
text: Have you seen the coastguard?

speaker: Lucy
text: 'That every stone in the churchyard lies, and that you can tell which by doing sums. He is a terrible old humbug. He says the dead are not more than a dozen yards from the sea, and that the sea does not give them up.'

speaker: Lucy
text: 'The one with the telescope? He is a dear. He lets me look at the ships. He will let you, too, if you ask him about the tides: it is the only thing he is ever vain of.'

speaker: Mrs. Westenra
text: 'Mina, dear. You must not stand about. And the damp! Lucy, put a shawl on. I have been told the sea air is excellent for the nerves, and my nerves are certainly in need of something.' She sips her tea and looks thoughtfully at the window. 'I am so glad you came.'

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: 'Eh, lass. Ye're the one wi' the notebook. Sit ye down and ask. I'll tell ye nowt for nowt, but I'll tell ye plenty for a good question.'

speaker: player
text: They say the stones here lie, Mr. Swales.
