text: Which of these three tombs tells the biggest lie?

speaker: player
text: How do the tides run, Mr. Swales?

speaker: player
text: What do you make of the creak and the lap of the sea?

speaker: player
text: Good evening, Mr. Swales. [Leave]

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: 'Aye, every one. They bury a man and write down what pleases the widow. But there's one o' them three as cannot do a sum, and a stone that cannot count is a stone that's lying. Find it, and I'll show ye summat the parson doesn't know.'

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: 'Well, lass? Which stone cannot count?' (Read the three stones: Hannah Brough, John Anson, Mary Dale. Compare birth, death and age.)

speaker: player
text: Hannah Brough: born 1785, died 1830, aged 43.

speaker: player
text: John Anson: born 1765, died 1795, aged 30.

speaker: player
text: Mary Dale: born 1790, died 1810, aged 20.

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: 'Nay. Count it again, lass, from the year she was born to the year she died.'

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: 'Aye! Eighteen thirty less seventeen eighty-five is forty-five, and the stone says forty-three. The widower paid the mason by the letter, ye see.' He chuckles, then rummages in his coat and produces a dog-eared almanac. 'Here. The sea keeps a calendar, too. Tides run later by fifty minutes each day. Every sailor knows it. Take it, and make the coastguard a fool for once.'

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: 'Ask me that when ye've shown me ye can count.'

speaker: Mr. Swales
text: 'The sea speaks to them as listens, lass. I've heard it call my name on a dead-calm night. Ye'd best not answer it till ye're sure who is calling.' He looks at me sideways. 'Ye've a listening face, lass. Mind it.'

speaker: Mina
text: 'Hannah Brough, born 1785, died 1830, aged 43 years. She was a faithful wife and a good neighbour, and a boat's width from her husband.' Born 1785, died 1830; I put the numbers away to be added up in a quiet moment.

speaker: Mina
text: 'John Anson, master mariner, born 1765, died 1795, aged 30 years. Lost off the Scar and not found.' A stone over an empty grave. The figures are neat and the sum is good.

speaker: Mina
text: 'Mary Dale, spinster, born 1790, died 1810, aged 20 years. She died as she lived: quietly.' The lettering is deep and clean and the sum is exactly right.

speaker: Mina
text: The coastguard's tide-table, pinned flat with a mug. It lists only Monday: high water at 4.10 in the morning and 4.35 in the afternoon. 'Next high water on Wednesday?' has been pencilled in the margin by a hand that has clearly given up on its own arithmetic.

speaker: Coastguard
text: 'Miss. Come in, mind the cat.' He is very proud of the tide-table and a little embarrassed about the pencil in the margin. 'Hmm. Tell me, now you are here: Monday's afternoon high water is at 4.35. When will it be on Wednesday afternoon?'

speaker: player
text: A quarter past six, by my reckoning.

speaker: player
text: Half past five.

speaker: player
text: Seven o'clock.

speaker: player
text: Four o'clock, the same as Monday.

speaker: player
text: Tell me about the telescope.

speaker: Coastguard
text: 'No, miss. The tide does not keep pace with the town clock. Look at the table again, and ask someone who knows the rule.'

speaker: Coastguard
text: 'Fifty minutes later each day, two days on: a hundred minutes. Four thirty-five and an hour forty makes a quarter past six. Right to the minute, miss!' He is delighted, and a little hurt. 'Here, a gift for a young woman who can count.' He unhooks a brass plumb-bob from a lead-line, a cord knotted round the neck. 'A plumb is a pendulum, miss; hang it in a room and it will tell you what the room is thinking.'

speaker: Coastguard
text: 'It looks at what I cannot see. That's the whole of the trade. A coastguard is a man paid to expect something.' He glances out at the sea, and for a moment looks very tired. 'I have been expecting it for thirty years.'

speaker: Mina
text: Outside: the cliff, the churchyard, the sea. On the sill, a damp mark the shape of a small hand, as of someone who stood outside and looked in. It dries as I watch. I tell myself it is only the sea air. I do not tell Lucy.

speaker: Lucy
text: She murmurs 'Arthur...' and turns over. I tuck the sheet round her. Whatever else the summer brings, she is happy tonight, and I should like that to be the first thing recorded about it.

speaker: Mina
text: The rocking-chair stands in the middle of the room, as if it had been put there for the purpose. The candle is lit, the water waits in the basin, the plumb hangs from the bracket. I sit.

speaker: player
text: Begin.

speaker: player
text: I am not ready: there is something in the room still unprepared.

speaker: Mina
text: A trance wants three things: a flame to look at, water to listen to, and something that hangs and turns. The candle, the basin, the plumb. I must prepare them before I sit.

speaker: Mina
text: The room goes quiet. What should I do first? In my dream notes there is an order, and I have always obeyed it.

speaker: player
text: Listen to the water lapping in the basin.

speaker: player
text: Rock the chair so that the boards creak.

speaker: player
text: Watch the plumb turn in the candle-light.

speaker: Mina
text: Lap. Lap. A small, slow water, very near, like a hand being passed gently over a face. I forget the room.

speaker: player
text: Rock the chair so that the boards creak.

speaker: player
text: Watch the plumb turn in the candle-light.

speaker: Mina
text: The chair rocks. The boards creak: one, two, a long groan like a ship at her moorings. I am not in the room any more, or only the least part of me is.

speaker: player
text: Watch the plumb turn in the candle-light.

speaker: player
text: Listen to the water again.

speaker: Mina
text: It does not work. The water is only water, the boards only boards, and the plumb a dull weight on a string. I feel foolish and a little relieved. The old order must be kept. I try again.

speaker: Mina
text: The plumb turns: a small bright eye. The candle lengthens into a line. The lapping comes from everywhere, and I am no longer Mina Murray in a rocking-chair, but a listening thing in a very dark place that is also a very quiet one...

speaker: Narrator
text: She did not know it, but it was the first time she had walked into that country on purpose. Years later, in a London drawing-room, the Professor would say: 'Where are you now, Madam Mina? What do you hear?' And she would answer him with the very words she found tonight.

speaker: Mina
text: The barrel drips: a slow, loud plink into a puddle that has no bottom. I put a hand on it and the lapping rises through the wood into my wrist. Water, near and rhythmic. This is the first of the three, as it always is.

speaker: Mina
text: The great timber groans as the hull settles. It has a voice, long and patient, like an old man shifting in his sleep. I listen until I can tell it from my own heartbeat. Wood, the second of the three.

speaker: Mina
text: The cord is thin as a hair and cold as a wire. It leads up the ladder and out of the hold. I cannot see its end.

speaker: player
text: Follow the cord, and listen for what it is tied to.

speaker: player
text: Not yet: I have not listened enough.

speaker: Mina
text: I know better than to climb a thing I have not first listened to. The water, the wood: I must hear them both.

speaker: Mina
text:
I take the cord between two fingers, and it hums. Somewhere far above me a bell is struck; somewhere far away a man is breathing, deep in the dark, and does not know I am here. I open my eyes in Whitby, in the rocking-chair, with the candle burned to a stub, the plumb still, and Lucy sound asleep.

I shall tell no one. Not yet.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Typewriter and the Trance. She kept the ribbon from the Remington and the notebook from Whitby in the same drawer, and neither was ever empty of use. When Dr. Seward's asylum, the Count's Carfax and a ship called the Demeter drew the threads together, she knew the sound of the dark, because she had been listening to it for years.

speaker: Wash
text: Mornin', Mr. Quincey. Dunning's crowd come in the night. Sawed the rail, took the whole remuda, eleven head, and your Santa Fe along with 'em. I got this for sayin' no.

speaker: player
text: Who would dare?

speaker: player
text: Where do I start?

speaker: player
text: Any sugar? She'll want something sweet.

speaker: player
text: Rest, Wash. I'll bring them home.

speaker: Wash
text: Black Jack Dunning, who else? He's been running the brakes of the Brazos since the drought, cattle first, now horses. The rail was filed so quiet the dogs never barked. He fed them first.

speaker: Wash
text: Tracks leave by the east gate onto the range. But don't you ride out with an empty cylinder. Powder's up in the stable somewhere. I hid it out of the damp, so look sharp. Lead you can dig out of the old target post. Cast the lead and charge the cases at the loading bench and you'll have your rounds, and the rope you'll want is in my tack chest.

speaker: Wash
text: Santa Fe'd follow you to Mexico for a lump. Cook keeps it in the tin. Here.

speaker: Maria
text: I heard them, Señor Quincey. A horse blew twice near the barn and I thought it was the wind. I should have gone out. I should have gone out with the lamp.

speaker: player
text: Maria, it was not your doing.

speaker: player
text: Which way did you hear them go?

speaker: Maria
text: You are kind. Eat the corn bread. A man who tracks hungry makes foolish choices.

speaker: Maria
text: East, toward the creek bottoms. That is all I know. And a man laughing. A laugh like a saw.

speaker: Hobbs
text: Morning. You look like a man who lost a horse.

speaker: player
text: Eleven, and my mare. Seen any riders?

speaker: player
text: What about the creek?

speaker: Hobbs
text: Three riders came through at dusk yesterday, driving a string of loose horses. They had a pretty paint mare at the tail, fighting her rope. They headed for the low country. There is only one low country around here.

speaker: Hobbs
text: Wolves are thick down there since the dry year. If you find the channel too deep to cross, there is an old cottonwood snag that leans halfway over it, with a stub on the limb. A good lariat will do the rest. I crossed that way in '71.

speaker: Tomas
text: My grandfather read the grass like a book. 'A man who is hunted leaves marks that are not on the ground,' he said. 'Look at ash, at cloth, at hooves, and wait.'

speaker: player
text: Good advice. Thank you.

speaker: player
text: Where did he learn that?

speaker: Tomas
text: From the Comanches, who stole his horses. Everyone learns from whoever is stealing their horses.

speaker: Quincey
text: Three trails leave the water-hole: north to the Cap Rock, east to the cottonwood bottoms, south across the mesquite flat. Dunning's men and my mare took one of them. I can't afford to guess.

speaker: player
text: North, over the Cap Rock.

speaker: player
text: South, across the mesquite flat.

speaker: player
text: East, down to the cottonwood bottoms.

speaker: player
text: East? I would like some proof from the hoofprints first.

speaker: player
text: East? I would like some proof from the ashes first.

speaker: player
text: East? I would like some proof from the thorn bush first.

speaker: Quincey
text: Nothing up there but bare stone. A rustler doesn't drive eleven horses where there is no water and no cover.

speaker: Quincey
text: Mesquite would flay the horses' hides. Not a single hair on those thorns. Whoever went through here didn't drive horses through it.

speaker: Quincey
text: A hunch is a poor thing to ride on. There are three signs on this ground: the hoofprints at the water-hole, the dead camp-fire, and a bush with something snagged on it. Read all three, then choose.

speaker: Quincey
text: Hoofprints turning east to low ground, cottonwood ash, canebrake burrs on red flannel. All three agree: the bottoms. They think they are safe in the reeds. I'll show them different.

speaker: Rustler
text: (snores) ... Jack says the paint is worth four hundred in Fort Worth. Four hundred dollars... (snores)

speaker: player
text: Tip his hat over his eyes and go on.

speaker: player
text: Listen a while longer.

speaker: Rustler
text: ... don't tell Pike I lost his spur ... damn river ... (snores)

speaker: Dunning
text: Well, if it ain't the Morris boy, come all the way down to the bottoms for a pony. Sit. Have a drink. The mare's a fine one. I may keep her.

speaker: player
text: Give her up, Dunning. Ride away and I'll let you.

speaker: player
text: Then I'll take her myself.

speaker: Dunning
text: Ride away? We are three to your one, and you are in my camp. You come mighty bold for a rancher's son.

speaker: Dunning
text: (his eyes narrow) Pike's spur. You've been down at the ford, then. Well. That settles it. Nobody leaves who's seen the bottoms.

speaker: Dunning
text: My iron! You went through my... (his hand slides toward his belt) That is a hanging matter, Morris. Once I put you under the cottonwoods, there's no one to say it.

speaker: Quincey
text: I came for my mare, and for the others. You can hand them over, or I'll take them out of your hands.

speaker: Quincey
text: Easy, girl. It's me. It's Quincey.

speaker: player
text: Whistle the three notes she knows.

speaker: player
text: Ride her out of here, now.

speaker: player
text: What stops me from riding her out?

speaker: Quincey
text: Her ears swing round. She knows. She has known me since she was a wet-legged foal and I was a boy of fifteen with a bucket of oats. But there is a raw wild look in her eye. The picket has galled her, and the fire has frightened her.

speaker: Quincey
text: Dunning and his men still hold the camp. Her picket-line has to be cut, and she's too wild with fright to carry a man. A lump of sugar would settle her faster than any words of mine.

speaker: Quincey
text: Up she comes under me. We go out of the hollow at a gallop, with the wind in our faces, and the horses of the remuda running behind us, as if there'd never been any other life.

speaker: Narrator
text: One year later. The Pampas of Argentina, winter 1885. Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, my friends, had asked me to hunt with them in the south. Santa Fe came too.

speaker: Arthur
text: Quincey! Come and sit. Seward says the fire will do us good. Anselmo says it will bring the bats. They cannot both be right.

speaker: player
text: What are you cleaning that for?

speaker: player
text: Do you hear the horses?

speaker: player
text: How is the hunt?

speaker: Arthur
text: My father says a gentleman should never let a gun go unattended for a night. My father has never been within a thousand miles of the Pampas.

speaker: Arthur
text: They have been restless since sunset. Anselmo says it is nothing. Anselmo says it is nothing the way a man says 'it is nothing' while looking at the sky.

speaker: Arthur
text: We have seen rhea, guanaco and a puma at a distance. We have not seen what Anselmo keeps warning me about, which I suspect is the only sensible policy.

speaker: Seward
text: I am writing up the day's notes. Tell me, Quincey, did you know that Darwin recorded bats biting horses on this very continent? A small incision, and the animal bleeds a little at the neck.

speaker: player
text: A little? That doesn't sound serious.

speaker: player
text: Have you any bandage to spare?

speaker: Seward
text: No. Darwin says the horse is only inconvenienced. But Darwin did not say how many nights it might continue. I would not leave a horse uncovered.

speaker: Seward
text: A roll, from my own bag. I'd keep the rest for Arthur, who thinks pain is a form of bad manners.

speaker: Anselmo
text: Señor. The horses are afraid. They smell the thing that comes. You see how the stars are clear? It is a clear night. A night for the vampiro.

speaker: player
text: What can a man do against a bat?

speaker: player
text: The bats here are only bats.

speaker: Anselmo
text: Three things, Señor. First, smoke: the vampiro hates it. A fire of something that smokes thick, thistle, not dung. Second, light: a lantern hung high, so he will not come out of the dark. Third, a cloth over the neck of the animal, a cloth it knows, because the bat goes for the bare skin, always the neck.

speaker: Anselmo
text: Bats, Señor, are small. The thing that comes here, when it comes, has no size at all. I have seen a steer drained white by morning, without a mark you could put a finger in. (He crosses himself.) Smoke, light, cloth.

speaker: Arthur
text: A story, Quincey. We have an hour before bed and nothing to look at but stars. Tell us one of yours.

speaker: player
text: The night I bought Santa Fe.

speaker: player
text: The Marquesas, and the shark that ate my hat.

speaker: player
text: Titicaca, and the boat that sank in a calm.

speaker: Quincey
text: She was a three-day foal in a Comanche pony-herd, and I was fifteen, with six dollars and a tin of sardines. The old chief said the foal was marked for a short life, born under a falling star. I said I would take the risk. I've had her ever since. The one horse in the world who knows what I am thinking before I do.

speaker: Quincey
text: We were becalmed off the Marquesas for eleven days. I'd lost my hat to a shark by Tuesday and my temper to a missionary by Friday. But the pearls... boys, you never saw such pearls. And not one of them mine.

speaker: Quincey
text: The boat sank in a flat calm, boys, at four thousand feet above the sea. I never learned why, and the Indians never told. But I learned that you can swim in cold water as long as you like, if the alternative is Bolivia.

speaker: Seward
text: Excellent, Quincey. Though if you ever write it down, I will insist on correcting the medical details.

speaker: Arthur
text: To Quincey! And to the friends one makes when one has no business being friends.

speaker: Quincey
text: (Santa Fe lays her head on my shoulder, nostrils wide.) You feel it too, girl. Something's wrong in the air.

speaker: player
text: Stroke her neck.

speaker: Quincey
text: Her skin shivers under my hand. She has never been like this, not at the pass, not in the storm off Cape Horn. If I were a praying man I would start now.

speaker: Quincey
text: The moon is as bright as a coin. The grass is tall enough to hide a man. I've sat watch over cattle in a norther, over a sick friend in Panama. Tonight I'll sit over a horse.

speaker: player
text: Begin the vigil.

speaker: player
text: What have I forgotten?

speaker: Quincey
text: Anselmo's three things: smoke at the lines (the pit and thistle), a lantern hung high on the post and filled with oil, and a cloth over Santa Fe's neck. I carry no lantern or oil with me: both are back at the fire.

speaker: Quincey
text: Smoke across the lines, light on the post, the blanket over her withers. I sit with my back to a picket-post and the Winchester across my knees. An hour goes by. Then another. The horses go still all at once, the way a room goes still when someone enters. Something moves against the moon.

speaker: Quincey
text: She doesn't shy when I come. Her head drops against my chest. The wound at her neck is two small punctures, clean, almost tidy. The blanket was soaked through.

speaker: player
text: Sit with her.

speaker: Quincey
text: Seward says she's lost too much and there is nothing to be done. Arthur turns away. I stay on my knees in the grass beside her, my hand on her neck, and I talk to her about nothing. The ranch. The Brazos. The sugar-tin.

speaker: Quincey
text: At sunrise she gives one long breath, like a horse settling for the night, and lays her head down in the grass. They say a horse goes to grass when it dies. She does not move again.

speaker: Seward
text: Two punctures, three-eighths of an inch apart, and no tearing. Bat teeth, I'd say, though I've never seen a bat bleed a horse white in a single night. Quincey, what do you make of the grass?

speaker: player
text: A bat did this, Jack, plain and simple.

speaker: player
text: Snake. A big one.

speaker: player
text: This was no ordinary bat. I've read the ground.

speaker: player
text: I haven't read the ground yet.

speaker: player
text: I haven't read the ground yet.

speaker: player
text: I haven't read the ground yet.

speaker: Seward
text: Perhaps. But a bat takes a thimbleful, not a mare. And a bat doesn't leave a ring in the grass. Look about you.

speaker: Seward
text: A snake, with two fangs so exactly paired, in a horse that was watched all night? No. Nothing slithered across the grass.

speaker: Seward
text: Then do. There are marks in the grass and I am no tracker. Look at the ring, the earth, and the prints near the posts.

speaker: Quincey
text: A ring where something stood and rose. Black earth carried across a continent. A line of bare human prints that begin at the ring and end at the picket-posts. The bat was only the shape it chose for the last part of the trip.

speaker: Seward
text: You are suggesting a thing that is not a bat, that comes and goes in the shape of one. I am a man of science, Quincey. And I find, to my surprise, that I do not wish to argue.

speaker: Arthur
text: I held her rope, Quincey. All night, not twenty feet away, and I saw nothing. I heard nothing. I'm sorry.

speaker: player
text: It was not your fault, Art.

speaker: player
text: It was there and none of us saw it. That's what I mean to remember.

speaker: Arthur
text: You are kinder than I deserve. If you ever want a man at your back... I will be there. Wherever it is.

speaker: Arthur
text: Then we remember it together. Whatever it was, we'll know it if it comes again.

speaker: Quincey
text: A mound of red clay under a cross of picket-posts. I stand with my hat in my hand. I think of a foal in the Comanche herd under a falling star, and a boy with a tin of sardines.

speaker: player
text: Lay the sheath on the grave, then take it up again.

speaker: player
text: I haven't understood what took her yet.

speaker: Quincey
text: I'll not leave this place until I know what to call the thing that did it. Seward is by the posts, and the ground is still readable.

speaker: Quincey
text: Santa Fe's bridle and my bowie's sheath: I laid one on the other, as a kind of promise. The sheath she once bit through, on the Brazos, in a fit of spite. I take it up again. 'Whatever you were,' I say to the empty grass, 'I'll know you the next time.'

speaker: Narrator
text: Years later, in London, a Dutch doctor with a pointed beard spoke of bats at a window and a girl who grew pale. I did not need him to say the word. I said it myself. I had already seen it on the Pampas, and I had not forgotten.

speaker: Hodge
text: Morning, Mr. Renfield. Slept? Your tray's there. The doctor says if you're quiet this morning he'll see you in his study. Well. Are you going to be quiet?

speaker: player
text: I am quite myself, Mr. Hodge. A man of sense, I hope, and a gentleman. May I be let out to the day-room?

speaker: player
text: Let me out! Every hour you keep me here, a thousand lives go by and none of them are mine!

speaker: Hodge
text: Ah, there you are. Well said, sir, and well said again. That's the voice they ought to put in the books. Come along, then. Mind the step; I'll leave the door off the latch. Dr. Seward'll want a word.

speaker: Hodge
text: Now then. NOW then. That's the other voice, is it? Steady, Mr. Renfield, steady, I've got you. There, there, there. A turn in the wet sheet and you'll be fit for company. Come on. Out you come; I'm sorry for it.

speaker: Hodge
text: Spoon? Gone again, I'll be bound. If you ever find it, it's no business of mine, but it'd be well to look under things. And you'd never use a spoon for anything wicked, sir. You'd be the first.

speaker: Hodge
text: Mr. Renfield. Keep to the day-room if you please. The doctor's in his study. And Cook'll want to see you, I fancy; she's had a soft spot since the business with the mice.

speaker: player
text: Where is the garden key kept?

speaker: player
text: Who is on the night round, Mr. Hodge?

speaker: Hodge
text: Garden key? I lost it, sir, three weeks back. Hung it on a hook in the scullery and it was gone by dinner. Dr. Seward does not know, so you'll oblige me by not knowing either. Between ourselves, I think the mice have it.

speaker: Hodge
text: Blunt. Ten and two. He walks out to the far wall, stops to light his pipe under the lamp there, and walks back. Same as he's done for ten years. Not a man for surprises. If he ever turned round before the pipe was lit, I'd call a doctor.

speaker: Hodge
text: Ho, who's that. Mr. Renfield? Back to your bed, sir. I'm on till six and the Doctor says no wandering after dark.

speaker: player
text: A drop of something, Mr. Hodge, for your nerves. I could not drink it myself. You have been so kind.

speaker: Hodge
text: None of us can, sir. Go on, now. Back to your room, and I'll bring you a cup of cocoa.

speaker: Hodge
text: Well. Well, that's very handsome of you, sir. Just the one, mind. For the damp. I never saw you do a mean thing in all the time I've known you, not once, whatever they write in the book...

speaker: Mr. Quill
text: Seven, seven, seven. One, two, three. Do you know, Mr. Renfield, that in this room there are nine lamps? I counted them as a boy of ten at my mother's. They all go out at the same hour, and still I count.

speaker: player
text: How many beds are in this room?

speaker: player
text: And windows?

speaker: player
text: Why do you count?

speaker: Mr. Quill
text: Seven beds. Seven. You'd say eight, because of the one by the stair, but it isn't a bed. It's a bier.

speaker: Mr. Quill
text: Three, with bars, and a fourth that is only a painting of one. The doctor calls them 'inventory'. He puts them in his book in the order: beds, windows, lamps. A tidy man, the doctor.

speaker: Mr. Quill
text: Because if I stop, sir, I begin to think about the things that can't be counted. And those are what put me in here.

speaker: Mr. Ashby
text: Renfield. You were once Mr. Renfield of the firm, I think. A good house. There is a crest on your handkerchief, and in my day we did not carry the crest of a bad house in our pockets.

speaker: player
text: I was a man of business once, Mr. Ashby. My father kept a good library.

speaker: player
text: Do you hear the voice, Mr. Ashby?

speaker: Mr. Ashby
text: I knew it. One can tell a man of breeding by what he does with the cutlery. Whatever they say of you, you have never once been vulgar. Hold to that, Renfield. It is the only furniture we are permitted to bring in with us.

speaker: Mr. Ashby
text: The voice? My dear fellow. Everyone in this house hears a voice. Mine tells me the price of consols. Yours, I think, promises you something. Be careful what you accept from a voice that has never once been in need.

speaker: Renfield
text: The ward inventory, under glass, in Dr. Seward's hand: 'Beds, 7. Windows (barred), 3. Lamps, 9. Clock, 1 (defective).' And below it, in a fainter pencil, 'Sugar ration: Press, key by dial. Do not tell R.'

speaker: Renfield
text: Seven. Three. Nine. In that order, beds, windows, lamps. I never forget a figure. It is the last sane thing about me.

speaker: Renfield
text: The linen-press, with its three brass wheels. The sugar ration is in there, and with it the whole of my little world of flies.

speaker: Renfield
text: The wheels turn and stop. The press does not budge. An error of arithmetic; I will not make another.

speaker: Renfield
text: Seven. Three. Nine. The wheels click, the latch drops and there it is, on a blue paper, fine as snow: a lump of sugar. Just one. Dr. Seward counts them. I count him.

speaker: Renfield
text: A case-book open on the blotter: 'R. M. Renfield, aet. 59. Zoophagous (life-eating) maniac. Sanguine temperament, great physical strength, morbid selfishness. Collects: flies (sugar), spiders, sparrows, a cat. Keeps accounts. Perfectly lucid on matters of family and law.'

speaker: Renfield
text: 'His dread of the unseen is genuine. He does not lie. He says a Master will come for the lives, and that he has been promised a great number. I do not know what to make of a delusion so well-regulated. He is the only patient who thanks me for my notes.'

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Renfield. Good morning. Sit, if you wish. I confess I did not expect to see you out and about so early. You look, if I may say, like a man who has not slept.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: My notes? I note what I see. You collect, you count, and you cannot be argued out of the account. I find it rather admirable and I do not know what to do with it.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Moved? Where? This is a good house, as houses go, and I have no other bed.

speaker: player
text: He is coming, doctor. I feel him through the wall. I beg you, send me away before he comes! [Raving]

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: I see. 'He is coming.' It is a symptom, Renfield, I wish it were not; I wish you could say it to me without rolling your eyes. I will note it. Come back when you can tell me what you mean in plain figures.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Your ledger. Good God, man. Every fly, every sparrow, in a clerk's hand. It is a perfectly rational document, and I have never read a sadder one. Very well. I shall move you to the quiet wing on Monday, and I want no more of this 'Master'. Take this note to the day-room; Hodge will see it honoured.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: You are the man who raised his voice at Hodge this morning, Renfield. But this ledger is the first honest thing you have shown me. Very well, Monday, the quiet wing. Hodge will keep an eye on you; you will not mind.

speaker: Dr. Seward
text: Do not thank me yet. Monday is Monday. Try to be quiet tonight, Renfield. It is a thing I can say to you without writing it down.

speaker: Mrs. Pargeter
text: Mr. Renfield! Get along with you, out from under my feet. Though if you've the wit for it, I've a riddle. Sing a song of sixpence, a pocket full of rye; four and twenty blackbirds, baked in a...?

speaker: player
text: ...pie.

speaker: player
text: ...cage.

speaker: player
text: ...net, with the wings still moving.

speaker: player
text: Why do you keep the cat so fat, Mrs. Pargeter?

speaker: Mrs. Pargeter
text: Ha. No, no, no. Not that. The nursery rhyme, dear. I had a brother who told it the wrong way too, God rest him, and they put him in a place like this one.

speaker: Mrs. Pargeter
text: He earns it, the beast. He's the bravest in the house, sir. Eats whatever the garden sends, and sleeps in the warm. I keep him fat so he doesn't need to hunt.

speaker: Mrs. Pargeter
text: ...Baked in a pie! There, you've a head on your shoulders. Now: Doctor says you're not to have anything stronger than cocoa, and I say a man who can finish a rhyme can have a drop in a cup for his nerves. Take it, hide it, and do not tell the Doctor that Cook says so.

speaker: Renfield
text: The cot, and the grey blanket. It is early afternoon and the whole house is waiting for something.

speaker: Renfield
text: A prudent man gets his house in order before the dark: a key to the garden, a drop of brandy for the keeper. And a ward to wait for, only when I hold them all.

speaker: Renfield
text: I lie down and let the afternoon pass over me. When I wake the lamps are lit and the house is quiet. Somewhere a bell strikes ten.

speaker: Narrator
text: That night, at Purfleet.

speaker: Renfield
text: I crouch behind the water-butt, in the wet. The night-man's lantern comes along the gravel, swinging. He is walking out to the far wall.

speaker: Renfield
text: I get three strides before the lantern swings round. 'Who's that?' I am back behind the butt with my heart in my mouth. He turns again. The lantern goes on.

speaker: Renfield
text: I wait, and wait. He does not go in; he is on the bench with his pipe. It is a long, cold, wet quarter of an hour. Nothing has changed.

speaker: Renfield
text: He reaches the far wall, stops under the lamp, bends to his pipe, a match flaring in his cupped hands. His back is to me. I cross twelve yards of gravel in my stockinged feet, and not a stone speaks.

speaker: The Voice
text: Renfield. You have come. You have kept my books faithfully, and I have kept my promise. I told you: lives. Not flies, not spiders, not a bird in the grass: lives. Great ones. Do you hold something for me?

speaker: Renfield
text: I tear a clean page from the back of the ledger and write, in the clerk's hand I have never lost: 'Doctor, he is real. The box is in the chapel. Do not come alone. Garlic, a cross, and the sunlight. I am sorry for the trouble. R. M. R.' I tuck it beneath the candle where the morning will find it.

speaker: The Voice
text: Ahh. Yes. Good servant. Give it me, and the bird shall be the first of many. Seven, then seventy, then seven thousand. You have only to be faithful.

speaker: player
text: ...No. Wait.

speaker: Renfield
text: I do what I have done a hundred times. It is a small, warm, brief thing and it is over before the voice has finished its blessing. And then there is no blessing: only the pale smell of earth, and a feather on my thumb, and the silence of a house that has taken what it asked for and will give nothing back.

speaker: The Voice
text: You dare. You, who ate a thousand little lives in my name! You are mine, Renfield. You are a vessel, a thing I fill. What is one sparrow to a man who has eaten ten thousand?

speaker: Renfield
text: The word 'Renfield' goes through the chapel like a coin on stone. The voice thins. I cross to the broken window, open my hands, and the sparrow shakes itself once, and flies out of my fingers and over the wall into the grey. It does not look back. It is the best bookkeeping I have ever done.

speaker: Renfield
text: I roar. I beat the lid until the voice is a sound like paper tearing, and when I come to myself I am on my knees with split hands, and the sparrow is still alive, trembling in the crook of my arm. I lift it to the window. It goes, in a flurry. I laugh, I think, or weep.

speaker: Seward
text: The phonograph waits, the wax cylinder in its place, the horn turned toward me like an ear.

speaker: Seward
text: It records a voice, so that I do not need to write by candlelight. I have kept a diary since I first saw a ward, but I cannot yet say a thing aloud and let it stand. The machine keeps its counsel better than I do.

speaker: Seward
text: 'Twenty-fifth May. Lucy Westenra has refused me. She was gentle, and clear, and entirely right. I do not blame her, nor Arthur, nor myself, which is a nuisance, since a man wants someone to blame. I shall not sleep. I shall dose myself with chloral, in the proper measure, and be a better doctor for it.'

speaker: Seward
text: I let the cylinder run out. The voice that comes back is thinner than my own, and braver.

speaker: Seward
text: Dawn comes grey over Purfleet. The dispensary is a black ruin of one shelf, Pettit is bargaining with his conscience in the ward, and Renfield sleeps in Room 12 with his sugar untouched. I wind the cylinder and begin.

speaker: Seward
text: 'Case notes, the twenty-sixth. A night in which three things went wrong and none was the worst. I used judgment where I might have used force, medicine where I might have used a stick, and nerve, I hope, where I might have run. I write this partly for the Board, but chiefly for myself, who must not forget it.'

speaker: Seward
text: 'I shall write to Van Helsing in Amsterdam tomorrow. He taught me that a doctor's chief duty is to doubt himself carefully. I shall tell him that I doubted, and went on.'

speaker: Seward
text: Lucy's note, on thick cream paper in her round, schoolgirl hand. It has been folded and unfolded until the creases are soft.

speaker: Lucy (letter)
text: 'Dear Dr. Seward, I cannot say what you wish. You have been kind and gentle and clever, and I would not lose your friendship for the world. But I am promised, in my heart, to another, and it would be cruel to let you hope. Please do not think the less of me. Lucy.'

speaker: Seward
text: I stood in the Hillingham drawing-room with my hat in my hand and she said it more kindly than I deserved. I said I understood. I said I wished her happy. I said it twice, to be sure that I had.

speaker: player
text: Burn the note.

speaker: player
text: Keep it. A doctor should keep his case-notes.

speaker: Seward
text: I hold it to the candle. And I cannot. I fold it back along the creases and put it in the drawer, which is a different kind of weakness, but a more honest one.

speaker: Seward
text: I shall keep it. It is no use to anyone, which is the best reason I know for keeping a thing.

speaker: Seward
text: The armchair, with a dent in it the shape of my sleeplessness.

speaker: Seward
text: I have the draught measured, the letters read, and Renfield's secret half understood. If I am to sit up with any of it, it may as well be tonight.

speaker: Seward
text: A bundle of letters from Amsterdam in a crabbed, forceful hand. Van Helsing, my old master.

speaker: Van Helsing (letter)
text: 'My dear John. On the chloral, remember the three lines I taught you. Fifteen grains for a woman or a frail man; twenty for a strong man in his full strength; never more than thirty for anyone; and sixty is not a sedative but a funeral. Weigh twice. A sleepy patient is a patient; a sleeping doctor is a catastrophe.'

speaker: Van Helsing (letter)
text: 'John, you doubt too much, and then you believe too much, and the middle you never visit. Believe nothing because I say it; doubt nothing because you have not seen it. Write it all down, and then look at what is written. Madness is often a theory the world has not yet been told.'

speaker: Van Helsing (letter)
text: 'You thanked me again in your last. I do not recall that winter's dying, John. I recall only that you sat for three nights with a man who was nothing to you, and that I could not leave a fever to do what you had not allowed it. You owe me nothing. But if you wish to pay, then be to some other sleepless fool what I was to you.'

speaker: Hennessey
text: Good afternoon, sir. All quiet, bar Mr. Pym, who is taking an interest in the weather again.

speaker: player
text: Tell me about the ward.

speaker: player
text: Why is the ward clock stopped?

speaker: player
text: Who keeps the dispensary key?

speaker: player
text: Can you write the ward log tonight, if I am busy?

speaker: Hennessey
text: Mr. Pym, the watchmaker; Miss Vane, who writes letters to a man who died in India; old Mr. Greer, who sits in the garden talking to the sea. And Number Twelve, sir, who you know. All good as gold, so long as the weather holds.

speaker: Hennessey
text: Ah. That was Mrs. Pym's clock. Stopped at ten past three, the hour she went, and he's never allowed it touched. Not once. If you tell him you know what the hour was, I think he might be persuaded. But only just.

speaker: Hennessey
text: Safe, sir. I've put it where Mr. Pym would never let anyone look. That's the safest place in the house.

speaker: Hennessey
text: I'd be glad to, sir, but I can't, being no scholar. I sign with my mark, and a bad one. Mother couldn't spare me to the school. The log's best left to Nurse Dowling.

speaker: Mr. Pym
text: Don't touch it. Don't touch the clock. It is quite right. It has been right ever since.

speaker: player
text: Why is it stopped, Mr. Pym?

speaker: player
text: It stopped at ten past three, the hour your wife died.

speaker: player
text: Thank you, Mr. Pym.

speaker: Mr. Pym
text: Because it is my clock, doctor, and it has told the time quite long enough.

speaker: Mr. Pym
text: ...Who told you? Hennessey. He is a kind man and a poor liar. Ten past three, in the morning. I had the watch in my hand, and I counted her breaths, and they stopped. I was a watchmaker forty years and I could not mend that.

speaker: player
text: It need not stay stopped. A clock that runs again is not a clock that forgets.

speaker: Mr. Pym
text: Hm. Hm. Perhaps. Here, doctor: the winding key. Wind it, and set it, and then give me back the key. I am not ready to hold it. But I would like to hear it tick.

speaker: Miss Vane
text: Dr. Seward. I am writing to Edmund, as you see. He is a poor correspondent, but a very faithful one.

speaker: player
text: How is the ward at night, Miss Vane?

speaker: player
text: Who is Edmund?

speaker: Miss Vane
text: He was to be my husband. He is in India. Mrs. Pritchard tells me he is dead, but I am sure that is a mistake of the post.

speaker: Miss Vane
text: Oh, quiet enough. The boy comes in at night, you know, the one with the violet fingers. He sits in the dispensary with the lamp and practises writing a name on the back of old labels, over and over. I thought it a love-letter. It is rather a long way to travel for a love-letter, to practise one signature.

speaker: Mr. Greer
text: Sit, doctor. I was mate on the old Lizzie out of Sunderland, forty years back. D'you know what happens when spirit catches in a hold?

speaker: player
text: Tell me.

speaker: player
text: What do you see out there?

speaker: Mr. Greer
text: You never throw water on it. The spirit floats and spreads it, burning, to every plank. We wet the blankets and smothered it. That's all there is to it, doctor: soak the blanket, drop it on, and lean. Mind you, I've forgotten my own wife's name, but I never forgot that.

speaker: Mr. Greer
text: A ship, doctor. She will come in out of the east with a dead crew and a dead master lashed to her wheel. Mind you, we all know that story. Do you? Well, then.

speaker: Pettit
text: Doctor. Shall I do the dispensary jars again, sir?

speaker: player
text: Where do you learn your Latin, Pettit?

speaker: player
text: Pettit, I have a slip for sixty grains of morphia. Written in my name.

speaker: Pettit
text: From the labels, sir, and from the dispenser. He lets me copy the prescriptions so as I learn the hands. My mother's very ill, sir, in Barking. She cannot be left alone.

speaker: Pettit
text: I don't... what slip, sir?

speaker: player
text: The ink is violet, and Miss Vane saw you practising. Hennessey cannot write, and Mrs. Dowling was on the ward. Only one person could have done it.

speaker: player
text: Someone has been practising my hand, Pettit. Who might it be?

speaker: Pettit
text: I don't know, sir. I swear I don't. Perhaps Mr. Hennessey. Perhaps...

speaker: Pettit
text: ...It was for my mother, sir. The doctor in Barking has given her up and the pain is... she begged me. I thought sixty grains would carry her through a month. I tried it three times before I could do your S. Then I couldn't, and I started the fire to burn the slip, and it caught the ether...

speaker: Seward
text: I do the thing the law requires, which is to say, I write to the Board and let a boy of seventeen pay for what a doctor ought to have prevented. I do not feel clean. I do not think I am meant to.

speaker: Seward
text: I make a bargain: a proper prescription, signed in my own hand, to be dispensed by the dispenser and no one else; a bed for his mother in the cottage hospital at Purfleet; a boy who works off the damage in the dispensary under Hennessey's eye. It is not in any book of regulations. It is, I think, in one of Van Helsing's.

speaker: Nurse Dowling
text: Doctor, thank God. Number Twelve is empty; the grating was forced from within. Hennessey's gone out after him. And there's smoke in the dispensary.

speaker: player
text: Where could Renfield have gone?

speaker: player
text: Who was last in the dispensary?

speaker: Nurse Dowling
text: The garden, sir. He always goes to the garden wall, to look at Carfax. If I may say so, doctor, leave the stick at home. Three men would be needed.

speaker: Nurse Dowling
text: Pettit, to sweep. And me. And I don't write, sir, except the log, and my hand's not a bit like yours.

speaker: Seward
text: A prescription slip, half-burnt at the corner. 'Morph. mur. gr. lx. Pro J. Pettit.' The body of the slip is clerkly. The signature, 'J. Seward', is a very careful forgery.

speaker: Seward
text: The ink is violet, the clerk's copying ink, which stains the fingers for a week. Sixty grains of morphia: enough to kill three men. The signature is perfect, and somewhere a hand has practised my S fifty times to get it.

speaker: Seward
text: The brass scales and the tray of weights. I have measured chloral on them a hundred times. I will not do it by guesswork tonight.

speaker: Seward
text: For Renfield. If he breaks out, and the garden wall keeps its mortar poorly, a draught that is neither too weak nor too strong may be the difference between a man put to bed and a man put in the ground. I need both chloral and a clean glass of water, and I need to know the right number.

speaker: Seward
text: Ten grains. For Renfield, who is strong and wakeful, it would simply make him cross. I pour it away.

speaker: Seward
text: Thirty grains: the limit, not the dose. It might put him down; it might stop his heart. I pour it away.

speaker: Seward
text: Sixty grains is not a sedative but a funeral. I set it down before I have thought about it, and wash my hands.

speaker: Seward
text: Twenty grains for a strong man in his full strength, as Van Helsing wrote. I weigh it twice and dissolve it in the water. Clear, bitter-sweet, innocent. A bottle I hope never to use.

speaker: Seward
text: The poison register, a ledger of every grain that has left this room, in my hand and the dispenser's.

speaker: Seward
text: 'R. M. Renfield, aet. 59. Sanguine; great physical strength; fourteen stone; sleeps ill. Chloral, if needed, to the full strong-man dose, to be witnessed by the attendant.' I wrote that three months ago, and have been careful with it since.

speaker: Seward
text: Hennessey's diet ledger for Room 12, his big round hand, week after week. I have read it a dozen times, but not as a series.

speaker: Seward
text: 'Flies, caught on sugar, 3-4 a day. Mr. R. keeps them in a jar, to hold the lives, in his own words. Eats none for first fortnight. Third week: eats them. Says they are quite delicious, and so full of life.'

speaker: Seward
text: 'Spiders. He feeds the flies to spiders, and swallows the spiders. Says: one spider is worth a hundred flies, for the life in it.'

speaker: Seward
text: 'Sparrows. He tamed one. Wanted a cat to eat the sparrows. Now keeps them, begs for more, and one morning there is a heap of feathers. He says he should like a cat, for the spider's life is little, and the sparrow's is more. Not a word to the doctor.'

speaker: Seward
text: 'A kitten, brought by the housemaid. Wanted by him, begged for. The kitten went into his room on Tuesday and came out on Wednesday as a cap-ribbon of fur and a smear. Mr. R. ill, afterwards, as if he had been sick with grief.' I have written nothing under it. I do not need to.

speaker: Renfield
text: Doctor Seward. I am quite at your service, and as sane as any man in England. Might I trouble you for another saucer of sugar?

speaker: player
text: How are you sleeping, Mr. Renfield?

speaker: player
text: Tell me about the flies.

speaker: player
text: I have read the ledger. I think I understand what the flies were for.

speaker: Renfield
text: Poorly, Doctor. A man in my position has so much to keep track of. I find I count, and the counting does not stop.

speaker: Renfield
text: Flies are lives, Doctor. Small lives, but each a life. I keep them, as you keep your patients. Is it so different?

speaker: Seward
text: You do not eat the flies because you are hungry, Mr. Renfield. You eat them because each one is a bit of life, and you wish to gather more life into yourself. The spider for the flies, the sparrow for the spiders, and the cat for the sparrows. Each is a step up a ladder. And what did you wish to be at the top?

speaker: Renfield
text: ...Doctor. You have a cleverer head than I took you for. Life, Doctor. 'The blood is the life.' I am a collector of it, in a small way. You see how the system works. I am not at all mad; I am merely early.

speaker: Seward
text: I write that down, in the ledger, in my own hand: 'Zoophagous mania, systematised; the patient believes life may be taken in by eating living things; progression from small to large.' It is a good case. It is a very bad case. I wonder what he is waiting for, that he must be early.

speaker: Seward
text: Renfield, hunched under the wall, eyes on the moon. I take a step and he turns his head, and for a moment I see the whole ladder of lives written on his face.

speaker: player
text: Mr. Renfield. You are not hungry. You are afraid of being too late.

speaker: Renfield
text: ...Afraid? Yes. Of being late. Doctor, you are the first who has ever said so. I thought there was time. I kept the flies, and the spiders, and now the wall is so high. Something is coming. Something is coming and I should like to be tidy, if it comes.

speaker: Seward
text: 'Come in out of the dew, Mr. Renfield. Number Twelve is warm, and the sugar is still there. We shall be tidy together.' He lets me take his arm, and I walk him in across the gravel while the moon sets behind Carfax.

speaker: Renfield
text: Doctor. Forgive me. I was not myself, which is perhaps a mercy. I should like the sugar, in the morning.

speaker: player
text: You shall have it.

speaker: Renfield
text: And Doctor: I was truthful, about being early. Be a little early yourself.

speaker: Latin note
text: 'Mortuus non est qui nocte surgit. Per diem in terra sua iacet. Ligno cor transfige, caput abscinde, os allio imple.' Beneath: 'And beware of the sacrament, A. - it is a thing, not a sentiment.'

speaker: player
text: 'He who rises at night is not dead. By day he sleeps in his own earth. Pierce the heart with iron, burn the body, fill the mouth with earth.'

speaker: player
text: 'He who rises at night is not dead. By day he lies in his own earth. Pierce the heart with wood, cut off the head, fill the mouth with garlic.'

speaker: player
text: 'The dead do not rise at night. By night he lies in his own earth. Bind the heart with wood, hide the head, fill the mouth with salt.'

speaker: Van Helsing
text: No. 'Ligno' is wood and 'transfige' is pierce; 'os allio imple' will not turn into salt however much I wish it. And 'per diem' is by day. A careless translation could get a man killed.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Wood, not iron; day, not night; garlic, not earth. It is exact, and it is horrible, and my friend Arminius has not troubled himself to say how he came to know.

speaker: Arminius's letters
text: Three letters, tied with black tape. The paper is Hungarian, the hand beautiful, the content not.

speaker: Arminius
text: 'My dear Abraham, you ask who he was. A Voivode of the Wallachian line, a general, a statesman, a man of cunning and of iron. Beaten at Kossovo and, they say, betrayed. In the Szekelys' tales his blood is the river of a nation. I do not believe a word, my friend, but I have never found his grave.'

speaker: Arminius
text: 'The tales speak of a school: the Scholomance, in the mountains over the Hermannstadt lake, where the Devil himself was said to take ten scholars in seven, and keep the tenth as his due. They learned the language of beasts, the weather, the use of thunder. One of those scholars, the Szekelys say, was of this Voivode's blood.'

speaker: Arminius
text: 'Now a practical matter. Pfarrer Albrecht of Kirchdorf, in Styria, has written me about a grave in his churchyard. The village will not let him open it. I cannot go, being old and immovable. You are neither. Go prepared, Abraham, and do not go to disprove it. Go to find out.'

speaker: My wife
text: You are late, Abraham, which means you have found a theory. Tell me, quickly, before Mevrouw Bakker scolds us both.

speaker: player
text: How are you today?

speaker: player
text: Tell me about the little coat.

speaker: player
text: Is there anything you need?

speaker: My wife
text: The doctor says my lungs are 'no worse'. I told him that was not a diagnosis, it was a courtesy. I watched the skaters today. One boy fell and got up again. I counted it a sign.

speaker: My wife
text: I began it in March, for a boy who would have been four. I stop when I think I will finish it. Do not look at me like a case. It is only wool.

speaker: My wife
text: You are the cleverest man in Amsterdam, my dear, and you cannot save a child who has already gone. But you will save somebody's. I think that is why you read the heresies.

speaker: My wife
text: Yes. There is a silver cross in the cradle, under the wool. It was his christening gift from Arminius. It is made for a small hand. I would rather it went into the world doing a work than lay in a cradle. Take it, Abraham. Take it for the next one.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: I sit by her until the lamp needs trimming. We do not talk of the child. We talk of Boerhaave and her father's boat and whether the ice will hold until Sunday. It is the best afternoon of the winter.

speaker: Mevrouw Bakker
text: She ate two spoons of the barley broth, Herr Professor. Two! If you could see your face, you would think it was the end of the world.

speaker: player
text: Mevrouw, I need garlic for a ward.

speaker: player
text: What do you make of all this, Mevrouw?

speaker: Mevrouw Bakker
text: A ward? Is that what they call it at the University? My grandmother hung garlic in Zeeland to keep the plague away. Take the best braid, Professor, and put it where it does the most good.

speaker: Mevrouw Bakker
text: I think you work too hard, I think she is braver than any of us, and I think a house with a sick-room needs one woman who says nothing clever. That is me. Eat something.

speaker: Jan
text: Cold, Herr Professor. Colder than the Zuider Zee in March. Cab? The coach for Cologne goes from the corner when you are ready, and not before.

speaker: player
text: What do you hear of the south?

speaker: player
text: Where might a man lose a key in my house?

speaker: Jan
text: The post-boys say the Styrian road is cut at Kirchdorf with snow, and that no one in the village will say why they close their doors at four. A rumour, Professor. I always say: a rumour is a draught that has found a keyhole.

speaker: Jan
text: Where would a clever man hide a thing from himself, Professor? Under his own nose. I once found my watch in my boot. Check what you look at every day without seeing it.

speaker: The student
text: Professor! Is it true the Dean means to have you disgraced on Friday? They say he has the whole Faculty behind him.

speaker: player
text: Never mind the Dean. What does he say about me?

speaker: player
text: What are you reading under that Boerhaave?

speaker: The student
text: That you put stories of ghouls in your lectures and call them medicine. That a physician who believes in peasants' tales has no business teaching the sons of the Burghers.

speaker: The student
text: Calmet. On vampires. I thought it was a joke, but Herr Seward from London says you gave it him to read. Are you cross?

speaker: Van Helsing
text: I am delighted. A student who reads the foolish book is a student who learns to ask what is true in it. Keep it. But read the column that is written in the margin, not the one that is printed.

speaker: John Seward
text: Professor! I thought it best to be early, in case the Dean tried to take the best seat.

speaker: player
text: How is your hand, Mr. Seward?

speaker: player
text: Does the Dean ask the same questions every time?

speaker: John Seward
text: Healed, Sir. Thanks entirely to you. I cut myself at the dissection of the septic case, and the surgeon wished to take the hand. You would not allow it. You opened the wound with your own knife and drew out the poison with your mouth. I remember thinking you were mad.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: I was mad with fear, Mr. Seward. I had lost enough that winter. A physician may refuse to lose another. It is a very stupid thing and an excellent reason.

speaker: John Seward
text: Always the same three, Sir: the peasant's remedy, the mesmerist, and the thing he calls your 'Carpathian superstition'. If I were you I would look at your own blackboard. Everything he needs is there, and everything you need.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: Van Helsing. Still pinning ghost-stories to your lectures, I hear. The Faculty is gravely concerned that a physician of your gifts has gone to the dogs.

speaker: player
text: I have come for the key to the rare-book press, Dean.

speaker: player
text: I think we should settle this today, in the open.

speaker: player
text: (That blackboard has the answers. I should read it first.)

speaker: Van Helsing
text: I will study the board before I give him my reasons. A man ought to know his own argument.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: The key stays where it is. Prove to me that you are a man of science and not a man of rumours, and you shall have it. I shall ask you three questions. Fail one, and we begin again.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: Splendid. Three questions, then. The first: the peasants of this country swear that a hanged man's rope, bound round the brow, cures a fever. Fact, or superstition?

speaker: player
text: Fact. The peasants have observed it for centuries.

speaker: player
text: Superstition. It has never been tested.

speaker: player
text: It is none of a physician's business what peasants believe.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: Centuries of observation by whom? By people who also stopped hail with bells? It seems your own blackboard disagrees with you, Van Helsing. Again.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: A physician who will not look at what the peasants believe will never learn what the peasants know. That is no answer. Again.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: Good. The second: the mesmerism in the Salpetriere, where a sleeper obeys a command given hours before. Another peasants' marvel?

speaker: player
text: No. It is observed under witness and repeated; it is fact, though we do not understand it.

speaker: player
text: Yes. If we cannot explain it, it cannot be real.

speaker: player
text: It is a hoax of the French.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: 'If we cannot explain it, it cannot be real.' You wrote the opposite on the board. Begin again.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: And the third. In the Carpathians, they say, the dead rise by night and drink the blood of the living. I take it you will call that superstition by your own rule.

speaker: player
text: By my rule I may not call it so until I have tested it. I will not deny what I have not examined.

speaker: player
text: It is nonsense, of course, as I have always said.

speaker: player
text: It is certainly true. I have seen it.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: Neither of those is your own doctrine. You are either lying to me or to yourself. Begin again.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: ...Hm. 'Disbelieve nothing you have not tested.' You have beaten me with my own favourite sentence. Very well. Take the key. But understand I will watch the day you bring the Faculty a case.

speaker: Professor Verhoeven
text: And, Van Helsing. For what it is worth, my own grandmother hung garlic at her door. I should be very sorry to find she was right.

speaker: Mijnheer de Vries
text: (whispering) Professor. The Ordo you want is in the press. The Dean has the key. The Dean also has the opinion that you should not have it.

speaker: player
text: What is the Ordo, exactly?

speaker: player
text: What have you in the way of Styrian travellers?

speaker: player
text: Does the Dean ever read the rare books himself?

speaker: Mijnheer de Vries
text: A rituale of the old Dutch rite. It is dull in ordinary hands. The chapter on the blessing of bread and the making of a circle is the only part anyone has ever read, and that only once, in 1731.

speaker: Mijnheer de Vries
text: The Folklore and Travels. Third shelf from the west, among the Natural History where they cannot do any harm.

speaker: Mijnheer de Vries
text: Every Sunday, in the dark, with the lamp turned down. He thinks I do not know. I should hate to be the one to tell him I have always known.

speaker: Father Pieter
text: Professor. You come into my chapel perhaps twice in the year. Either you are very troubled, or you are working.

speaker: player
text: I have the Ordo and a tin of wafers. I need to consecrate them, Father.

speaker: player
text: What do you think of a man who tests his religion?

speaker: player
text: What makes the Host the Host, Father?

speaker: Father Pieter
text: I think he is a better Christian than the man who never tests it. Faith that cannot bear a question is not faith but fear.

speaker: Father Pieter
text: Nothing you could measure on a scale. The bread is bread, until the words and the intent are laid on it in the right order, and then it is what it is. The order matters, Professor. Do not let any man tell you it is only ceremony.

speaker: Father Pieter
text: Hm. You have the Ordo. Then let us do this properly. I will not guess at the order; you shall read it to me, and I will do as you direct. What comes first?

speaker: player
text: The priest is shriven.

speaker: player
text: The hands are washed.

speaker: player
text: The Collect is said over the bread.

speaker: player
text: The pyx is sealed.

speaker: Father Pieter
text: (frowning) No, that is not what the Ordo says. 'Before the bread is blessed the hands must be washed; before the hands are washed the priest must be shriven.' Let us begin again.

speaker: Father Pieter
text: (He kneels, speaks low, rises lighter.) I am shriven. What now?

speaker: player
text: The hands are washed.

speaker: player
text: The Collect is said over the bread.

speaker: player
text: The pyx is sealed.

speaker: Father Pieter
text: (He washes his hands in the font, breaking the ice with his knuckles.) Clean. And now?

speaker: player
text: The Collect is said over the bread.

speaker: player
text: The pyx is sealed.

speaker: Father Pieter
text: (Over the wafers, in a voice I have not heard him use before, the Latin runs like water.) And last?

speaker: player
text: The pyx is sealed.

speaker: Father Pieter
text: (He closes the little silver box and presses the cross on its lid.) It is done. These are no longer bread. Take them with the blessing of this house, and may you never need them. And if you do, Professor, remember that the Host is not a charm but a reproach: it works only on those who know what it is.

speaker: Old Gerrit
text: WHAT? Ah, the Professor! I was saying, the Father is a good man but he washes his hands with a great deal of ice about it.

speaker: player
text: Is there anything in the order of the Mass that people forget?

speaker: Old Gerrit
text: Forget? Forty years I have set the table for it. Confess first, wash after, bless the bread, close the box. The Father mutters if I put the water out before he has been to the box. Sacristans know these things, Professor. We just never get asked.

speaker: Pfarrer Albrecht
text: Professor Van Helsing? Thank God. I have written to nine men and been answered by one. I had begun to think my letter was a kind of madness.

speaker: player
text: Tell me what you know.

speaker: player
text: I wish to see the churchyard, Pfarrer.

speaker: Pfarrer Albrecht
text: Four children of the village have wasted this winter. Pale, listless, two small marks at the throat. I buried one of them. Then I found, at dawn, that the snow on the north side of the churchyard had gone as if a fire had been lit under it. One grave only. I will not say which, for I have not the courage. Ask the old ones.

speaker: Pfarrer Albrecht
text: (He closes his eyes.) You will do it by night? I have no right to refuse; I have only the fear of a priest who has seen what a Christian burial cannot hold. Go. Matthias has the gate. Say a Pater for me at whichever grave it is.

speaker: Matthias
text: I do not talk of it, Herr. I dig. I do not ask who it is I dig for.

speaker: player
text: The grave that has no snow upon it. Do you know which?

speaker: player
text: A girl, nineteen. A wedding-dress. Is it Katharina Lindner?

speaker: player
text: Is there anything I should know about the gate?

speaker: Matthias
text: Three stones are by the north wall. Anna Pfeifer, who was a saint. Josef Hauer, who was a thief. And a third. Ask the old Frau Lindner; she is the only one who still says the name.

speaker: Matthias
text: (He crosses himself.) I have driven three iron nails into that stone with my own hand. Twice the nails were out by morning. Yes, Herr. She is the one. God help me for saying it aloud.

speaker: Matthias
text: The lantern will not stay lit beyond the third stone. Go by the moon. And, Herr, do not step on the snow where it has thawed.

speaker: Frau Lindner
text: A stranger. A doctor, they say. Then you are the one who will open the grave, and I will tell you what I should have said to the Pfarrer's face seventy years ago.

speaker: player
text: Who lies there, Frau Lindner?

speaker: Frau Lindner
text: My aunt. She was nineteen, a bride of the spring, and the prettiest girl in three parishes. Ask me no more until you have listened.

speaker: Frau Lindner
text: It was the year of the great snow, when the wolves came into the street. My aunt Katharina wed the miller's son in March and was dead by Easter. She lay in the church for three days with a bloom on her cheek like a living girl. The priest, who was old and wise, drove an ash-nail through the coffin-lid, and the sexton nailed three more to the stone. Still the children sickened.

speaker: Frau Lindner
text: My mother used to say she walked on the night of the great thaw, and that she asked for her husband by name at his window. Katharina Lindner. A bride of the spring. Say it once to the sexton, Herr, and he will give you the gate.

speaker: Landlord Huber
text: A hot wine for the Herr Doctor. Or a hot soup. We have both, and I fear that is all we have.

speaker: player
text: Why so much garlic on the windows?

speaker: player
text: When did the trouble begin?

speaker: Landlord Huber
text: My wife's idea. Do not ask me if it works; ask me if I sleep. I do. That is all the evidence I need.

speaker: Landlord Huber
text: At the first thaw. A child at the Meyer farm, then a girl at the mill. By the Feast of the Three Kings the village shut its doors at four. They say the Pfarrer wrote for help to a man in Holland. We did not think he would come.

speaker: The herdsman
text: You are the learned gentleman. Tell me, Herr, is it true that you can tell by looking at a man whether he is sick of body or sick of mind?

speaker: player
text: Sometimes. Why?

speaker: The herdsman
text: My daughter Resi has been weak since the thaw. She says a pretty lady stands at her window and sings. I told her it was a dream. The Pfarrer says it is not, and I dare not hear him say why.

speaker: Van Helsing
text: Arminius has written again. The black edge is not for himself; it is for the friend who died in Buda-Pesth last month. At the foot, in his shaking hand, a postscript: 'Abraham, what I told you of the Voivode - a letter came to me from a Transylvanian monk. The name that he used for the family in the end was not Voivode, but Dracula.'

speaker: Van Helsing
text: I sit with it for a long time, the lamp low, the snow falling across the canal. Upstairs she coughs and sleeps. I had thought I was putting a ghost to rest. It is very clear to me tonight that I have only learned what the ghost looks like. The fight is not over, and I am not, I think, the man who will finish it. But I shall teach the man who will.

speaker: Narrator
text: Years later, a London doctor wrote to an old teacher in Amsterdam: 'Come at once, if convenient; if not, come anyhow.'

speaker: Narrator
text: A smoky fire. The landlord's family keep it burning all night. A half-burnt stick of ash wood lies in the hearth.

speaker: Narrator
text: I pulled out a half-burnt stick of ash wood.

speaker: Narrator
text: The remains of my paprika hendl. Excellent, if thirsty work.

speaker: Narrator
text: A rough chair with a scrap of homespun cloth over the back.

speaker: Narrator
text: I took the scrap of homespun cloth. It may bind or wrap something.

speaker: Narrator
text: A coil of rope hangs over the back.

speaker: Narrator
text: I took the coil of rope.

speaker: Narrator
text: Plum brandy, by the smell.

speaker: Narrator
text: I filled a flask from the barrel. Slivovitz: it will steady the nerves.

speaker: Narrator
text: Golden Tokay, left by the hostess.

speaker: Narrator
text: I pocketed the bottle. It gives courage for the road ahead.

speaker: Narrator
text: The door to the yard, where the coach waits.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Golden Krone Hotel. 'Mittel Land' - the Middle Land, as Bistritz calls itself.

speaker: Narrator
text: An oil lamp, nearly full.

speaker: Narrator
text: I decanted a little lamp oil into a flask.

speaker: Narrator
text: A plain table knife lies by the plates.

speaker: Narrator
text: I slipped the table knife into my pocket.

speaker: Narrator
text: The landlord's wife. She wrings her hands, and weeps for me.

speaker: Narrator
text: A broad man, anxious to speak and unable to.

speaker: Narrator
text: A black calèche with four black horses' worth of harness and no horses. The driver waits, tall and silent.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Borgo Pass. A track climbing toward the Carpathian night.

speaker: Narrator
text: A faint blue flame flickers over the grass. They say gold is buried where it burns.

speaker: Narrator
text: I mark the spot, and pull up a sharpened stake that someone left nearby. It may serve.

speaker: Narrator
text: Bare against the clouds.

speaker: Narrator
text: A tall driver with a long brown beard, a black hat, and eyes that shine red in the lamp.

speaker: Narrator
text: Yellow eyes in the dark. The howling is close.

speaker: Narrator
text: The pack grows bold. Near the driver, they cower.

speaker: Narrator
text: A great door, old and studded with large iron nails. No light, no sound.

speaker: Narrator
text: Stagnant water. A bat flits across the surface.

speaker: Narrator
text: A rusted lantern, long burned dry.

speaker: Narrator
text: A path leads toward the ruined chapel at the edge of the castle.

speaker: Narrator
text: A fire the size of a man burns in the grate. It is the only warmth in the castle.

speaker: Narrator
text: Laid for one. The Count says he has already dined, and does not drink... wine.

speaker: Narrator
text: Set for me.

speaker: Narrator
text: Empty. He does not eat in my presence.

speaker: Narrator
text: Golden Tokay, old and rich.

speaker: Narrator
text: I took the bottle.

speaker: Narrator
text: A bowl of garlic flowers, set out unaccountably on the Count's table.

speaker: Narrator
text: I took a handful of garlic flowers.

speaker: Narrator
text: Golden candlesticks, long past polishing.

speaker: Narrator
text: My bedroom. The Count showed me there himself.

speaker: Narrator
text: The library.

speaker: Narrator
text: The door to the courtyard.

speaker: Narrator
text: A carved face of some forgotten ancestor, scarred with age.

speaker: Narrator
text: A tall old man, clean shaven save for a long white moustache, clad in black from head to foot. His hand is cold as ice.

speaker: Narrator
text: A four-poster. I sleep here, though not easily.

speaker: Narrator
text: Cutting myself shaving, the Count's hand seized my throat... and in the glass there was no reflection of him at all.

speaker: Narrator
text: I unhooked the little glass. Whatever he is, he cannot be seen in it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Paper, ink, and no one to write to.

speaker: Narrator
text: My journal, kept in shorthand.

speaker: Narrator
text: I will not be parted from my journal.

speaker: Narrator
text: A locked chest. Forced from within? Or from without?

speaker: Narrator
text: Four candles. A fifth would not hurt.

speaker: Narrator
text: The hall.

speaker: Narrator
text: English books on every subject - law, history, geography... and 'Bradshaw's Guide'. The Count has studied England thoroughly.

speaker: Narrator
text: More English books, thick and well-thumbed.

speaker: Narrator
text: Magazines, newspapers, and a London directory.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Count's favourite chair, I think.

speaker: Narrator
text: It burns day and night.

speaker: Narrator
text: The hall.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'Whatever you do, do not sleep in any other part of the castle.' This door leads there.

speaker: Narrator
text: Here, in the moonlight, I let myself fall asleep. I should not have.

speaker: Narrator
text: A lady's embroidery frame, dusty with years.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dried garlic flowers, left on the table. They are old.

speaker: Narrator
text: I took the garlic flowers. A superstition? Maybe not.

speaker: Narrator
text: Back to the library.

speaker: Narrator
text: Black with age. Nothing stares back.

speaker: Narrator
text: One was dark, and had great aquiline nose, like the Count; the other fair, with great masses of golden hair and eyes like pale sapphires.

speaker: Narrator
text: They whispered together and laughed - a silvery, musical laugh, as hard as glass.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'He is young and strong; there are kisses for us all.'

speaker: Narrator
text: One of fifty boxes of earth, newly dug, I think.

speaker: Narrator
text: The lid is open. The Count lies within, eyes open, stony and without colour. Not breathing. A key hangs at his belt.

speaker: Narrator
text: With shaking hands I take the keys from his belt. He does not stir.

speaker: Narrator
text: Worn letters. 'Dracula'. The rest is lost.

speaker: Narrator
text: Even here, the cross endures. The Count would flinch from it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Its flames lean toward the coffin.

speaker: Narrator
text: Back to the night air.

speaker: Narrator
text: A narrow stair beneath the chapel. Perhaps the road to freedom - perhaps worse.

speaker: Narrator
text: Cold in August, with a vase of sea-pinks in the grate. Mrs. Westenra says the chimney draws better empty.

speaker: Narrator
text: Guide-books, a Bible and three novels with their pages uncut. Lucy reads only the ends.

speaker: Narrator
text: My shorthand notebook, the blotter, and a place where I have written 'Jonathan' and nothing after it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lucy's long letter, three pages crossed. I have read it twice and shall read it again.

speaker: Narrator
text: I put Lucy's letter in my pocket. It is the only complete account of that wild afternoon.

speaker: Narrator
text: My notebook of Whitby: tides, the price of tea, and the unanswered questions about Jonathan.

speaker: Narrator
text: My own chair, with the cushion Lucy embroidered badly.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lucy's favourite. She says the springs are exactly right for novel-reading.

speaker: Narrator
text: Cottons, a thimble, a card of buttons and a paper of safety-pins, which Lucy borrows daily.

speaker: Narrator
text: I take the largest safety-pin. One never knows.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lucy gathers them on the cliff every morning.

speaker: Narrator
text: The door to the room Lucy and I share.

speaker: Narrator
text: The way down to the town and the East Cliff.

speaker: Narrator
text: The way down to the town and the East Cliff.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ajar, and the night air coming in. She has gone out into the fog.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lucy, pretty and fair, smiling over her tea. She has the colour of a girl who sleeps well.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lucy, pretty and fair, smiling over her tea. She has the colour of a girl who sleeps well.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lucy's mother, in grey silk and a lace cap, with a weak heart and a strong opinion on draughts.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lucy's mother, in grey silk and a lace cap, with a weak heart and a strong opinion on draughts.

speaker: Narrator
text: A plain, quick girl from the town. She knows everything the fishwives know.

speaker: Narrator
text: A plain, quick girl from the town. She knows everything the fishwives know.

speaker: Narrator
text: A postman in a sea-damp coat, holding a foreign envelope with a convent seal.

speaker: Narrator
text: Papers in rows, a blotter, and the case-book of the asylum, open at a name I cannot read from here.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'R. M. Renfield, aetat 59. Sanguine temperament; great physical strength; morbidly excitable; periods of gloom ending in some fixed idea.'

speaker: Narrator
text: Maudsley, Esquirol, Pinel, and a row of bottles with tight stoppers and tighter labels.

speaker: Narrator
text: Chloral, morphia and brandy, all measured, all locked. The key is left in because Seward trusts himself.

speaker: Narrator
text: Seward waves a hand: 'Take one dose, Miss Murray, in case Miss Lucy cannot sleep.' I bottle it carefully.

speaker: Narrator
text: A sugar-smeared jar of flies, confiscated from the patient in Room 12. They buzz without hope.

speaker: Narrator
text: Well sat in. Many a mad man has told his story here.

speaker: Narrator
text: Banked low. The room smells of carbolic and cigar smoke.

speaker: Narrator
text: A large, kind man in a white coat who has been bitten twice and bears no grudge.

speaker: Narrator
text: A thin, pale man of nearly sixty, quite calm, with a little line of sugar on the table before him and an eye on the window.

speaker: Narrator
text: A seat fixed on the flat tomb of the suicide's grave. Lucy and I come here every fine afternoon, and the sea breathes up at us.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'HERE LYETH THE BODY OF GEORGE CANON, WHO DIED, IN HOPE OF A GLORIOUS RESURRECTION, ON JULY 29, 1873, FALLING FROM THE ROCKS AT KETTLENESS. THIS TOMB WAS ERECTED BY HIS SORROWING MOTHER TO HER DEARLY BELOVED SON. HE WAS THE ONLY SON OF HIS MOTHER, AND SHE WAS A WIDOW.' Lichen at the foot has been disturbed.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pressed into the moss at the stone's foot, a small iron key on a loop of tarred twine. The coastguard's spare, if Mr. Swales is to be believed.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'Sacred to the memory of Thomas Wilson, mariner, lost with all hands in the Providence, 1859. His wife and five children mourn.' Fresh flowers lie at the base.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'Mary Jonas, widow, aged 91 years. She was beloved of many.' She had, the stone suggests, several sons.

speaker: Narrator
text: Worn smooth. A carved anchor and a ship. The inscription began 'In loving memory' and then lost patience.

speaker: Narrator
text: A plain cross for a child. Someone has set a shell on it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Square, grey and enduring, with the hundred and ninety-nine steps going down beside it.
