text: I told the villagers they could not have the grain, and the army ate. Some of the villagers walked away at dawn. Not all of them could. Stanciu says it was prudent, and does not meet my eyes. The army is fed. I cannot be sure of the rest of us.

speaker: Narrator
text: I read the letter aloud to Radu, and then I let him go. He walked out of the gate with a cloak and a horse, and his face was the face of a boy who has been caught and not whipped. I will see him again, and I will not know what he intends.

speaker: Narrator
text: I read the letter aloud to Radu and gave him to the guard. He did not resist. The key in my hand felt as though it belonged to some more severe person. My brother is below my feet in the dark, and I tell myself it is justice.

speaker: Narrator
text: Old Dan told me what the tower needs: lamp-oil from the hall and a torch from the stair-door bracket. Without a signal the ridge garrison will not know we have left. I am a prince whose first order is to arrange a bonfire.

speaker: Narrator
text: Oil, a torch, and a pillar of fire above the pass. Across the valley a small light answered, and then another. Forty spears on the far crag. I stood and watched it burn until Dan said politely that the wind would soon turn the sparks onto the thatch.

speaker: Narrator
text: The levy goes one way down the mountain and the refugees come the other, and between them the road is no wider than a wagon. A child asked me if the Turk had a face. I said yes. She asked if I had seen it. I said no. She nodded, as one who knew better.

speaker: Narrator
text: I gave her bread and a blanket from my pack. She did not thank me for the bread, only for the blanket. She said the bread was just, but the blanket was kind, and kindness was the thing nobody had spared for her. It cost me nothing, and I am still thinking of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: A hundred fires, ten thousand men, and none of them certain whose war this is. Mircea tells stories of Kossova and I try not to look too closely at what he leaves out. I am to put them in a ford by the dark of the moon, and I do not yet know which.

speaker: Narrator
text: He gave me his name, Ahmed, and the ford, for a blanket and a cup of water. The old way says never trust a captive. The newer way, mine, says never trust a man you have starved. I think I am a poor student of both.

speaker: Narrator
text: He told me the ford. It took a quarter of an hour. I do not intend to remember how it was done, and I know I shall remember nothing else. Mircea, who has seen worse, put his hand on my shoulder and said it was necessary. That is how it begins.

speaker: Narrator
text: Felt on the hooves, reeds on the banks, a creek from the north-east: the Stone Ford would ring, and the Wolf's Ford is too far. Reed Ford it must be. I placed three hundred spears among the reeds myself, and a hundred archers at the bend, and then I waited.

speaker: Narrator
text: They came as Cristea said, low and silent, with their horses in felt. I never knew how loud a river could be until it was full of men trying not to be heard. The first one saw me at ten paces. I had my father's hammer, and I did not hesitate.

speaker: Narrator
text: He knew what I had not told my captains: that the ford was sold. I did not ask who sold it. I think I knew. He offered me a school, and a lesson, and an eternity, in the voice of a man selling a horse. I took the token. I cannot say why, except that I was tired of being beaten.

speaker: Narrator
text: A black lake, a ferryman with no breath and a mountain with its door open. 'The tenth pays more,' said the scratched post. I did not ask what. I paid the first toll in silver, taken from a drowned scholar's cairn. It felt like stealing from a man who was too proud to mind.

speaker: Narrator
text: A stone school under the mountain. The Master teaches with the amused patience of a thing that has had a thousand pupils and remembers each. The lessons are of names, of weather, of the speech of wolves. Nobody laughs. Nobody leaves. In spring, they say, the tenth is taken.

speaker: Narrator
text: I offered him a share of what I learned instead of a threat. He looked at me as though I had spoken Greek, and then he laughed, and gave me the key. It is a small thing. I find I am proud of it, and ashamed that I am surprised.

speaker: Narrator
text: I laid a hand on my dagger and Vasile gave me the library key as quickly as a child gives up an apple. He has not spoken to me since. I did not need to draw. That, I suppose, is what a prince's reputation is for.

speaker: Narrator
text: Chained books, black candles and a cold that has nothing to do with the weather. I read the Clavis Minor with my teeth clenched. Water to open the way, silver to bind, flame to seal. The order matters more than the things. It always does.

speaker: Narrator
text: Water, silver, flame. The altar accepted them in that order and hummed like a struck bell. I felt, for one moment, that something large had noticed me and been pleased. I do not know how to make that feeling stop being pleasant.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ten seats in a ring, a green fire that gives no heat and, below the floor, something breathing. The Master read the roll in a flat kind voice. Nobody looked at anyone else. Everyone knew that one of us would not be rising from the ring.

speaker: Narrator
text: I wrote another man's name in my place. The ink dried at once. I told myself it was a prince's choice, and that Vasile would have done the same, and that it made no difference to the Master. The more I told myself, the less any of it was true.

speaker: Narrator
text: I stood in the ring and said that the tenth was mine. The Master was surprised, I think, and then very attentive. Something came up out of the grate. I do not remember what happened, only that I was cold when it ended and have been, since, one way or another.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vasile went down the stair with his head up. I saw his face as he passed, and I will see it as long as I have eyes. He did not accuse me. That was the cruellest thing he could have done, and I think he knew.

speaker: Narrator
text: I woke in a box. I have no idea how long. My throat was dry, and my father's stone lay on the left, and there was a scratching in my mouth as if my teeth were something else. The lid was lead-sealed, and I was strong enough to want it open.

speaker: Narrator
text: The altar candles are down to stubs and the doors are unbarred. A priest lies against a pew with a spear-wound. Ileana's tomb is new. The hunger in me is not a hunger I know the name of, and I am afraid it knows mine.

speaker: Narrator
text: I took what I needed from Father Dragomir. He did not resist. That was what was unbearable. He had given me the sacraments at my christening, and I gave him this. Whatever begins here, it begins with a priest's blood and my own choice.

speaker: Narrator
text: I called the wolves and fed on the oldest, and kept the priest alive. It was the lesser sin. It was still a sin. They looked at me with a kind of recognition, and I understood that I was now something wolves could follow.

speaker: Narrator
text: I knelt by her stone and asked to be spared, and the sun rose and spared me, and spared the priest, and that was the worst of all. There was no one to punish me, so I began to punish myself, and have not stopped.

speaker: Narrator
text: Exeter, May. Cathedral bells, a fine sun, and Mr. Hawkins's letter in my pocket. I am to go to Transylvania, a country I know only as a smudge on the school globe. The firm trusts me; I wish I trusted myself as much.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mr. Hawkins has taken a foreign client, a Count Dracula of Castle Dracula, for the purchase of an English house. His letters are formal and exact. I am to prepare the file and, if all goes well, go to him in person. I am rather proud.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Count wants a house in England: large, old, solitary, with a chapel and a high wall, and no neighbour near enough to overlook him. The surveys are in the muniment room; Mr. Pell has the key, and Mr. Pell is not a man to be hurried.

speaker: Narrator
text: The deed-box held three surveys: a Hampstead villa, a house at Whitby, and a place at Purfleet called Carfax. Only one was old, walled and furnished with a chapel. I begin to see which the Count would choose.

speaker: Narrator
text: Carfax, then. An old house at Purfleet, walled in stone, with a chapel and a pond, and only a lunatic asylum for a neighbour. Mr. Hawkins agrees. I hope the Count is as pleased with it as we are with ourselves.

speaker: Narrator
text: I read the Count's letters again. They are admirable: grave, patient, correct. But I notice what he never asks about: price. A man who does not ask the price has too much to lose, or too much to spend.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mr. Hawkins gives me a letter of credit and sends me to the British Museum. Then I am to go east, find the Count and have the deed signed. And, he says, say goodbye to Mina. He says it with the air of a man who is not asking.

speaker: Narrator
text: London. The great dome of the Reading Room is like the inside of a giant's skull, and the readers sit under it like thoughts. I stand a long time in the door and feel very small, and very provincial.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the Museum I learn that Transylvania lies within the Carpathians, a whirlpool of Saxon, Wallach, Magyar and Szekely, with the Szgany among them. The people believe in the Evil Eye and in a name, Dracula, which means both dragon and devil.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mina in her classroom, with chalk on her cuff. She says I am foolish to go so far, and hopes I will write every day. There is a blackboard of shorthand behind her. I shall pretend not to read it.

speaker: Narrator
text: The trunk is open at last. Inside, camphor, tissue, my mother's ring, a small crucifix and a letter in my father's hand. I did not know I had missed him so much. I must wear the ring, at least, to Mina.

speaker: Narrator
text: I gave Mina my mother's ring this evening, and she put it on a chain round her neck. She says she will wear it openly when I come home. I have never before had so good a reason to come home.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mina gave me the ribbon from her hair for my diary. She says I must write in shorthand and she will learn to read it. I tie it round the book and put it next to my heart.

speaker: Narrator
text: Valise strapped, diary in my breast pocket, the Count's papers and the Museum notes in the lining. Mrs. Dunmore wept a little into her apron, and denied it. I am, I think, as ready as a man can be for a country he has only read about.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mrs. Dunmore has laid out my shirts. My father's trunk sits under the window, locked. I will take nothing from it, because I have never opened it, and I wonder whether I should.

speaker: Narrator
text: I walked to St. Petroc's to see my parents' stone. The snowdrops were fresh. Somebody tends it; I know who. Mina has never said a word about it.

speaker: Narrator
text: I am a prisoner in the Count's castle. All doors are locked; the only way is a ledge and a wall. The Count went down the wall like a lizard. If he can, I can. The alternative is waiting for the women.

speaker: Narrator
text: I went down the castle wall by ivy, iron ring and loose stone, and in through the Count's open window. My hands bleed; my coat is torn. I have crossed a threshold I do not understand, and I cannot go back.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the Count's room, a heap of gold, Roman, Austrian, Turkish, Hungarian, all coated with dust, none newer than three hundred years. There is no mirror in the castle. There is not even a nail left.

speaker: Narrator
text: Down the stair to the old chapel: fifty great boxes of earth. In one lay the Count, as if asleep, his eyes open, but nothing living in them. It is the most terrible thing I have ever seen, and I am not yet mad.

speaker: Narrator
text: I searched the Count's body for the key and found none. A few gold coins in a pocket; no watch, no purse. He does not breathe. He does not wake. I wonder which of us is more afraid.

speaker: Narrator
text: Out through the postern in the moonlight, down a goat-path under the stars. The wolves are near; I can smell them. A fire burns below, with a Szgany wagon. I do not know whether I am escaping or falling.

speaker: Narrator
text: A Szgany woman sold me bread and a flask for a handful of the Count's gold, and refused to say more. Her people carry his boxes and ask no questions. I envy them both.

speaker: Narrator
text: I crossed the gully on a plank with the roar of the river under me. On the far side the track runs down. Then my legs gave way, and the dark came, and I do not know what I did next.

speaker: Narrator
text: I woke in a hospital in Buda-Pesth. Sister Agatha says I have had a brain fever, and have been here six weeks. I have a white streak in my hair, they tell me, and I believe them.

speaker: Narrator
text: A small, quick Sister of St. Joseph has sat by my bed, and sent word to Mr. Hawkins. She says I spoke of wolves and a wall and three women. I told her nothing. I do not trust words yet.

speaker: Narrator
text: Again the dream: three women in the moonlight, laughing like silver bells. One fair, two dark. I wake wet to the skin. Sister Agatha says I called a woman's name, and not a kind one. She does not ask whose.

speaker: Narrator
text: Sister Agatha has written for me; I signed. 'I am safe, in Buda-Pesth, ill but mending.' Nothing more. She said the letter must say nothing that would frighten Mina, and I agreed. I hope that I shall always be able to.

speaker: Narrator
text: I have sealed my diary with Mina's ribbon and the chapel's wax. I do not know whether it is true or the delirium of a sick man. I will not know unless some solemn duty come upon me. So be it.

speaker: Narrator
text: I left a letter to my parents at the Virgin's feet in the chapel. They never said that they were proud of me. I think I know now why a man writes to the dead: because he can say it, and nobody can say no.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mina arrived in Buda-Pesth this morning, in a cab, with a carpet-bag and a face like a lamp. She did not ask what had happened. She took my hand, and said, 'I am not going away.'

speaker: Narrator
text: Mina has said yes. Here, in a hospital ward in Buda-Pesth, to a man half-mad with fever and white at the temples. I do not deserve it, and I have never wanted anything so much.

speaker: Narrator
text: I gave Mina my sealed diary. 'Keep it,' I said, 'and do not read it unless a solemn duty requires.' She tied the ribbon again, as she had before, and kissed my forehead. She is wiser than I am.

speaker: Narrator
text: A small white chapel with roses on the altar, and a vase of candles. The Sisters have decked it for us. The chaplain, they say, has been an Englishman in Buda-Pesth for thirty years.

speaker: Narrator
text: I sit in the garden under the limes and listen to the bees. I have not been in sunlight for six weeks. The old gardener says I look better. I do not remember when I last looked at all.

speaker: Narrator
text: Tomorrow we shall be married, with a white rose, a borrowed ring and a chaplain who says he has been waiting thirty years to see an Englishman and a girl turn up with matching faces. I am very happy.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mina and I leave Buda-Pesth for England, with the sealed book in her trunk and the white streak in my hair. I have the road behind me. I shall not look at it again, unless some solemn duty come upon me.

speaker: Narrator
text: We were married in the chapel at Buda-Pesth this morning. Sister Agatha wept. I was happy, truly, for the first time since the Borgo Pass. Whatever the sealed book contains, it is not this.

speaker: Narrator
text: Two wolves on the mountain path, hungry and bold. I fought them with a poker and a spade. One tooth I kept. I think I was braver than I have ever been, and certainly sillier.

speaker: Narrator
text: The window is open, there is a lawn outside it and three gentlemen coming to tea. I have never felt so bright in my life. Hannah says I am rosy, Mamma says I am tired, and the mirror says I look like a girl who has been told a secret.

speaker: Narrator
text: The parlour is chintz and bad piano music. Mamma has a theory about flowers and a larger one about gentlemen. I have decided to ignore both and arrange the vase myself.

speaker: Narrator
text: Lilies like bridesmaids, a sundial that counts only sunny hours, a bench in the shade. Dr. Seward left a note on it. I read it and pretended not to.

speaker: Narrator
text: Tallest at the back, the rose in the middle, forget-me-nots in front. Mamma wept a little, which is how she shows she is pleased, and handed me the key of the escritoire as though she were giving me the Crown jewels.

speaker: Narrator
text: A bundle of them in blue ribbon. She writes with a straight back, if letters can; every page begins with the weather and ends with love. I envy her, but only a little.

speaker: Narrator
text: He asked, and I refused, plainly, because he asked to be refused plainly. He took it like the good man he is, and asked if we might still be friends. I could have wept. He is the sort of man one wishes were one's brother.

speaker: Narrator
text: He asked in four sentences and I answered in two. We shook hands like a pair of fellow-conspirators. He told me there was a gentleman behind the rose-bush who had been standing there half an hour. I am quite fond of him.

speaker: Narrator
text: Oh, my dear Arthur! He dropped his speech in the lilies and gave me his mother's ring instead. I said yes in the plainest words I knew. Why can't a girl marry three men? Jack to heal me, Quincey to defend me, Arthur to love me.

speaker: Narrator
text: I wrote in order, as she told me: the window, the house, the secret, and the love. It is the first letter I have ever written without a postscript. She will read it on Friday and write me four pages by return, and I shall love every line.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mamma wants sea air for me, Mina has taken the Crescent, and I am to bring my trunk and my appetite. The Hillingham lawn looked so well as I left it that I felt, for a moment, as if I were leaving a person.

speaker: Narrator
text: Two beds under a sloping roof, a window full of sea and a landlady who has opinions about draughts. Mina has taken the bed nearest the door. She says it is for the light. I think it is for the key.

speaker: Narrator
text: Papa's letter has gone. I had it in my hand at Hillingham; I may have put it down anywhere in Whitby. If I find it I shall never put it down again. Mamma thinks the trunk, the window-seat, or the seat on the cliff.

speaker: Narrator
text: A churchyard over the sea, an Abbey over the churchyard, and a seat over everything. Mina writes. I watch the ships and the gulls and the great red sun. Everyone is kind. I am so tired, and I cannot think why.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mina tells me I walked in my sleep last night. She found me at the window, in my nightgown, looking at the Abbey. I remember nothing. She has taken the key of our door and put it under her pillow, and she says she shall not sleep until I am well.

speaker: Narrator
text: A hundred and ninety-nine, he said. He has carried coffins on his shoulder down every one. It is a curious thing to know exactly how far it is from the cliff to the town. I shall remember it.

speaker: Narrator
text: I woke on the seat on the cliff. I did not walk there. There was a bell, and a man on the Abbey wall, tall and dark and red-eyed, watching me with the patience of the grave. I was not afraid. That was the terrible part.

speaker: Narrator
text: I said 'Arthur,' and he flinched. Arthur's ring was cold in my hand, and his name was warm in my mouth, and for that moment I was Lucy Westenra and not a thing on a seat.

speaker: Narrator
text: I said 'Mina.' Her letter was folded in four in my hand, and the first line was a rule for finding the way. Begin with what you see out of the window. I saw a Moon and a dark man and a path.

speaker: Narrator
text: I said 'Papa.' I held his letter against my heart with its stiff old forget-me-nots, and the man on the seat looked at it and could not look at me.

speaker: Narrator
text: I turned my back on him and walked. It was the hardest thing I ever did. There was no footstep behind me. In front, the steps went down into the dark, and I went with three names in my mouth like pebbles.

speaker: Narrator
text: A hundred and ninety-nine steps in a nightgown, between graves, with the sea below and the bell behind. If I lose count I shall be on the cliff all night, and there will be nothing to hold me but the seat.

speaker: Narrator
text: One hundred and ninety-nine, aloud, as I would count Arthur's name. At the bottom, a lamp swung, and somebody ran toward me with a shawl and a plait of dark hair.

speaker: Narrator
text: She ran all the way in her dressing-gown. She said she woke and the key was under her pillow and the door was locked and I was gone. She has a gift for being right when I am wrong. I am so glad. I am so tired.

speaker: Narrator
text: Home, and no better. The pallor has stayed. Dr. Seward sits with me, and Dr. Van Helsing, and Arthur comes when he can. Everyone is very kind, and everyone looks at me as though I were already a photograph. I do not want to be a photograph.

speaker: Narrator
text: I wrote: 'Do not be small with grief. Live, and love again, when you can. I shall not mind.' It is the hardest line I have ever written. It is also the truest.

speaker: Narrator
text: I wrote: 'Remember me in the garden, with the rose in my hair, and be the man I knew.' He will do it. He does everything I ask, bless him, even when it hurts him.

speaker: Narrator
text: I wrote: 'Watch over Arthur for me; he does not know how to be alone.' She will. She keeps promises as she keeps her letters, in order and in blue ribbon.

speaker: Narrator
text: I wrote: 'Keep writing, everything you see, in order, as you taught me. One day someone will need it.' She has always written for the pleasure of it. I would like her to write for the use of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Papa's letter, with the forget-me-nots, tied with the ring-ribbon. Arthur will understand. He always does, in the end.

speaker: Narrator
text: Papa's letter, tucked in with her own letters in blue ribbon. She keeps everything, and what she keeps, she keeps right.

speaker: Narrator
text: I folded Papa's letter in my hands. If it is to be forgotten, let it be forgotten with me. The forget-me-nots, I think, will be glad of the company.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'Hannah Brough, born 1785, died 1830, aged 43.' A faithful wife and a good neighbour. I copy the figures to be added up in a quiet moment.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'John Anson, master mariner, born 1765, died 1795, aged 30.' Lost off the Scar and not found. The figures are neat and the sum is good.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'Mary Dale, spinster, born 1790, died 1810, aged 20.' She died as she lived: quietly. The lettering is clean and the sum exactly right.

speaker: Narrator
text: Miss Hallam's speech-day prize, the Tennyson in green morocco, has vanished from a locked cupboard. I am to look into it, as I seem to be the only member of staff who reads the small print. I am rather pleased.

speaker: Narrator
text: Miss Hallam will give me the key to the typewriting room if I find the book. I have wanted that key since Christmas. Cupboard, blotter, girls, she said, in that order. I shall keep the order but not, I think, the temper.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dora Pike dusts the staff-room on Wednesdays for a penny. Her mother is ill in Heavitree, and she sews at night to pay the doctor. I do not like where this points; I like it less that it points so clearly.

speaker: Narrator
text: Held to the glass, Miss Hallam's blotter gives a backward letter in a girl's round hand, with a looped capital D: 'Dearest Mama, I have it safe...' So the thief is a daughter, not a magpie. That is a different crime and wants a different kindness.

speaker: Narrator
text: No scratch on the lock, no mark on the hasp. Only a tiny shining thumb-print of red ink on the brass. Whoever took the book had the staff-room key and had been writing with the staff's red ink. Not a burglar: a borrower.

speaker: Narrator
text: The red ink is a quarter lower than last week. Red ink is for the staff alone, so someone has been where she should not, and for longer than a moment.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dora Pike's hands are clean, but her sleeve-cuff carries a red thumb-mark the exact colour of the staff ink. She keeps turning it inward. I like her, and I wish I did not know what I now know.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dora confessed: she wanted to read the Lady of Shalott to her mother. The book is back in my hands, undamaged. What we do with a child who steals for love is not in any rule-book, and I am glad of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Miss Hallam asked no questions and gave me the key. A small iron thing; I wear it on a ribbon at my throat like a cross. Tomorrow I shall learn to make a machine speak.

speaker: Narrator
text: From Mr. Hawkins's office: the house at Purfleet, called Carfax, with its chapel and twenty acres, secured for the Count, deeds to follow by the post of the ninth instant. A dull letter; I copy it as I would any other, with all my care.

speaker: Narrator
text: I freed the type-bars, oiled the pivots and wound on a new ribbon. Eleven lines, no errors. If Jonathan's firm ever wants a typist, here is one who has never been told she could not.

speaker: Narrator
text: A clerk writes for Mr. Hawkins: a registered letter for me, in Jonathan's hand, was posted at Exeter and has been lost on the Bristol line. So Jonathan wrote. Whatever else the silence means, he wrote.

speaker: Narrator
text: The morning trains: 10.20, stopping at Tiverton, Taunton at 11.30; 10.50, express, Taunton at 11.40; 11.15, stopping at Tiverton, Taunton at 12.05. I could set a clock by it. I would rather set a man free.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mr. Pomfret: the bag went on the first train after the half-past-ten sorting, and the guard saw it on the van floor as the train roared through Tiverton. So not a stopper, and not before half-past ten.

speaker: Narrator
text: After the sorting, clean through Tiverton: the 10.50 express. Mr. Pomfret has had Hobbs wire Taunton. Nobody has ever called me a detective, but I do believe I solved a thing with Bradshaw today.

speaker: Narrator
text: Under a van seat at Taunton for twelve days. Soft at the corners, smelling of coal and tobacco, and the dearest paper I own. Bistritz, the Golden Krone, the little cross the landlady pressed on him. He wrote. He did write.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'I wish you were beside me, with your shorthand and your timetables. Wait for me, and do not be anxious.' I read it twice aloud to Lucy and a third time alone. I shall wait. It is what I am best at, though I wish it were not.

speaker: Narrator
text: I told Lucy of the dream: water lapping, wood creaking, and a call I cannot catch. I thought she would laugh; she did not. It is odd how heavy a thing becomes once it is said aloud.

speaker: Narrator
text: We lay awake until the rooks began, and Lucy told me of three suitors and I told her of one absent man. She says I shall come to Whitby, and that the sea air will cure my dreams. I am less sure that I want them cured.

speaker: Narrator
text: Whitby, on the West Cliff. The harbour, the Abbey, the church on its hill, and Lucy at the window counting boats. I took one look at the sea and felt at once that it knew my name.

speaker: Narrator
text: Old Mr. Swales swears that every stone in this churchyard lies and that one of three cannot count. I am to find it. He told me this with the cheerful malice of a man who has been telling it for fifty years.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mr. Swales gave me his almanac: tides run later by fifty minutes each day. The stone that could not count was Hannah Brough's: forty-five by the calendar, and forty-three on the stone. I shall remember that when anyone tells me a sum is no matter.

speaker: Narrator
text: The table gives only Monday: high water 4.10 in the morning and 4.35 in the afternoon. Somebody has pencilled 'Wednesday?' in the margin and given up. I would not mind helping.

speaker: Narrator
text: The coastguard gave me a brass plumb on a cord: 'A pendulum, miss; hang it in a room and it will tell you what the room is thinking.' I have thought of something else to do with it, and I am a little ashamed.

speaker: Narrator
text: Two bats at dusk, rather too close to my hair. I took the umbrella to them like a sensible woman, and they went. I do not think they were bats only. I do not know why I think so.

speaker: Narrator
text: The ninth stair complained behind me, and when I turned the curtain was moving, though the window was shut. Lucy slept through it. I told myself it was the draught. I lit the candle all the same.

speaker: Narrator
text: On the sill, a damp mark the shape of a small hand, drying as I watched. The sea air, the damp, a cat. I have a great many reasonable explanations and not one I would put my name to.

speaker: Narrator
text: From my dream notes: it begins with the water, lapping near; then the wood, a creak; then the dark, a single point turning, and I forget my name. Water, wood, swing. Always in that order, before I wake.

speaker: Narrator
text: I sat in the rocking-chair, listened to the water in the basin, rocked until the boards creaked, and watched the plumb turn. It worked. I do not know whether to be proud or afraid, and I suspect the two are the same.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the dark hold, a barrel drips. The water is near and slow and the sound comes up through the wood into my wrist. Water first, always.

speaker: Narrator
text: The great timber groans as the hull settles. Wood is the second sound, patient and old. I can tell it now from my own heartbeat.

speaker: Narrator
text: I woke with a candle-stub and a still plumb and a fine cord between my fingers that was not there. Somewhere, a man is breathing in the dark. I shall tell no one yet. But I know that I can follow the thread when I must.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dunning's gang filed through the corral rail while the dogs were fed. Eleven head gone, and Santa Fe among them. Wash has a gash on his skull. I mean to bring every horse home, and Santa Fe first of all.

speaker: Narrator
text: Wash says powder is hidden in the stable, out of the damp, and lead can be dug from the target post. With both in hand the loading bench will make ten cartridges. I mean to ride out loaded, not hopeful.

speaker: Narrator
text: Old Hobbs says the creek bottoms are thick with wolves and that the channel is too deep to ford. But there is a cottonwood snag leaning over it with a stub on the limb, and a good lariat will swing a man across.

speaker: Narrator
text: Hoofprints bent east to low ground. Cottonwood ash at the dead fire. Red flannel with canebrake burrs on a thorn. Three signs, one answer: Dunning and my mare are in the bottoms.

speaker: Narrator
text: A throw and a half to catch the stub, then hand over hand across black water. It is a boy's trick and I still know it. The wolves have not forgiven me for being on their side of the river.

speaker: Narrator
text: Two grey wolves, thin as rails and twice as mean. The Winchester settled one and the bowie the other. I take no pride in it. They only wanted the same supper I wanted.

speaker: Narrator
text: One against two, in the open, by firelight, and the odds do not improve as one gets older. The bowie settled Dunning's man and the Winchester settled Dunning. His running-iron I mean to take to the sheriff.

speaker: Narrator
text: She took sugar from my hand and stood still for the saddle. We rode out of the hollow with eleven horses running behind. A man can lose almost everything and keep his life, but not this mare.

speaker: Narrator
text: Anselmo says the vampire bat goes for the bare neck. Against it: smoke across the lines, a high lantern, and a cloth the horse knows laid over the neck. He says it as though it were common sense. It is, if you have lost enough steers.

speaker: Narrator
text: I told a tale by the fire, and Art laughed in the right places, and Seward corrected the facts. It was the best hour of the whole trip. Odd how often the best hour comes just before the worst.

speaker: Narrator
text: They came out of the moon, three of them, with a sound like wet leather. The smoke thickened and the lantern swung and the Winchester spoke. One went down. Two flew off. The third did not run: it circled twice, looked at me, and then it was gone.

speaker: Narrator
text: She was bled in the small hours, through the blanket, through everything we did right. By sunrise she was gone. I buried her under a cross of picket-posts, and Art helped dig. I do not remember the rest.

speaker: Narrator
text: A flattened ring, black earth foreign to the plain, and bare prints that begin at the ring and end at the posts. No bat made these. Something came on its own feet and left on wings. I wrote it all down, and told no one but Seward.

speaker: Narrator
text: I have the bowie, the Winchester, and a sheath that a mare once chewed. And a name for a thing nobody believes in. Some day I may need to use it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Morning at Purfleet. A cell padded in grey, a tin tray, a window with the first flies. I am R. M. Renfield, once of a good house and sound mind. Today I must be a gentleman to Hodge, find my ledger, and make myself reasonable to the doctor.

speaker: Narrator
text: I said, 'I am quite myself, Mr. Hodge,' and Hodge opened the door. It is astonishing what a civil tongue will do for a man in a grey ticking cell. I wish I had known as much in the Strand.

speaker: Narrator
text: I raved at Hodge. He held me in his arms until the strength had left me, then opened the door as gently as for a child. I should not have shouted. It costs me more than it costs him.

speaker: Narrator
text: Under the loose board, wrapped in my father's handkerchief: my notebook. Eleven flies, forty spiders, three hundred sparrows, a cat. A column of figures that grows and never closes. It is the only honest document in this house.

speaker: Narrator
text: Quill counts everything. The doctor's inventory board gives beds, windows, lamps: seven, three, nine. That is the order in which the doctor writes it, and so the wheels of the linen-press must be set.

speaker: Narrator
text: Seven, three, nine, and the press gave up one lump of sugar on a blue paper. Dr. Seward locks it away so we cannot hoard. I have hoarded other things from him, and will go on.

speaker: Narrator
text: Sugar on the sill, and in a minute the flies came. Eleven. Dr. Seward would call it a dozen flies on a lump of sugar. I call it a tithe. I am not certain which of us is the more honest.

speaker: Narrator
text: Hodge dropped the garden key in the scullery three weeks ago and told nobody. Between ourselves, he thinks the mice have it. I think the spider has it. We are both of us probably right.

speaker: Narrator
text: Fed the spider eleven flies; she dropped the key from her web, an iron key on a loop of tape marked 'GARDEN'. Hodge's, the doctor would say. The spider's, I say. It does not matter which, only that I have it.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'Baked in a pie.' Mrs. Pargeter laughed, gave me brandy in a cup and swore me to secrecy. Her brother died in a place like mine. People are kinder than a case-book allows.

speaker: Narrator
text: In Seward's notes: 'He does not lie. His dread of the unseen is genuine. I do not know what to make of a delusion so well-regulated.' It is the kindest thing anyone has written of me since my father's will.

speaker: Narrator
text: I asked Dr. Seward to send me away before the Master comes. The ledger did it: a clerk's hand speaks better than a madman's mouth. He has written a note: the quiet wing, on Monday. Monday is too far, but it is a start.

speaker: Narrator
text: Hodge says Blunt does the garden at ten and two: out to the far wall, a pause to light his pipe, and back. Same every night for ten years. A man who is predictable is a man who can be avoided.

speaker: Narrator
text: The lamps are low and the house is quiet. I have the key, the brandy and the list. Hodge sits his watch in the day-room, and I feel the Master through the wall like a second pulse.

speaker: Narrator
text: A cup of Cook's brandy for his nerves, and Hodge sleeps in his chair. I did not hurt him, or lie to him, except in the matter of why. I leave him a blanket.

speaker: Narrator
text: Behind the water-butt I waited for the pipe, and when the night-man bent to his match I crossed the gravel without a sound. A man who counts can wait. It is the only virtue that madness has left me.

speaker: Narrator
text: The chapel at Carfax, the box in its aisle and the voice about it. He has not touched the ledger. He has not paid one penny of what he promised. I am quite steady, for once, and quite sure I can add.

speaker: Narrator
text: I totalled the ledger on his box: eleven flies, forty spiders, three hundred sparrows, the cat. It never closes, and neither does his promise. He has taken my lives and given me none. A bookkeeper knows a bad debtor when he meets one.

speaker: Narrator
text: I wrote Seward a page and left it under the candle: the box, the voice, the garlic, the cross, the sun. It is the first letter I have written in years. I signed it with my initials and the crest.

speaker: Narrator
text: I opened my hand at the window. The sparrow went over the wall. It is the only life I ever gave back, and I will take it with me wherever I am sent. I think the doctor will have my notebook. I would rather he had that than anything else.

speaker: Narrator
text: The sparrow was warm for a moment and then it was not. The voice said I had done well. I have never felt smaller. I think I understand now what the doctor meant by 'delusion'. It is a debt that cannot be paid.

speaker: Narrator
text: Three nights without sleep. Lucy Westenra refused me at Hillingham, with great kindness, and I have gone on doctoring as if the thing had not happened. I shall find the ward key, make my rounds and try to tire myself properly. Chloral, in the right measure, will do the rest.

speaker: Narrator
text: I keep her note, though a doctor should know better. 'I am promised, in my heart, to another.' She was gentle, and clear, and right. I said I understood, and I did. It is the understanding that keeps me awake.

speaker: Narrator
text: I spoke my grief aloud to the cylinder, and it sounded smaller than it felt. I shall not blame Lucy, nor Arthur, nor myself. I shall be a better doctor for it, if I am not a worse man.

speaker: Narrator
text: Fifteen grains for a woman or a frail man; twenty for a strong man in his full strength; never more than thirty; sixty is a funeral. Weigh twice. Renfield is fourteen stone and in his strength: twenty grains, witnessed.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'Believe nothing because I say it; doubt nothing because you have not seen it. Write it all down, and then look at what is written.' He wrote this to me about a case of fever. I find it applies to nearly everything.

speaker: Narrator
text: That winter I was ill, and Van Helsing sat three nights with me when he could have been abed. He says I owe him nothing but to be, to some other sleepless fool, what he was to me. I shall try. I do not yet know how.

speaker: Narrator
text: The ward clock stopped at ten past three the night Mrs. Pym died, and her husband has let no one touch it since. Hennessey says that if I name the hour, the old man may give me the winding key. I think I understand the lock he means.

speaker: Narrator
text: Old Greer, mate of the Lizzie out of Sunderland: never water on a spirit fire, since the spirit floats and spreads. Wet the blanket, drop it on, and lean. A mad sailor's memory is better than my own on the subject.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pym's clock ticks again, and the dispensary key hung behind it on a nail where Hennessey, wisely, hid it. Pym watched me with the face of a man receiving a verdict. I think it was a good one.

speaker: Narrator
text: Miss Vane, who writes to a man dead in India, notes that a boy with violet-stained fingers sits in the dispensary at night practising a signature on the backs of old labels. She thinks it a love-letter. I wonder who is being courted.

speaker: Narrator
text: Hennessey signs with a mark, being no scholar. It had not occurred to me in three years. A man who cannot write cannot forge, so I may strike one name from any list. I feel foolish for having needed to ask.

speaker: Narrator
text: Renfield's room, as I always find it: the cot made tight, the sugar in lines on the saucer, the jar of flies on the sill. I have read his ledger a dozen times, but I have never read it as a series, and Van Helsing would say that is the whole of the art.

speaker: Narrator
text: Flies caught on sugar, kept in a jar 'to hold the lives'. For a fortnight he eats none. In the third week he begins, and calls them quite delicious, and 'so full of life'.

speaker: Narrator
text: He feeds the flies to spiders, and then eats the spiders. 'One spider is worth a hundred flies, for the life in it.' The system has a ladder in it; I should have seen that sooner.

speaker: Narrator
text: He tamed a sparrow, wanted a cat to eat the sparrows, and kept a heap of feathers for his pains. 'The spider's life is little, and the sparrow's is more.' The ladder climbs, as I thought.

speaker: Narrator
text: The housemaid's kitten went into Room 12 on Tuesday and came out on Wednesday as a smear of fur. He was ill afterwards, as if from grief. I have written nothing under it. I did not need to.

speaker: Narrator
text: Zoophagous mania, systematised: the patient believes life may be gathered by eating living things, in ascending order. 'The blood is the life.' He says he is not mad, merely early. I wonder what he is early for.

speaker: Narrator
text: Twenty grains of chloral for a strong man, weighed twice and witnessed by the register. A bottle I hope never to use. The house may break, but it will be broken by the book.

speaker: Narrator
text: Smoke under the dispensary door, Room 12 standing open, and a lad crying in the ward. Three things at once, and a doctor who has not slept in three days. Good. A man with nothing to lose makes a cool physician.

speaker: Narrator
text: Old Greer told me, with the memory of forty years, never to put water on a spirit fire. I smothered it with a soaked blanket, and the chloral was saved. I must remember to thank a mad sailor in the morning.

speaker: Narrator
text: Sixty grains of morphia, in my name, in my hand, forged beautifully, in violet copying ink. Hennessey cannot write. Miss Vane saw a lad with violet fingers practise my S. I think I know the signatory, and it breaks my heart.

speaker: Narrator
text: He did it for his mother, in Barking, in pain. I could report him, and the law would be on my side. I could help him, and the law would not. I choose, and write the choice in the book, so that I cannot pretend I did not.

speaker: Narrator
text: I found him in the garden under the Carfax wall, staring at the moon. I did not need force. Judgment, a measure of medicine and a steady voice did it. He said something is coming, and he would like to be tidy. I wrote it down.

speaker: Narrator
text: A night in which three things went wrong and none was the worst. I used judgment where I might have used force, medicine where I might have used a stick, and nerve where I might have run. I shall write to Van Helsing. I think I may sleep.

speaker: Narrator
text: My study, with the lamp lit before dark. Arminius's last parcel lies half-opened: a Latin note, a locked cabinet, and a letter I have not dared to read twice. I must see to my wife, my lecture, my friend, and at last that terrible village in Styria.

speaker: Narrator
text: 'Wood not iron; day not night; garlic not earth.' Arminius has the exactness of a man who has had it wrong once and paid. I wrote it out three times, since a physician who mistranslates a prescription kills a man.

speaker: Narrator
text: She lay turned to the window, with the little grey coat in her lap. Mevrouw Bakker says the broth is a triumph. I stood in the doorway and could not enter for a full minute. We have lost one child. I do not intend to lose the rest of the world.

speaker: Narrator
text: She gave me the christening cross from the cradle. 'Take it for the next one', she said. I am a Doctor of Medicine and Law, but I could find no word, and so I held her hand. Some wounds are not the business of surgery.

speaker: Narrator
text: Skaters, a barrel-organ, the bells of the Oude Kerk. The Dean of the Faculty means to humiliate me on Friday. My students are afraid for me. They are fond of me, which is more than I deserve and a great deal more than I can bear in the open street.

speaker: Narrator
text: Verhoeven stood where I stand, with his gloves in one hand and my own board behind him. He has the key to the rare books, and a rule: no man gets it who cannot defend his methods. Young Seward, with that scar on his hand, whispered that I should read what I wrote.

speaker: Narrator
text: Three questions, three answers from my own blackboard. Verhoeven gave me the key and a word I shall not forget: his grandmother hung garlic at her door. Everyone has one such grandmother. The trick is to listen to her before the Faculty tells you not to.

speaker: Narrator
text: Calf, vellum and a smell of mice. Mijnheer de Vries whispers, and the Dean's press is oak and brass. Inside it is the only book I wanted: a rituale of the old rite, and the order of the blessing of bread, in a Latin that has lasted since the Reformation.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Voivode, the Scholomance, the Devil's tenth scholar. Arminius does not believe a word, but he copies every one. And at the end a request: a churchyard in Styria, a priest afraid of his own graves. I shall go, but not to disprove. To find out.

speaker: Narrator
text: Father Pieter at his altar, Gerrit counting the candle-ends. The sacrament is not a charm but a rite, and a rite has its order. That is the one thing a physician and a priest can agree on: if you do it out of sequence, you have done something else.

speaker: Narrator
text: Confession, ablution, the Collect, the seal. I read the order and Father Pieter followed it, and when the little silver box closed, something in the room changed that I have no instrument to measure. I did not pretend that I understood it. I merely wrote it down.

speaker: Narrator
text: Snow, an onion-spire, doors shut at four. A priest with a month of sleeplessness in his face. The village is afraid of its own churchyard. I have not yet asked what it is afraid of. I have only looked at the garlic on the windows, and counted.

speaker: Narrator
text: Four children weak, one buried, and a grave that melts the snow. He asked me to say a Pater at whichever one it is. I said I would. I did not say that I had never until that night said a Pater with a stake in my other hand.

speaker: Narrator
text: A bride of nineteen, dead by Easter in the year of the great snow, nailed in by an old priest and an older sexton. Three nails on the stone, and the earth about it not frozen. It is not a theory any longer. It is a name.

speaker: Narrator
text: She came at midnight, hair pale in the moon, as lovely as the legend said. The circle held. She did not. When she lay helpless in the snow, I did what must be done, and I said the Pater, and I wept afterward, as a physician does when a patient is lost. She was somebody's niece.

speaker: Narrator
text: Verhoeven was right to demand evidence, and the peasants were right to be afraid, and the truth was in neither camp but between them. Arminius has sent a name: Dracula. I do not know what lies behind it. I have a casebook, a ward, and a certain faith that works when the evidence runs out.
